div.head: WILL THE PUBLIC GET IT?
div.p: WILL THE PUBLIC GET IT?

There has recently been some talk of preserving to the nation the house at Whitby, where Captain Cook, the great explorer, lived. In -some of his writings Captain Co-ok commented on the wonderful health of the Australian natives, due to their use of herbs and vegetable essences. It is a fact, of which some people are still unaware, that the best of Australian herbal essences are yet ob- tainable (in purified medicinal form) in the well known household remedy, alas. Forde's bile beans. Chas. Forde, irepressed with the superiority of vegetable medicines ever those containing harmful mineral substances, such as iron, bismuth, ect., thoroughly investigated the rich profusion of Australian herbs. After long research he found himself the dis- coverer of a vegetable substance which acted on the liver and digestive organs differently and better than any medicine known. The best 'laboratories, the most modern plant, and all that science dictated as being best for the purpose was requisitioned in the compounding of this substance into convenient !form. The result of it all war the production of a medicine in the form of small beans, which, being unequillled in their operation upon the liver and its secretion of liile,were called" bile beans." Being the products of modern scientific research bile beans are thoroughly up-to-date. They do not merely purge, give temporary relief only, arid leave the patient weakened; like the eut-of-date, so-called remedies of forty or fifty years ago, which contain probably aloes, mercury, and other harmful drugs. Without causing the slightest discomfort, bile beans prompt the diver and digestive organs to act in Nature's normal way, leaving those organs strengthened and stimulated to continue the Performance of their duties without farther assistance. They thus cure indigestion, headaclie. xliniia.femdle ailments, biliousness, constipa- tion, piles, kc., and tone up the whnle•system. Obtain- able from medicine vendors the world over.

At Runcorn on Thursday the body of Chttrles Haley, a sailor, of the sschooner Esmeralda, was taken from Runcorn Docks. Deceased who is a native a Hull, has been missing since Saturday, April 16th.

RESIGNATION OF SUPERINTENDENT KEIGIILEI7,WIDNES. Widnes is about to lose one of its prominent figures in the person of Superintendent Keighley, who is,abortly to resign after forty years' service in the Lantashire county constabulary. his career has been •tery interest- ing and full of adventure. His early days were went a; Presto and ha intends to take up his abode at ftibchesteramongst what few relatives remain.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY EXPLOSION AT RUNCORN.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY EXPLOSION AT RUNCORN.

On Monday evening an extraordinary explosion occurred at the residence f Mr. A. Rigby, Greenway_ road, Runcorn. The house was being decorated, and a. Painter named Cousins was in the act of burning the paint off the drawing-room door, when the benzine lamp he was using exploded with a loud report. The force of the explosion was such that the bay window was dislodged, and the ceiling of the room badly split across. The glass from the window was blown into the middle of the road, and several children narrowly escaped beirv,l struck by it. Luckily the plinter sus- tained no other injury than burns on his hands.
RUNCORN URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday morn- ing, under the presidency of Mr. S. Taylor. The medical officer reported that during April there were 20 deaths and 41 births, as compared with 20 deaths arid 52 birth in April last you. The Health Committee recommended that the plans of the proposed addition to the ward at the infectious diseases hospital. the erection of a new pavilion, the extension of the administrative block, and the erectionsof outbuildings, at an estimated cost of £4,003 be approved. Mr. Dean, chairman of the committee, explained that these exten- -sions had been forced upon them by the County Council who would, however, make a contribution to the cost Whencompleted the hospital would be one of the most up-to-date in the county. The plans were approved. It was reported that the profit on the market for the past year was £39 13s. 9d. Mr. James Pritchard, J.P., was re-appointed a member of the Upper Mersey Navigation Commission.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
THEFT OF , A CHICKEN AT GOLBOM:E.

At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednes- day, Michael Hanley, School-street, Golborne, was charged with stealing a chicken of the value of 4s. 6d., the property of Emma Dearden, from the hen cote at the rear of the "Cross Keys "Inn, Bridge-street, Golborne.—Prosecutrix stated that on the 2nd inst., she heard a noise in the hen cote, and on going into the yard saw the prisoner in the cote with the chicken in his possession. He ran away but Anthony Yates gave chase and caught him.—A fine of 10s. was imposed.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Women Visitors at the Houses of Parliament- —The fine river terrace of the Houses of Parliament promises to be as popular as ever for fashionable afternoon gatherings this season. The inconveniences of the Ladies' Gallery in the House of Commons find no counterpart in the arrangement made for their welcome on the Terrace, and the gathering there on the fine warm days usually includes many of the best dressed women in London. History is a little erratic as regards the admittance of women to the House of Commons, but it is said that their limited privileges are the result of their own misbehaviour. In 1778 they were on &Tel terms, as visitors, with men, 'but the galleries having been ordered to be cleared, they refused to leave. This story is on all fours with that of the Peeresses, who being shot oat of the House of Lords, made such a knooking and noise that proceedings could not go on. Then keeping quiet for half an hour, the doors were opened, it being thought they had gone, when in they rushed and took possession of their places. It was not however until 1831 that wonen regained admittance to the House of Commons, and in 1835 a motion was carried, though never given effect, to throw open a por- tion of the Strangers' Gallery to them. The great O'Connell supported it, because, he said, in the Irish Parliament, the presence of women had tended to pre- vent members from coming there drunk. Nellie Farren, and the first of the Gilbert Sullivan Pieces.—The death of Miss Nellie Farren reminds us that but for her there Might never have been the wonder- ful series of Gilbert Sullivan productions, which have proved the delight of the whole world. It was some- time after Miss Farren began her remarkable career at the Gaity Theatre in London, that Mr. John Hollings- head was badly in want of something specially suitable for that brilliant little comedienne, and it was at his suggestion that Messrs. Gilbert and Sullivan first worked together, and produced " Thespis or the Gods grown old." That was the commencement of the famous collaboration,and,as neither Nellie Farren,ner Mr. John L. Toole had any musical talent, Sullivan rcenfessed it rather difficult to" compose vocal music for people who had no voices." It was her personality, and not her singing, or her beauty, that made Nellie Farren such a great favourite with the theatre going pahlic. For twelve years before her death the other day, she had been more or less of an invalid, but from the time when she first went to the Gaiety Theatre in 18G8, to 1892 when she retired into private life, Miss Farren was cer- tainly the most worshipped Member of her profession. From Actress to Couatess.—The late Miss Nellie Farren came from an old family of play-actors, butthey bore no relation to the actress, Miss Eliza Farren, who became the Countess of Derby in 1797. She was an Irish girl, the daughter of Mr. 'George Farren, a doctor living in Cork, who, however, took to the life of a strolling player, when she was but a child, and finally attained fame on the stage in London. The, daughter also took to the stage, for which she thus obtained early trainincabut in 1797 she married Lord Derby and lived till 1829. The present Earl of Wilton is one of her grandsons. Passing the doctor at Civil Service Examinations.— Among the keenest of disappointments must be that experienced by the young girl, who, having spent per- haps two or three years in working up the subjects for a Civil Service Examination, and having secured. it may be, a good place in the list of successful candidates, finds herself rejected by the doctor on the ground of some weakness of which she knew nothing. A case in point was furnished in some recent examinations con- ducted by the Post Office. One young woman passed an examination for the telephone service. Then she was sent by the doctor to have four teeth extracted at a London hospital. The teeth were only slightly at fault, and a dentist said it was quite unnecessary to have thorn out. They were nevertheless extracted, and the candidate was thee rejected on the ground that she was anwmic. Such treatment can only be described as cruel in the extreme, and it would surely be possible for Government Departments to make arrangements by which candidates could be medically examined beforehand.

Anwmia.--Many girls with a natural colour take that as a proof that they are not ana3mic, but unless the gums, and insides of the eyelids are a deep healthy colour, that on the cheeks is apt to he deceptive. People who suffer from bloodlessness, skin eruptions, and a bad complexion, usually go to the doctor, take a few bottles of tonic, and then go on as before, but these cases which are much more common amongst girls than is generally supposed, really require careful and patient treatment for months, and perhaps for years. The essential thing is to improve the condition of the blood, and for this the special food preparations are better than physic. Amongst the most reliable of these is Viral, which is prepared by a firm of great repute. and is especially desigr ed for enriching the blood. Similarly the iron in such vegetables as spinach and rhubarb is better than that taken out of a bottle, and great importance should be attached to the ordinary rules of health, such as outdoor exercise, proper ventilation, and the daily bath.

A Healthful Exercise.—A leading physician tells us that stair climbing is an excellent exercise fen-dyspeptic or consumptive people, and indeed a capital thing for health, when performed in the proper manner. This means that the feet should be placed squarely down on each step, heal and ell, that the chest should be well thrown back, and the ascent performed slowly and deliberately.

Dress at the Royal Academy.—lt would have been difficult to decide from the toilettes donned on the occasion of the private view at the Royal Academy, what kind of weather prevailed outside. Some women appeared warmly wrapped in firs, others had evidently come to the conclusion that spring had arrived, while others again seemed to be under the impression that summer was already with us. Doubtless the latter con- tingent had taken the precaution to don warm vests and underskirts, still the effect of an airy fairy toilette, on a treacherous April day is not altogether pleasing. The same extremes were noticeable as regards style. The much beflounced and trimmed early Victorian toilette was there, so also was the severely tailor-made costume, in which perhaps.the women of our country look their best. In the way of wraps, little that is new was to be seen. The always becoming, round feather boa, was again inTevidence,also the flat pelerine feather cape,with lon ends, but the wrap most in favour was the little earry Victorian cape, in black taffeta 'silk, the ends be- ing gathered, and finished with frayed-out ruches of the same fabric. Black headgear, with the exception of the ever popular picture hat was little seen, and taken alto- gether this full dress rehearsal of the new fashions for the season was a very brilliant and instructive one. Dainty Accessories.—The attention given to cravats, neck bands, ties, and wrist frills, is considerable just now, and one marvels how one could ever have done without these attractive and becoming little accessories. Yet the fact remains that only a season or so back we were content without anything of this description at all. Nothing at the moment is too elaborate in the way of fine embroidery for ties, stocks, jabots. and cravats whether carried out in lawn and cambric, or in soft silk,

and the most fascinating ruffles for the wrist, both for dressy and morning wear are to be found in all the best shops. The former are in net, tulle, lace, and chiffon, the latter in fine lawn, accordion pleated. The quaint lace tuckers run through with narrow black velvet ribbon, which are finishing all the newest evening bodices, are also to be found ready to tack in. Dress Fabrics.—Shot materials ave having a great vogue, and when these are not possible, shot effects are sought after. For instance, voile made up over silk of another colour, affords a charming shot effect. Pale grey voile, over deep yellow silk is esquisite, so also is forget-me-not blue voile over pale grey silk. An attempt has been made to give us shot voiles, but it has not so far proved.st. success. MADGE.

div.head: Examiner Saturday, May 7 1904.
div.p: The Examiner Saturday, May 7 1904.
FASHIONS OF TO-DAy.

There are no remarkable revolutions in the style of our clothes this season, and fashions have not varied much from those of twelve months ago. The new skirts are still gauged or pleated round the waist and fall unlined in soft graceful folds over an under- skirt of silk or some other material which is more durable, but in all other respects closely resemble silk. The line of the shoulder and upper arm, both in indoor blouses and out- door coats, and pelerines, is plainly defined in the fashion of the early Victorian era, while the fulness of the sleeve starts just above the elbow, where it is released from gaugings, pleats or strappings and goes on increasing till it forms a full pouch below the wrist, where it is caught into a tight band or cuff. Sometimes this cuff is made very deep and extends halfway up the arm towards the
UG
ELorsz

elbow as many people find the superabundant folds of silk or muslin at the wrist in the way, especially at meals, where they seem posses- sed with the knack of dipping into one's cup or dragging over their plate, and therefore by substituting a deep cuff the fulness is kept further up the arm and out oi the way. Blouses are, if possible, more fashionable than ever, and prettier than we have ever known them_

My first sketch depicts a charming blouse of white washing silk simply and plainly made with the full bodice part springing from a deep shaped yoke which extends well down over the shoulder and is made of the silk covered with lace motifs of graduated serges, the wrist bands being to match while the throat is finished by a, folded silk band. It is a very pretty design and could be expressed in lawn or cambric or some cheap washing material suited for morning wear. It is necessary, of course, to possess a•good natural line of shoul- ders before attempting to wear a long- shouldered yoke such as this, and anyone who is very narrow or has very sloping shoulders should preferably adopt the Sleeve which springs from the 'top of the 'arm, as in the majority oflast season's models. There never was a time when one could put short lengths of thin 'washing materials•to as good a use as

div.head: L ACS-DR APED HAT.
div.p: A L ACS-DR APED HAT.

now, for really short lengths which -would otherwise be useless and can, therefore, be picked up for a few pence can always be eked out by the aid of face yokes or embroi- dered muslin. Half yards of piece lace left over from former dresses can be used up in this manner, while another method is to alternate strips of ribbon and lace insertion herring- boned together to form the ,yOke, etc. Lace is much us,l both as a.dress or blouse trimming and also in millinery. Indeed, a drapery of lace often forms the sole trimming of some of the large picture hats of fancy straw such as is given in my second sketch. It is arranged of soft folds round the ,brim which droop over the face in front and form a cur- tain at the back. Indeed, almost no hat seems complete at present without a veil of some sort whether it is the -variety which is worn loosely over the face and is generally of fine Chantilly lace covered with tiny rings and handsomely borderedwith a floral pattern, or else the veil is so arranged as-to permanent- ly float down the back, and -in this case it is generally as long as the wearer's purse will permit her to secure, for these veils are apt to be costly. Some fortunate individuals pos- sessed of heirlooms in the form of lace veils which have been preserved tintact in spite cif

numerous temptations to cut them up for one purpose or another are using these, and, of course, nothing really looks so well as a good lace veil skilfully draped. The mushroom hat is again making a bid for popularity, and I fancy we shall see a good deal of it this sum- mer although it is not, generally speaking, a very becoming kind of hat. There are also some very pretty basket straws which are most attractive and in natural wood tints of brown and green are loosely plaited into various shapes. The dainty cape, or pelerine, depicted in my last sketch forms a very useful addition to one's dress for out of doors, especially for those people who live in town and object to appearing on the streets without some sort of covering to the blouse and find a jacket rather warm in the hot summer days. The shoulder ruffle and the deep ostrich feathers and marabout stoles or shawls, look certainly very nice but somehow do not give the idea of a finished toilette when worn with a blouse, while a little wrap like this looks very dressy, and is cut on the latest lines. It is often made of the same material as the skirt, and many people are contemplating something .of this kind to take the place of the bolero coat, of which they have wearied. The formation of a cape of this style is not a difficult task nor at 11 beyond the capabilities of a home worker. COQUETTE.

The oft discussed subject of the widening of War- rington Bridge again occupied the attention of the Town Council on Tuesday evening. The General Purposes Committee had had under consideration the Borough Surveyor's report on Mr. J. J. Webster's scheme for widening the bridge by means of canti- levers and had resolved "that the following resolution of the Bridge Sub-committee be approved: That the General Purposes Committee he recommended to pro- ceed with the widening of Warrington Bridge by means of cantilevers in accordance with the scheme prepared by Mr. J. J. Webster" ; also "that a specifica- tion be prepared and tenders for the widening of the bridge as proposed be advertised for." In his report the Borough Surveyor stated that at the present time the total width of the carriageway between kerbs is 20 feet and from the side of, the tramlines to the kerbs averages four feet. The width of the foot- ways on each side are four feet. It is proposed to widen the carriageway to 301 t. Gin, between kerbs and 81t. 9in. from the side of the tram lines to the kerbs on each side. The width of each footway will be 10ft. ' The MAYOR moved the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor Tinsion seconded. - Councillor JAMES EVANS moved as an amendment, ' that the minutes of the committee be confirmed with the exception of .the one relating to the widening of the bridge. He said he felt, and had done so all along, that the time had not yet come for the widening of the bridge. It was astonishing to hear some men crying out about keeping down the rates. The way to keep down the rates was to give over spending; if they did ---- not, the rates would continue to grow... He ,maintained His Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, K.C., made some that the bridge was serving its trurpose better today strong comments during the hearing of a case at the than it was before the tramways were put across it. Warrington County Court on Thursday. John Tonkin - The question of the widening of the bridge might rest sonlof 194, Liverpool-road, puddle-,sued Messrs. Monks, for another year if not fora longer period. SEQUEL TO A COMPENSATION CLAIM.
Magistrates and the "Long Pull."

At the Warrington Transfer Sessi-ons, on Monday, the Chairman of the Licensing Bench (Mr. F. Mks) said he wished to make a remark with reference to the practice of the "long pull." The magistrates, some two or three years ago, decided that it should be abandoned as far as possihle, and there was a promise given that it should be abandoned, but he had it on the very best authority that it still continued, and that in many respects it was as bad as ever. He wished to publicly request the Licensed Victuallers' Associa- tion, as far as they could, to put a stop to the practice, and he hoped Mr. Browne would be able to .make some representation on the matter,and have something to communicate about it at the next opportunity of renewing licences—Mr.Browne said he would be only tco pleased to do so, but he understood that so far as the members of the Licensed Victuallers' Association were rconcerned the practice had been stopped. All the licencees in the town were not members of the association, but those who were had, he felt sure carried out the wishes of the magistrates.—Mr. Monks : I called attention to it as I had it on the most reliable information that in many districts the practice was as bad as ever.

It is expected that the china, plate, and snuff-boxes which belonged to the late Duke of Cambridge will be sold about the third week in June. There is some beautiful gold plate, which was bequeathed by the Duchess of Gloucester, but which the Duke seldom used, and which, indeed, has not been seen for a great many years.

div.head: WARRINGTON BRIDGE.
div.p: WARRINGTON BRIDGE.
CANTILEVER SCHEME AGAIN APPROVED BY THE COUNCIL.
Long Discussion.
An Unnbstantiateci Charge.
STRONG REMARKS BY THE JUDGE.
Alderman SUTTON: What about the loss on the in- terest for_the_cantilevers ?
Councillor A. PiracocK: I have allowed for all that in my calculation.

_ Councillor TINNION thought the Council had finished with the question of whether they were going to widen the bridge by means of cantilevers or erect a new bridge. It was remarkable that every time they had reached that stage someone had raised the question as to whether it would be desirable to go any further and pointed out the advantages of building a new bridge. He was not going to impute motives to anyone, but it was remarkable that that should happen. There was a resolution on the Council's books that the bridge be widened by cantilevers, and it had never been rescinded. The present resolution simply authorised the obtaining of a specification and tenders. If when those were forthcoming it was thought that a very large expenditure would be involved, it would be time to raise objections. The widening by cantilevers would cost about £4,000 and the improvement would serve for fifteen or twenty years. What would it cost to build a suitable bridge to replace the present handsome structure? Several members had run up the cost of widening to a much higher figure than £4,000. Therefore it would be just as reasonable for him to say that a new bridge would involve an outlay of £40,000 or £50,000. Alderman SUTTON: Why do you keep repeatinc, such nonsensical things? Nobody ever mentioned £50,000. It is simply your own imagination. Councillor TINNION objected to the interruption. The 41AvoR thought the Council should have some regard to discipline and allow speakers to proceed with- out interruptions. Councillor TINNION said Alderman Sutton had no need to be so testy about the matter. "You might be gouty or something of that sort" he added amid some laughter. Continuing, he asked the Council whether they were going to be content with the present bridge, which everybody admitted was a nuisance, for ten or fifteen years ? It was dangerous to pedestrians and vehicular traffic—in fact the only time that he felt safe in crossing it was when he was in a tramcar. The figures given by Councillor Peacock were perfectly accurate. They would be saving money by adopting the cantilever scheme, instead of spending a much larger stun on a new bridge and having to pro- vide a sinking fund and pay interest. If he had his wish he would provide a one-span bridge which would improve the waterway and the road, but they could not afford to do that. By the cantilever scheme they would be improving the road and they hoped they would not be damaging the water way. In ten or fifteen years they would probably be able to erect a new bridge. The present scheme was a reasonable one, and would, he be- lieved, repay the ratepayers for the expenditure. Councillor BURTON said it seemed very strange to him that a man who could steer a boat through the 29ft. lock at Walton could not steer it through a 401 t. span at Warrington Bridge. Alderman SUTTON: Did you ever steer one? Councillor BURTON: This Council takes some steer- ing. (plughter.)._

, The MAYOR : Quite right. Councillor BURTON pointed out that the bridge was 10 inches higher above the surface of the water than the Arpley railway bridge. He did not think anything would be gained by raising Warrington Bridge. He could not understand why a certain number of aldermen and councillors should from time to time throw cold water on that scheme, especially as it had been passed in the Council Chamber time after time. (Hear, hear.) Councillor JAMES EVANS : We want to save the ratepayers' money. (Hear, hear, and " 'No no.") Councillor BURTON said that if the question of widen- ing the bridge was deferred for twelve months simply to MIT money he would say Amen ! but he saw some- thing behind all this. If the matter was left over, instead of spending .£3,100 they would probably spend £30,000 or £40,000 and, therefore,he should go in for the widening of the bridge at once. He was not an engineer, but he had never seen a bridge so engineered as this had been. (Laughter.) They had far too many engineers about it. (Laughter). He advised the Coun- cil if they were true friends of the ratepayers, to pass the cantilever scheme.

The DEPUTY MAYOR said he had listened to all the speeches that had been delivered that evening about the bridge. A great deal had been said about the top of the bridge, but little about what happened below it. It was said that the water wag deeper, but the flood ran twice as strong as it used to do and when there was a, flood it was impossible to steer under the bridge with- out going backwards and tying up their ropes at the far side. They got the archway full of steam and they could nut steer the boat. If they widened the bridge on both sides the steam would be worse than ever and down they would go to the bottom. They had beard a great deal that evening about the fear of men being , killed on the top of the bridge, but suppose men got I drowned beneath, who would be to blame when it came to an inquiry, and there would have to be one if they ' passed the resolution that night? He could say that their firm would oppose the scheme tooth and nail. The MAYOR said the question resolved itself into this,that the footpath was too narrow and that the only way to widen it was to take down the walls or put up cantilevers. The road was certainly too narrow for ordinary pedestrian traffic, considering that tram cars went over it so frequently. The traffic was regulated by a policeman at each end of the bridge, and it was owing to that fact that there had not been accidents. How did the bridge affect the general public ? In the first place as it at present stood it cost them nothing. They could go on year after year doing nothing to it, but if they widened the bridge by means of cantilevers it would cost them £3,100. The sinking fund and interest for the time over which the loan would be extended would cost about £270 per year. A new bridge would cost £20,000 and that would mean £l2OO a year. They had also to consider the cost of pulling down the old bridge, altering the approaches, and other details which might possibly raise the expenditure to t 30,000. If the cantilevers were too wide and interfered with naviga- tion they might be altered. Anything was better than the present state of the footpaths. The question was whether to go on with the estimates or to defer the scheme for ten et. a dozen years. The widening by cantilevers would probably be sufficient to serve the present generation, and the next generation might have more money to spend on the bridge. Alderman Surros : Do you attach any importance to the navigation of the river.? The MAYOR : The navigation as a rule looks after itself—(hear, hear)—and as far as the cantilevers are concerned if they are too wide and interfere with the navigation of the river they would be shortened so that they would Not interfere.

Voting then took place as follows :-- For the amendment: Aldermen Ffl irclou eh, Bennett, and Sutton ; Councillors Willcnson, James Evans, John Evans, Barton, Hulse and Maginn-9. Against: The Mayor, Alderman Smethurst and Pier- point, Councillors Davies, Brough, Tinnion, Thornton, Roberts, Burton, Ashcroft, Wilson, P. Peacock, A. Peacock, Petnberton, Stott, Lord, Ellison and Rogers- -18.
The amendment was therefore lost, and the minutes were confirmed.
Warrington Polyglot Society.

The Society had a most successful outing at Halton on Saturday last, this being the first excursion of the season. The cyclists,under the leadership of Mr. May, seated the battlements of the precipitous east side, in the hope of surprising those who had come by train. The surprise was complete, the enemy being found fortifying their courage with potations from sundry stone bottles containing a light coloured fluid. Friend and The, however, were s-,on engaged in the ancient frame of bowls and other diversions, untft the 'shades of night (or Widnes smoke) warned them that it was time to leave. Warrington was reached abdut nine o'clock, the trip having been all that could be desired.

LOUIS EXHIBITION: te The largest international exhibition ever beell is now open, although it will at least „a• month from all accounts before it is ;,..-nuY completed, and at present many features --`e in a very unfinished state. America alwaYs does things upon a Brobdigna.gian but the St. Louis Exhibition—or World's Fair, as it is popularly called—in !heir vernacular. "licks creation." In magni- plde of area alone it not only eclipses all 118 predecessors, but is practically as large as -rariS, Buffalo, and Chicago rolled into one, '4 all it covers 1,240 acres, or close on two 'aquare miles, and it is reckoned that 410,000,000 has been expended upon it. here are some fifteen departments, consist- ing of '44 groups, which are themselves s'ubdivided into 807 classes, .and there are endless buildings devoted to every country nd every branch of art, agriculture, engineer • ;Ig, science, and every subject under the )1,.,11- Fifty foreign nations, including Great ,s "thin, are exhibiting, and forty American taes have buildings of their own. The 111.1a,,1n building of all is the great Festival and facing it is the Grand Basin, the St enormous expanse of artificial water ver consgucted, and hard by are three wonderful cascades over which nearly too,ooo !all°ns of water fall each minute. There is "sn intramural railway with numerous stations Zili_si:ch conveys passengers all over the Ex-- on, to save time and make it possible ocl things properly. Then there is the .Ic. the haunt 61 the pleasure-seeker, 'onstructed at the cost of a million and a 'quart -er, and there the visitor can travel from -;°sc,ow to Port Arthur and follow the Whole,l course of the war in the Far East, i-Crting Lake Baikal and stopping at Seoul. ,zn the Pike there are also " sky-scrapers " in arnes, battles between Britons and Boers, ;lava battles in miniature, an Eiffel Tower :rtY feet high with a Paris in parvo be- 'ifath, constructed out of cardboard to give he effect of the real city fifty times as far „away, and other wonders too numerous to Zention. There is a fleet of gondolas, won- .erful illuminations, a stupendous menagerie, ,ups, submarine dinners, wireless tele- tuaPhic stations, the most wonderful electric Zght installation ever seen, and everything itP°ll a similar scale. The English Pavilion, 4-, may be mentioned, is a copy of Wren's Uee Anne Orangery at Kensington Palace k'''lth an Adams ceiling, and several historical erican buildings, such as Constitution ,u,se, Windsor, Vermont, General Grant's 'euin, and Daniel Webster's New Hampshire home have been moved holus-bolus into the V'3uads.

MISS NELLIE FARREN. The death of Miss Nellie Farren, who wan Th'ur Nellie" to her countless admirers for -a—anY years, came after a long time of illness si suffering, and it is now twelve years she appeared upon the stage, except .413°11 two memorable occasions. These were bPorl the occasion of her great and historic venefit at Drury Lane on St. Patrick's Day, 98, when 7,000 was taken, and just over Year ago on the last night of the old .oaletY, from which her name was inseparable. EL neither occasion was she fit to take any Pail in the programme, but words fail to (lescribe her receptions. Both were a touch- ing t • ribute to a never-to-be-forgotten favour- ile and a proof of the loyalty of the tneatrical public. After playing various ~_Parts, Miss Nellie Farren joined the Olympia ‘,-"nipany in 1864 and stayed there until she ,went on to the Gaiety in 1870 under Mr. John Hollingshead's management, and from That time onwards she was "Our Nellie" to London and drew the whole town. Never

THE LATE MISS NELLIE FARREN. 111-s there been such a burlesque actress or Zrl a "principal boy," and so many were 1.„,e. Parts she played under Mr. Hollingshead's -Pine that once when she tried in later ,30.,''ars to draw out a complete list of them, it lbais, found that sh had forgotten nearly Jack Sheppard, Aladdin, Monte Cristo, Ruy Bias, and many others come ck to recollection at once, and in all her ter successes she played with the equally li)l°Pular Fred Leslie. Then in 1892, during ttie_, run of "Cinder-Ellen Up -to - date," he e't and she broke down, ending what was rer',3bablv. the most popular and successful tl3llllaboration ever seen on the stage. From .e,at time Miss Farren has never been well tulugh to play again, but she has once or e,e essayed management. The funeral Place on Monday at Brompton Cemetery Was followed by a great procession of vi.,`" friends and admirers, hnd the wreaths z,:re innumerable. It was not only Nellie tli'rren's playing, but her personality which e public loved, and last Monday bore testiraol v to the fact.

THE KING'S IRISH VIT.:- visit of the King and Queen to Ire- has been one great and glorious success, Iv- enthusiastic triumphal procession. It t„;ltild appear that, wherever their Majesties a'ff-, 'whatever the previous rumours of dis- anAection, they command loyalty and affection I,:a;t carry peace and good will with them. week was mainly spent in Dublin, and attir afternoons were devoted to racing—two 11, ,Punchestoi,vn and one each at Phcenix and Leopardstown. Last Saturday the the and Queen went to Kilkenny to spend week-end with the Marquis and March- turir ess of Ormonde, visiting the local agricul- fo,i show. On Monday they left for Water- w. where again the local agricultural show :so visited, arriving in the evening at Lis- rice Castle for a two days' visit to the retl„,e and Duchess of Devonshire, prior to Alr—Vjig home. • Durina the visit to Dublin a „ eerbohm Tree, on Thursday night- gave /zo„ T3nlinand " performance at the Theatre dee, for which the house was magnificently znororated. Leaving town on Wednesday bersnj at a.m. with the leading mem- his company, Mr. Tree arrived in
THE EXHIBITION.

Dublin in the evening, and after dinner at the close of the evening performance at the Theatre Royal he held a rehearsal which lasted all night. After two or three hours' sleep another rehearsal was held which con- tinued until four in .the afternoon, and at 8.30 the curtain went up. The programme consisted of two scenes from " Richard II." and the first acts of "The Last of the Dandies" and "Trilby." Mr. Tree, of

. BEERI3OHM TREE. course, played Count D'Orsay and Svengali, showing his great versatility, and an ex- tremely interesting feature of the performance was the appearance of his daughter, Miss Viola Tree, as Trilby. In the small hours of ad ay morning, after a most brilliant and Arcessful trip. ,the company returned to London in time for Friday night's perform- ance at His Majesty's. It was an excep- tionally busy week for Mr. Tree, as on Monday he opened his new "Academy of Dramatic Art," which promises to prove a great success.

div.head: DEATH OF DVORAK.
div.p: DEATH OF DVORAK.

The music world is the poorer to-day by the death of the well-known composer, Antonin Dvorak, which occurred on Saturday last at Prague, as the result of ,an attack of apoplexy; The deceased composer was in his 62nd year, having been born at Muhlhau- sen, in Bo- hemia, and was
the son of a butcher. It
was intended that he should follow the same
calling, but the passion for
music was in-
nate, and re-
markable ability displayed as a
chorister
violinist
caused an alter-
ation of plans. He was sent to
Prague to study music_ and sup-.
ported himself
there by play-
ing the v'iolin in
the theatre. He became an or-

ganist in 1873, 'and shortly afterwards wrote an opera ior which he r3ceived a pension of Lso a year from Vienna. Brains became greatly interested in the rising composer, who in 1878 wrote the " Slavische Tanze " for pianoforte cluet, wh:ch was taken up every- where, and as arranged for orchestra was played at the Crystal Palace in 1880. His later works are well known to English music lovers. His " Stabat Matcr " was given in London in 1883 and at the Worcester Festi- val in the following year. In 1885 "The was produced at the Birm- ingham Spectre's eßsrtiidvea l" and conducted by the com- poser as was the oratoria, "St. Ludwela," at the Leeds Festival in 1886. His impressive " Requiem " and his chamber music, with his vivid contrasts, are generally admired and will always be remembered.

div.head: OPENING OF THE CRICKET SEASON.
div.p: OPENING OF THE CRICKET SEASON.

The cricket season for 1904 has indeed started well, favoured as it was by com- paratively dry weather and good wickets. The dreary ,wet summer of last year will long remain memorable to the club cricketer as the most disastrous in cricket history, and with many organisations things almost reached a crisis. Consequently the early start in April has been thoroughly appre- ciated and already two or three achievements of more than ordinary Merit are to be noted. The chief of them all is that of the G.O.M. of cricket—W.. G. Grace--who, defying the burden of years, gave proof on Thursday afternoon last that he was Still to be reckoned a power in first-class cricket. Since the inauguration of the London County C.C. Dr. W. G. Grace has rendered 'invaluable aid to the metropolitan cricket, and besides his
W. G. GRACE.

first-class programme. an extensive list oi club games are annually arranged with the chief teams.. Thus, since this sterling cricketer came to town to take up his per- manent residence at the Crystal Palace, he has been instrumental in unearthing many a clever young exponent of our national game. The Essex professional, Sewell, has also sur- passed all his previous efforts in this count') by scoring the magnificent total of 181: which was obtained in less than three hours. and his innings is described as sound as ii was brilliant. Apropos of the match betweer the M.C.C.'s Australian team and the Rest 0: England, it is now practically settled that jl will be played at Lords on May 9th, loth, and nth, the original date—June i6th— being found an inconvenient one, as so mans itunty teams have fixtures.

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
The County Council and Road Improvements.

A meeting of this Council was held at • Bewsey Chambers on Wednesday afternoon, Mr. T. Halton pre- siding. There were also present : —Dr. Murray. Messrs. Brooks, Houghton, Mather, with Dr. Sephton (medical officer of health), Messrs. J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), F. Kerfoot (inspector of nuisances), B. S. Newcombe (surveyor), and H. H. Burnage (assistant surveyor.)
THE PROPOSED CONTRTBUTION TO 3'IRE IRRIGADE EXPENSES.

A letter was receivedit:Ol-ii; Clerk of the Burton- wood Parish Council stating: "The question of provid- ing fire extinguishing appliances will be discussed at our next meeting, and I understand the Warrington Rural District Council contributes annually to the Warrington Corporation for the use of their fire engine."

The CLERK said he had replied stating that that was not so. He had simply written inquiring the scale upon which the Corporation proposed to fix a portion of their maintenance charge upon that Council. The Cor- poration's proposal must have become known to Messrs. Merryweather and Co. who wrote calling attention to the advantage of having appliances at hand as in that way fires could frequently be extinguished at the out- set with very little damage, whereas if a neighbouring brigade had to be summoned some time must elapse be- fore their arrival and the fire might get beyond control. The firm offered to supply any fire engine, hose or other apparatus it might be decided to procure. The CLERK said he had not yet received a reply to his letter to the Town Clerk.

Mr. MATHER asked if it would be possible, wherever water mains were laid, for that Council or the Parish Council to provide a hose pipe. It was pointed out that there was not sufficient water pressure In many districts to enable the appliances to be used.
The CHAIRMAN said he understood the Corporation contemplated making a kind of pond near the sanatorium at Sankey in order that water would be available in case of fire.
Mr. MATHER : That will be for trout, won't it ? (Laughter.) The Council decided that they could take no antion in the matter until the Town Clerk's reply was received.
A DEPUT AT ON.
The VICE-CHAIRMAN (Mr. Brooks) and the Clerk were appointed to represent the Council at the confer- ence of Rural District Councils to be held in London.
INCREASED COUNTY comicir, GRANTS.

A letter was received stating that the Main Roads and Buildings Committee of the Lancashire County Council had had under consideration the District Coun- cil's appeal against the offer made to them for the maintenance and improvement of main roads in their district. The committee had resolved that the sum of £BO per annum allowed to be charged against the oldin- ary maintenance account in respect of establishment charges be increased to £lOO and that the following amended offer be made to the Council :—For ordinary maintenance, £1,596.; for extra macadam (Winwick- road), £200; for reconstruction of Manchester-road, £200; for kerbing and channelling near Sankey schools, £7O • total £2,066. The SURVEYOR explained that as the result of his appeal, it was understood that the £2OO grant for extra macadam would be made a permanent annual payment to the district, thus praoticall v increasing the mainten- ance grant to £1,796. The £7O towards the expense of kerbings at Sankey was an extra special grant. The allowance towards salaries, &c., would be increased to £lOO per annum. Another permanent grant was £36 per annum for a new secondary road (Alder Root lane, Winwick). There was thus a permanent gain to the district of £256. Other additional grants towards secondary roads for this year were £5O each for improvements at Hood-lane and Cinnamon-lane. The County Council had also given a salary grant of £5O for the carrying out of the Halton's Bridge improvement.

div.head: HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.
div.p: HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.

FEARNHEAD SEWERAGE QUESTION. Dr. SEPHTON reported that during the fortnight end- ing that day there had been 5 births and 15 deaths. The death rate was 316 per 1000 against 306 the average for the past three months and 30.4 for the corresponding period last year. Ten deaths had ocfmrred in Winwick Asylum, so that the death-rate proper for the district was 105. VVith reference to Fearnhead sewage, he had met the Parish Council and submitted several schemes nd suggestions. The matter would be reported upon t the next meeting.
The Examiner, Saturday, May 7, 1904.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION.
THE OP FINAL.
WARRINGTON FAIL TO WIN AT • WASTE.
Halifax Retain the Cup.

Never did the Warrington enthusiasts go away with their tea n in a more Inpe.ful frame of mind than on Saturdav,when the final tie for the Northern Union Cup was played between Warrington and Halifax at Weaste, the headquarters of the Salford Club. The local team had done excellently in the Cup Competi- tion, and started favourites for the final seeing that all the incidentals of ground, crowd, and weather were favourable to Warrington. Halifax, however, pursued the old-headed close tactics that won them the Cup the previous year and succeeded in getting the upper hand of their cleverer, opponents and keeping it. Warrington madegreat efforts, but had to admit defeat by 8 paints to 3 points. There was a time when they might have won—but for excuses and miaht-have- beens the reader must turn to the notes by "Ovalist " on another page. In till eight seasons during which the competition for the Cap has bE,.en in existence, the trophy has been taken into Yorkshire on five occasions—three times to Batley, and twice to Halifax. There was a fine crowd, but it fell far short of the estimates some exuberant partizans indulged in. Stil it was very nearly a Rugby record for the Manchester district. The official returns of the turnstiles showed that the number who paid for admission was 16,011, with takings to the amount of £936 ss. 6d. To these figures have to be added tickets sold in advance, and the num- ber of members of the Salford club present, and it is computed that with these additions the full- attendance would reach 17,530, and the receipts about .21,000. The figures are satisfactory, so far as they go, thozagh they do not, of course, compare with the records of any of the final ties p!ayed at fleadingley within the last seven years. If financial reasons alone dominated the choice of ground, it is clear that all the IV orthern Union Cup finals would have to be played on the Leads Club's enclosure.
A complete list of the finals and gates under the Northern Union is as follows:

All the arratrzements at the S tlford around for Saturday's match were admirable, and from first to last the proceedings passed off without a hitch. The turf, though bare and pitchy, was in good, firm condition, and thoroughly suitable for a fast exhibition of foot- ball. The sun was perhaps a little too warm and bright for the players, but a pleasant breeze tempered it to the spectators, who could not have desired more agree- able conditions for an afternoon on the football field. The Salford Central Band played selections for an hour or so before the match started, and their efforts to beguile the dull period of waiting and anticipation were obviously appreciated by the ccowd. In finally deciding up in the constitution of the team, the Halifax Committee resolved to include Hadwen in the threequarter line in preference to Wedgwood. The last named was all right, but the C)mmittee thought that on the firm turf the old Salford man's speed would be useful. Warrington were represented by precisely the fifteen that defeated Bradford at the second attempt in the Denulimate wand of the tournament. Teams and officials:

Halifax—W. B. Little, back; H. Hartley, J. Riley, W. W. Williams, and H. Haciwen, -three-quarter backs ; A. Nettleton and J. Morley (captain), half backs; I. Bartle. J. W. Balmer, G. H. Langhorn, F. Mallinson Jack Riley, W. Morton, J. Swinbank, and R. S.Winskill, forwards.

Warrington—Haßarn, back; J. Fish, D. Isherwood,(cap- tain),G. Dickenson,anci E. Elarris,three-quarter backs; D. Davies and F. Hockenhsll, half backs; G. Thomas,A.B. Boardman, D. Morrison Lunt, G. Cook, S. Jolley J. Edmondson, and A. Naylor, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. H. Smith, Widnes. Touch judges, Messrs. J. Priestley, Salford, and E. H. Smirk, Wigan. A glance round the ground prior to the kick-off dis- closed club favours in abundance, the Warrington colours predominating. Far away—across on the popular stand—was a huge imitation "Fish" nailed to the mast, or to one of the pillars to be strictly accurate while at one end a primrose banner insc:ibed 'Play up Warrington" floated in the breeze as it was borne aloft by a couple of ent'uusiasts. Innumerable "Little Fishes" were to he seen pinned to coats and caps. In the 4/entre of the members' stand the Cup glittered in all its glory, while around itgathered the County officials and t'aeir lady friends. Warrington were out promptly to time, their appearance being greeted with a volume of encouraging cheers. Every man sported a brand new jersey and looked in the pink of condition. Halifax were a full ten minutes later, and met with nothing like so cordial a reception. The toss was won by Halifax, who had the wind behind them and the sun in their faces to start with. Dickenson commenced the game, and after the custom- ary exchanges, play settled just inside the Halifax half. Morley got possession from the first scrummage, but his pass was charged by Dickenson, andenatters remained as they were. Then Halifax were penalised, and a kick by Fish sent the ball into touch at the Halifax qaarter line. Thence the game was taken by the Halifax for- wards in a couple of loose rushes to the Warrington line, and Fish being tackled with the ball, Morley was all but over from the ensuing scrummage. The ball was kicked back to Little, who attempted to drop a goal, but the shot was wide, and Warrington touched &even an operation they had promptly to repeat from Little's return to the drop out. The Hali- fax back next placed the ball cleverly in touch, and from a fair catch by Joe Riley, Little took a place kick but was wide •of the mark. Little's strong punting kept Warrington on the defensive, Morley nearly rush- ing over on the blind side of the scrummage. Thomas and Boardman relieved the pressure with a short counter rush. This was but a momentary relief, for the Halifax forwards, playing in great style, were quickly in close quarters again. Then catne a free kick to each side in turn, and from the Halifax kick Little missed the goal by a narrow margin. Dickenson's kiek- ing subsequently caused Halifax to retire to midfield, and this movement was followed by a fast rush of the Warringtonians to the Halifax quarters. Little tem- porarily stayed their career, but the onslaught was renewed, and exciting play followed on the line. Fish kicked across and Dickenson rushed over with the ball near the posts, only to be recalled amict a groan of dis- appointment from the. crowd. The referee ordered a scrummage outside the line, and from this Morley got , the ball to safer quarters. A pass was given to Fish, but it was clearly off-side, and he was promptly whistled back. The advantage of a free kick gave Halifax the upper hand again, Hartley being bowled over into touch after some good passing by Morley and Williams. " Four in a row "at the scrummage caused Halifax to lose ground, and a hot rush to-aheir quarter line followed the Warrington men being very speedy in this move- ment. The defence of Joe Riley and Little kept the invaders within bounds, and the ingenuity shown by the Halifax forwards in wheeling the scrummage changed the scene of action once again. A combined attack by Morley,Nettleton,Joe Riley,and Hadwen catne to nothing, and though Halifax were proving distinctly the stronger side, they found the defence extremely good under pressure. When Warrington, through a free kick, had managed to raise the seige, Bulmer placed the cup. holders on the attack again with' a strong dashing run. Fish attempted to field the ball near the line, but by a piece of ill-luck the ball caught his knee and bounded over, a five yards' " serum" resulting. Here the Halifax men made a supreme effort. The ball came from the base of a scrummage to Nettleton,who handed it to Morley, and the last named passing to Joe Riley, the Halifax centre, with a strong burst, beat the opposi- tion and scored near the posts, for Hadwen to kick a goal. This, the first substantial point of the match,was obtained about ten minutes before half time. Warring- ton then spent a brief period hi. the Halifax quarters,but blundering by Hallam lost them a lot of ground, and a penalty kick being awarded to Halifax, Hadwen en- deavoured to place a goal without success. Halifax were attacking strongly up to the interval when they held a lead of a goal and a try (5 points) to nothing. After the customary rest, the teams faced each other , again, the ball now being put in motion by Little,whose kick was returned by Dickensoh. Warrington got pos- session from the first scrummage, and Davies smartly ' found touch, but the Halifax wheeling tactics were soon in evidence again,and the cup-holders' forwards ploughed their way through the opposing backs in great style, Only to be pulled up by a free kick, which Fish utilised SO well that the ball was landed in touch at the Halifax " 25 " flae,whence it was smartly removed by Nettleton and Morley. Then came a great rush of the Halifax forwards, led byßulmer and Bartle, and it required a heroic save by Hallam to avert a try. This effort of the Halifax forwards was to some extent neutralised by the concession of a free kick, bat Morley replied to this satisfactorily, and kept Warrington on the defensive: ,Smart work by Davies and Hockenhall changed the run of the playagatn. Fish ran well downlouch, and, putting I in a tall kick, a race ensued between Davies and Little, I with the result that the Welshmau had the advantage, and scored a try near the left-hand

corner. Fish failed at goal. Encouraged by the crowd, I Warrington now played up desperately, and were all I over their opponents. They were temporarily beaten off by the Halifax forwards' but Hallam picked the ball from the latter's toes, and dodging several men landed it in the Halifax quarters again, this being a really brilliant effort on the Warrington custodian's part. Warrington again got possession, and a bout of passing beat the Halifax defence, Isherwood and Harris running to the line with a certain try before them. Just on the rut, the centre passed, Harris gathered the ball, and then to the horror of the Warringtonians he stumbled and fell a foot short of the crease. Before he could get up Little had him, and the chance—the best of the game—was lost. At this stage Warrington looked probable winners, but Harris's misfortune seemed to break their hearts. The cup-holders quickly rallied, and were never again in danger. Morley and Little, using touch well, kept their opponents in neutral territory. Then a run by Williams put Halifax on the attack again, and a short dash by Morley sent Warrington still further back, but another penalty for trickiness in placing the ball in the pack lost Halifax the advantage of these movements. Morley was again conspicuous with his cool dashing runs through the opposing ranks, and though he did not part with the ball it was perhaps the correct game to play. The Halifax captain was conspicuous in other attacks, and after Joe Riley had got over from a pass by him, ruled to be informal by the referee, reward came to Morley for his great efforts. There was a scrummage near to the Warrington line, and the ball coming out to Morley, he with a rapid dive shOt past his opponents, and scored a well-deserved try. This settled the match, even though Little's kick at goal striking the post, was unsuccessful. One more raid by Warrington was changed in a twinkling to an attack by Hadwen, who nearly reached his opponents' line before being brought to book by Fish. H difax were attacking when " Time " was called, and had won the cup for the second succes- sive year with the score :—Halifax, 1 goal 2 tries (8 peints) ; Warrington. 1 try (3 points). THE CUP PRESENTED.

Immediately the match terminated there was the usual rush to the front of the grand stand to' witness the ceremony of presenting the Cup to the winning team and medals to both combatants. The presentation should have been made by 'Air. R,. Collinge, of Rochdale, the President of the Union, but indisposition caused him to forego the pleasure of performing this duty, and of wituessi lg the match. Accordingly the Cup was presented by Mr. F. Lister, of Bradford, vice-president of the Union, and Chairman of the Yorkshire County Club.

Mr. Lister, after an expression of regret at the absence of Mr. Coltinge, said that judging from the game played that day, and the large number of specta- tors who had assembled to witness it, Rugby football, so far from being dead, was very much alive. He congratulated the Halifax team upon their success, and expressed the opinion that the best side had won. At the same time he sympathised with. Warrington at be- ing defeated for the spcond time in the final contest for the cup. They must, however, persevere, and perhaps another time success would attend their efforts. Though beaten' Warrington had played good football. The defence had been strong on both sides,and the team that had won had been successful because they had taken advantage of the few opportunities that came their way. Mr. Lister then handed the Cup to Mr. Morley, the Halifax captain, and medals to the winners and to the runners-up. Morley and Fish each came in for an ovation from the crowd.

Mr. Morley said he was pleased to receive the Cup on behalf of the Halifax team. It was an honour to beat a team like Warrington, and he asked the Halifax men to drink to the health of the Warrington captain, Mr. Isherwood. This hiving been done, three cheers for Warrington were called for by the Halifax captain, and these being heartily given the formal proceedings came to an end.

div.head: First Division. SWINTON v. LEEDS.
div.p: First Division. SWINTON v. LEEDS.

Played at Swinton. The visitors opened strongly, and Jenkins scored an unimproved try. Grace kicked a penillty goal, after which Jenkins, Taylor, and Ward ran in tries, the second of these efforts being converted by Grace. In the second half Leeds still had much the best of matters, and Taylor scored, Grace kicking a goal. Swinton scored a try and a goal. Result—Leeds, 23 points; Swinton, 5 points. LEIGEI v. EIUDDERSFIELD.

Played at Leigh, before a poor attendance. The Leigh backs combined well, and Messer, Ganley. and Bennett scored tries, and Johnson kicked a goal before the interval. On resuming, Leigh again attacked, and Messer, Rirk, and Bennett scored, Towers improving one. At the close Lewis (twice) scored , unimproved tries for Huddersfield. Result—Leigh, 22 points; Huddersfield, 6 points. RUNCORN v. WIGAN.

Played at Runcorn, before 1,000 spectators. Runcorn was poorly represented. For Wigan, Barr scored a try and Mason kicked a goal. In the second half Runcorn pressed throughout. Butterworth scored a brilliant try, and Price kicked a penalty goal. Result—Runcorn, 1 goal 1 try; Wigan, 1 goal 1 try.

div.head: DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR. S. G. DAVEY.
div.p: DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR. S. G. DAVEY.

Warzington has lost ole of its het known and most respected tradesmen by the death of Mr. Samuel George Davey, who for some years had carried on business as a grocer in Butterinarket-street, He passed away at his residence 186, Padzate-lane, on Sunday, after having suffered for a long time from falvular disease of the heart. The deceased gentleman, who was 48 years of age, was the second son of the late Mr. W, H. Davey, of Truro, Cornwall. He had lived in Lancashire during the past thirty years, and for the greater part of that time in Warrington. He was with the well known firm of Messrs. Milling and Company for twenty years, and during the latter end of that period held the office of secretary and dire3tor. On severing his connection with the firm he opened the premises at the corner of Academy-street and Batermarket-street. Mr. Davey was a member of the Wesleyan denomination and was at one time identified with Bewsey-road Church. After- wards he worshipped at Bold-street Church and latterly at Padgate Church. He was a prominent Freemason, being a member of both chapter and lodge, of the "Gilbert Greenall " Lodge, 1250. He was also a mem- ber of the "Lodge of Equity," 1383, Widnes, and of the 2819 Widnes Lodge. rn connection with the former lodge he had passed through a number of offices, and WAS senior deacon up to a short time ago, when he was compelled to resign owing to failing health. The Warrington Grocers' and Provision Dealers' Association had in him a useful member, and he had occupied the post of vice-chairman. His genial and kindly disposition had gained for him a large circle of friends who deeply regret his death. He leaves a widow, two sons, and two daughters, with whom much sympathy is expressed. THE FUNERAL.

The funeral took place at the Cemetery on Wednes- day afternoon in the presence of many relatives an d friends. The cortbge left the house at 1.15 and pro- ceeded to Padgate Wesleyan Church where the first part of the burial service was conducted. The officiating ministers were the Revs. John Gunnell, of Penketh, and the Rev. R. Wilkins Rees, of Bewsev-road. There was a large congregation. The Rev. John Gunnell made a • synlpathetic allusion to the loss which the family, the • tradesmen of Warrington, and the Wesleyan body had sustained by the death of Mr. Davey who, Mr. Gunnell said, was a personal friend of his. Mr. Davey's "house was, in fact, a second home to him whenever he took an appointment in any of the Warrington Wesleyan Churches. The deceased gentleman's favourite hyma "Give me the wings of faith to rise" Was sung, and at the conclusion of the service Miss Nellie Bennett, who presided at the organ, played the Dead March in "Saul." The chief mourners were Mrs. D ivey (widow).Nlr. Reginald Davey and Master Sydney Davey (sons), Misses A. M, and L. Davey (daughters), Mr. W. H. Davey, Cressington (brother), Mr. Harold Davey(nephew). Three of Mr. Davey's oldest friends (Messrs. W. Winstanley, W. Roberts, and G. W. Weaver) attended, and others pre- sent in the church included Messrs. William and John Bennett, F. Dixon, J. Bailey and G. Mather. At the Cemetery the last rites were performed by the Revs. John Gunnell and R. Wilkins Roes. The mem- bers of "Gilbert, Greenall" lodge and "Lodge of Equity" (Widnes) of Freemasons lined the path along which the coffin was borne to the graveside, and at the Cemetery gates a number of the members of the Grocers' and Provision Dealers' Association had assembled. Amongst those present at the graveside were Dr. Reginald. Smith (Mr. Davey's medical attendant),

Mr. J'.' W. Hayward, Mr. J. Robinson, and Mr. Lawsonl The following represented the Freemasons :—" Gilbert Greenall "Lodge 1250, Brothers J. W. G. Craddock. W.M. ; T. div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Backley-strut P S.A. Sniety.

A largely-attended open 11133tirlg of the above society washeld on Sunday. Mrs. C. Simpson presided. The speaker was the Rev. J. F. Matthews who gave an address on "To do good, to be good." Air. J. Barrett read the lesson. The soloists were Miss C. Sumner, who gave an excellent rendering of "Lead kindly light," and Mr. W. R. Roberts who effectively sang the tenor 5010... "If with all your hearts" and "When I survey the wondrous cross." Miss M. Plinston, A.L.C.M., and Mr. A. Trow were the accompanists.

div.head: Services for the People.
div.p: Services for the People.

The Rev. H. Minnie() again preached at the Parr Hall on Sunday evening, taking his text from Galatians 6. 7. "Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap." God was an essential factor in human life, said the preacher, and could not be ignored. The law of retribution and the consequences of sin were discussed, it being seen that silt invariably left its mark on the body, on the intellect, and on the soul. The preacher also pointed out the possibilities of goodness, stating that in every good deed there was the element of infinity.

div.head: Ellesmere-street Wesleyan Mission.
div.p: Ellesmere-street Wesleyan Mission.

A good congregation assembled in the above place of worship 0n Sunday evening, when a special service was held and the collection devoted to the choir funds. The preacher was Mr. A. Perkins, who urged the choir to put all their soul and energy into the work that they were doing for the Nlaster. He also exhorted the con- gregation to give to the choir their fullest sympathy, so that all might be blessed and the Kingdom of God extended. The choir rendered the anthems "The earth is the Lord's," and "When I survey." A quartette, entitled "Perfect in Christ," was also sung by four members of the choir. A concert was given in the Mission on the following evening, and a good pro- gramme was submitted. The items rendered were of a high order, the artistes being the Misses Woodland, Taylor and Plinston, A.L.C.M., and Messrs. Roberts, Perry and Grounds (humorist). Mr. J. Ellison presided. Votes of thanks to all who had taken part in the pro- ceedings followed by tite singing of the Doxology, brought a pleasant and profitable evening to a close.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A.

There was a good attendanceat this meeting on Sun- day. Mr. George Colley presided, and spoke upon the ill effects of gambling. Mr. S. Hilton, of lVfarple was the speaker, and delivered an address upon "ways of living." There were, he said, many ways of living amongst old and young, high and low, rich and poor. Some lived for pure gratification, whilst many lived for impure gratification. Some men could go so far as to rob themselves, their w ives and families, •-to satisfy their own desires and gratifications. One man he knew, not long ago told him he had for some time spent one-third of his wages every week for his own gratification. Living to get, when legitimate, was honourable and right; getting to improve self and others was God-like. The man•of science gave to the world what he had got, and so helped to brighten life. The man getting knowledge became in his living and giving, a channel of good from God to man. A man living and getting for himself alone would some day find that what he had got was like a millstone around his neck, driving him further away from God. In giving we received more than we gave,---Mr. C. Eccles and Mr. G. Smiley also tobk part in themeeting. Mr. Payton, Mus. Bac., presided at the organ. The Secretary welcomed anew member, and gave him the usual greet- ing. He also gave a parting word to Miss M. V.Vomers- ley, who was leaving Warrington to go to another town. He said she had always been willing in every way to help in the musical portion of the services.

div.head: Anniversary Services at Bewsey-road.
div.p: Anniversary Services at Bewsey-road.

Large congregations assembled in Bewsey-road Wes- leyan Church on Sunday on the occasion of the Sunday school anniversary. At night, the congregation was one of the largest for many years chairs being placed in the aisles in order to afford additional accommodation. The preacher for the occasion was the Rev. John Grange Bennett, son of Mr. John Bennett, of Padgate. This is the second time in succession he has preached at the anniversary services in connection with Bewsey-road, but it will be remembered that for many years he performed a similar duty for Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Chapel. His morning discourse was based on the text "What lack I yet? " (Matthew 19c. 20v.), and "YetNackest thou one thing." (Luke 18c. 22v.) He pointed out that a good moral life was incomplete without there was love to God and to our neighbour. The evening discourse was based on Deuteronomy 14c. 14v. He spoke of a strong man with deep spiritual convictions and with courage to adhere to those convictions, as instanced in the life of Caleb. The choir, of which Mr. Wadsworth is the conductor, sang several anthems with taste and expression. The morning anthem was " 0 Praise the Lord of Heaven" (Redhead), and at the evening service "From Thy love as a Father" (Gounod). Mrs. A. Booth was the soloist. The children were accommodated on an impro vised platform. They bad been trained by Mr. B. Wadsworth, organist and choirmaster, and the duty of conducting devolved upon Mr. Williams. It is interest- ing to note that two hy-ans were sung to tunes composed bylocal friends. Mr. Catland a member of the choir, is the composer of the tune sung to " Lift the Gospel Banner,' and Mr. S. Horton, the composer of a new tune to the familiar hymn There's a friend for little chil- dren."

A musical service was held in the afternoon, presided over by Councillor Tinnion. Mr. S. Horton, formerly of Warrington but now of Leeds sang the silos "It with all your hearts" (Mendelssohn) and "Come ye Children" (Sullivan). Mrs. A.lilooth also sang two solos one in the anthem "From Thy love as a father, and Gounod's "0 Divine Redeemer." Mr. Councillor Brough gave the address and spoke on the influence of kindness, illustrating it with several pleasing and in- structivestories from life. The total collections for the day amounted to £5O Is.

div.head: ST. BARNABAS' CHURCH.
div.p: ST. BARNABAS' CHURCH.
Sale of Work °pull by Lady &mall.

To aid various funds connected with St. llarnabas' Church a sale of work was held in the Assembly Room at the Conservative Club on Wednesday and akursday. Lady Greenall performed the openiug ceremony on Wednesday afternoon in the presence of a large gather- ing. The objects:of the sale were explained by the Vicar (Rev. J. H. G. Hollingworth) who cordially thanked the workers for their willing assistance. One of the three funds which required support, he con- tinued, was the curacy fund. Each year £l6O had to be raised to provide the salary of an assistant curate, and towards that sum the Additional Curates' Society made a grant of £4O. The balance of £l2O had to he obtained by subscriptions and in other ways, and they hoped to be able to devote some of the prt,fits of the sale to that fulid. Then they had to help the thy schools. When the Education Act came into operation in Warrington their schools were free from debt, but unfortunately they had no funds in hand. About two months ago be received a notice from the Education Committee asking for certain alterations to be made to the build- ings at a cost of about £l5O. He did not want to hand over the schools to the authority, and therefore he hoped the proceeds of the sale would enable them to assist that work. In regard to the third item, it was felt that the time had arrived when the church should he enlarged. At present they had no chancel, and they also required an organ and organ chamber. Those improvements would involve an expenditure of between £2,003 and £3,030. The raising of funds should, he felt, be commenced immediately and as the result of the sale he hoped to be able to set aside some- thing for that large undertaking. He had pleasure in introducing Lady Greenall to whom they were much indebted for her kindness in coming to open the [sale. (Applause.) _ _ _

Idy GREENALL then declared the sale open. She asked all present to remember that the parochial objects about which they had heard were an ever-increasing anxiety to the Vicar. She hoped they would do every- thing they could to lessen that anxiety and to help Mr Hollingworth in his good work. (Applause.) On the proposition of Mr. JANIES IDDON (vicar's warden) a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Lady Greenall who briefly acknowledged the compliment. The stalls had been very pleasingly arranged, and were in charge. of the following ladies :—Refteshment stall, Mesdames Proud, Jones, and Grounds, Misses S. Whitehouse, &Whitehouse, Gerrard,and Snelson ; work stalls (I), Mesdames Hollingworth, Dowling, and Tom- kins. Misses Pickering and Clogs; (2), Mesdames Iddon, Siddall and Smith; (3), Mesdames Bracegirdle and Allen, and Miss Bracegirdle ;FM Mesdames Connell and Hassall,and Miss Jefferson; Japanese stall,Mesdames Furnival, Evans, and Billington ; toy and perfumery stall, Misses E. and A. Fry ; flower stall, Miss Alice Whitehouse and Mrs. Hands. Each evenine selections were creditably rendered by Master Toni Birton's boys' band. ' The proceeds for the two days amounted to £9.5.

div.head: After the Football Match.
div.p: After the Football Match.

At the close of the Northern Union cup final, at Weaste, on Saturday, there was a big rush on the tramcars, and Detective-Sergeant D ransfield and Detective Jones saw a couple of Men behaving suspiciously amongst the crowd. They eventually arrested the men, who gave the names of William Gordon and John Wilson, and at the spot where - they were arrested Detective-Sergeant Jackson found a purse containing a sum of money:and the return half of a ticket to Warrington. The men were also in .posses- sion of a walking stick. They refused to give any account of themselves, and on Monday they were [remanded until Saturday. •

The Padgate institute tourney was concluded this week, being won by El.Holcroft, who defeated J. Smith in thefinal. Mr. J. Roberts did not compete. In the earlier rounds of the tourney Holcroft defeated 3. Weston, W. Turner and J. Mercer, respectively.
