div.p: THE EXAMINER.
Mr. BALFOUR gaily lIRED UNIONISTS, suggested on Tues-

day that the present Parliament has still three years and a half to run. It is to the credit of his own cunning that his Government has not yet been shipwrecked ; but even his friends are dispnsed to regard his official life as a life from hand to mouth. The Budget and the Licensing bill are held up for our admira- tion as feats of political strategy which have dished the oppasit)on. Upon this we will only remark that the dishing is not over yet, and that some narrow divisions on the Budget may be the heralds of still narrower divisions in Committee on the Licensing Bill. The slackness of attendance on the Ministerial side is incurable. It is reported by the and bv some of their news- papers, enrtilayl withoutWhiepff journal, the Whips, and One unioni st that it is the natural course of hutnan nature. a pleasant choice of metaphors, "Whipping a demi donkey," says our contem- as useful and remunerative as the owr aoruyl ,d wb t jhu t castigation of a majority. If there is any peril overhanging Mr. BALFOUR'S Ministry of the kind that might be suggested by a series of unpleas- antly close divisions, it arises from conditions with I

which personal management has little control." A nice hint to Mr. BaLrounthat all his charming arts are of no avail. "The Unionist party,"continues the "Pall Mall" remorsely, "has been nine years in power, and is feeling some of the natural results of that prolonged strain—a strain which in its de- gree is just as telling upon the private member as on his leaders, who spend their days on their departments and their nights in the House. The exhilaration of Parliamentary life evaporates in some people before they have completed such a term of service. The wonder is that it endures six months in anyone who is not a bore or a hero." These are sufficiently plain words. The " Pall Mall "is evidently tired of this Government, and believes that many Unionist rnetnbers are tired, too. There are otters who loudly proclaim their resolve to keep Mr. BALFOUR at the helm in the interests of the State; but whether, they are bores or heroes, who can say? The point is that many gentlemen feel they have worn them- selves out in the service of Unionist principles, and are entitled to take their rest when the division bell is calling and the Government Whips are fuming. "The irksomeness of perpetual duty," as the "Pall Mall" says with such illumin- ating candour, "is a constant foe to the alacrity and zeal which are the only true safeguards of a Government, even with A large numerical advantage in the House of Commons." So irksome is the ' perpetual duty that one Unionist member - writing to the "Times," rebukes the Whips for expecting him to be constantly on the • alert. Why can't they let him dine in peace in the bosom of his family and get somebody , else to keep watch for "snap divisions " ? His mind reverts fondly to Disraeli's time, when the party was much better managed and the Whips were far more affable. This letter has drawn some • angry protests from other Unionists. Sir HERBERT . MAXWELL says it is a "ccwardly attack," and that instead of dining at home with his family the writer ought to invite them to dine with him at the House of Oommons. The offending Unionist will probably consider this a new form of dictation • and ask himself whether an independent citizen can remain in a party which coerces him even at his meals. But the truth is, as the " Pdl Mall" tells us, that the "prolonged strain " of keeping Mr. BALFJUR in office is growing too much for Unionist Constitutions, and if they are weary after nine years, what must be the condition of the , country to which Mr. BALFOUR graciously promises three years and a half more of his priceless leader- ship?

Our local Liberal leaders are putting forth splendid efforts to improve the organisation of the party and to educate the constituency on the political topics of the hour. During the week the committees of five wards have held joint meetings and there is a consensus of opinion amongst Liberals that the parcy organisation never made more rapid progress towards efficiency than it is doing at the present moment. The work of educating the constituency is also being carried forward with energy, and such excellent addresses as 3lr. Howes has delivered must bear good fruit. Mr. Crosfield struck the right note at the public meeting on Thursday when he emphasised the need of cohesion in the party and the sinking of particu- lar fads for the general good of the cause. Mr. Arthur Crosfield has not yet been formally adopted as the Liberal candidate for the next election, but there is not much doubt as to his ultimate selection. A more popular Liberal candidate could not be found, and unless present portents are altogether wrong we believe he will succeed at the next election in carrying the Liberal standard to victory. It is encouraging to learn from his speech on Thursday, that if the Liberal executive desire him to fight again the Liberal battle he will, to use his own words, "be there when the bell rings." We hope the bell this time will be the division bell in the House of Commons.

It is not likely that anything More will be heard for a while of the teachers and their revised scale of salaries. The Ethication Committee has triumphed in its little duel with the Town Coun- cil, which was in quite a repentent frame of mind on Tuesday when Alderman Bennett re-introduced the disputed scale. He devoted more time than was really necessary in advocating the teachers' claims, for the Council hits been almost reduced mentally to a state of :pulp by the storm of criticism levelled at it during the past few weeks, amid had not one opposition kick left. In defence of the municipal authority we ought in fairness to add that there was some misapprehension in the minds of many Councillors who voted against the scale of salaries on the first occasion. They have since obtained necessary enlightenment, and the teachers can go on their way rejoicing that they will not have to seek situations elsewhere in order to obtain a fair day's pay for a fair day's work.

Alderman Bennett also alluded to the necessity for more school accommodation, and announced that the Education Committee had abandoned the idea of erecting a temporary iron building on one of the open spaces. We agree with the Com- mittee that this would be false economy,for such a structure. could only relieve the congestion in a slight degree, and would be of no permanent service. The scheme for the provision of new schools cannot be shelved, and it will be the wisest course for the Committee to pro- ceed as early as possible with the erection of one of the three new schools decided upon. The Edu- cation authority in the neighbouring town of St. Helens has this week agreed to build three new schools at a total cost of £27,000, which is not at all an extravagant estimate. The sum of £lO,OOO per school has been mentioned as the probable figurs for Warrington, but if St. Helens can man- age with £l,OOO less there should be no difficulty in the Warrington authorities economising to a similar extent.

If time were really money, and talk of equal value, sufficient of both would have been expended ere this to have paid the interest on the capital required to widen Warrington Bridge by canti- levers. The whole scheme is discussed pro and con every time it advances one little step, and we have not the slightest doubt that the wordy warfare of Tuesday night will be renewed on some future occasion, fruitless and absurd as it all is. The cantilever scheme has been again and again affirmed, and it ill-becomes certain members of the Connell to obstruct at every opportunity when the feeling of the town is strongly in favour of the improvement. Were a poll taken on the subject we doubt not that the scheme would be ratified by a ten to one vote. It is simple, inexpensive, and will answer the purpose for a considerable number of years. Nothing could be more absurd than for members of the Town Council to argue that the Briuge at present is wide enough and not dangerous. They have only to stand ten minutes at Bridge Foot in the middle of any weekday to be convinced—if they are open to conviction—that the structure is a standing menace to the life and limb of all those who traverse it. As Councillor Pemberton son- ably pointed out, what is the use of spending hundreds of thousands of pounds to widen Bridge street when the approach to t from Cheshire is contracted by Warrington Bridge? Thera was not a single logical argument advanced on Tues- day night in favour of further postponement, un- less we are to deem the problematical changes on the railway as something to consider. No Let the scheme proceed without any further shilly-shallying.
Alderman Fairclough is,perhaps,the most hostile of any of the members of the Council to the

bridge. He apoarently hates the structure wit;hei whole-souled and undying hatred and presumably rather see it blown up than widens° Revertheless it is going to be widened or we vel much mistake the tone of the 18 to 9 majoritP The Alderman's threat that" our firm will °Ws: the scheme tooth and nail" will probably ll° dater anybody from supporting it. Oa the on- trary it should spur them on. Such a remark.,s the one quoted ill-becomes the Deputy-Mayor. Ca° it be that he has forgotten that he was elected tdd the Council to represent the ratepayers first an himself not at all?

Councillors John Evans and Stott gave thej! separate versions of the interview with Messir Rhodes and Son, of Stourbridge, in regard to tut/ standard wage question. Fortunately there ;no discrepancy in their statements, but the CO' elusions they drew from their observation.. were completely at variance. The Chair' of the Sanitary Committee expressed b self perfectly sati4fied that Messrs. Rhode: and Son paid the standard wage of t,he district, and asked the Council to confirm contract. On the other hand Councillor Stott 70 dissatisfied and expressed his belief that the r. in question did not pay the standard rate of wagel The sympathy of the Council, however, was 11°3 with the Trades Union representative, and as mie could not actually prove either that there was standard wage for the district, or that gessrs.4. Rhodes and Son did not pay it, the contract WTI ratified. This has been an unsatisfactory affair :9 along, and Councillor Stott, in our opinion, h failed to justify the extreme position he took 11% The Council must have a stronger case to go uP°O in future before refusing to sanction a contract the standard wage question.

At Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wed- ‘4l,7a7 Samuel -Warburton. and John Lilford, both of -"lnwick-road, Warrington, were charged with steal- lug a basket containing groceries of the value of 3s.Gd., „th,_, property of Mary Bold, Clambrook Cottage, wmwick. Prosecutrix went into the Longford Hotel, •and placed the basket on a form. A few minutes later he missed it, and on going outside saw the prisoners, 'who had also been in the hotel, running down the road with the basket in their possession. Warburton, 'who had a bad character, was sent to gaol for one Month. Lilford was fined 20s. and costs, or fourteen 'days.

Latchtord Man's Delusions. A young man named Benjamin Hatton, said to be from Latchford, was charged at Stockport on Tuesday With being a wandering lunatic. He was found Pacing the roadway just outside Stockport, and told a Police constable that he was a burglar, but had lorgotten his tools. He also said he would break Open all the doors in Bredburg, and that be was a -noted pugilist,having beaten Fitzsimmoas and all the best boxers of the world. The magistrates ordered him to the workhouse to be medically examined. 'Warrington and the Welsh Eisteddfod. Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at.the Police Station on Monday on the body of Ann Kirkham, 57 years of age, who resided at 291, I'lumpton-street.—John Kirkham, soapmaker, husband of the deceased, said he retired to bed shortly before le.n o'clock on Thursday, leaving his wife in the kitchen. At 11.50 he heard a noise as of someone laYing downstairs, and on getting up he found his wife lying at the botton; of the stairs, bleeding from the head, and in an unconscious condition. A clock an.d a broken jug, which had contained water, were lying by her side. Dr. Naden was sent for, and ordered her removal to the Infirmary, where she died '9,rt Saturday night.—A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. - _

WATERS.—Advt. Property Owners and the Increased Rates. The members of the Property Owners' Association met in Cain-street schools on Monday evening to consider in view of the increase of rates, the course of action to be adopted by the property owners of the borough. Mr. Joseph Mounfield presided. Many suggestions were made as to how the increase of rates should be met. Eventually the following committee was formed in addition to the ordinary committee of the• association, to consider the question of the tenants paying their just proportion of the increase in the rates :—Messrs. T. May, T. Pemberton, T. H. Pilking- ton, W. Gandy, J. Jameson and R. Dale.

Training College Musical Examination. Dr. Arthur Somervell visited the Warrington Training College yesterday for the purpose of con- ducting the annual musical examination. The collec- tive test took the form of a concert in thelevening, and by the invitation of the Principal (the Rev. Morley Stevenson) a number of ladies and gentlemen interested in the work of the college attended. The first part of the programme comprised some mis- cellaneous items by the first year students' and in the latter part, the second year students sang Parry's ode on St. Cecilia's Day. The principal vocalists were Miss ivy Adkin, Miss Ella Yates, Miss Daisy Haywood and Mr. H. A. Greenlees. Mr. W. S. Woods the musical instructor, conducted, and the perform- ance gave great pleasure to the audience. The choruses were given with precision and expression and the soloists acquitted themselves with marked ability. Valuable assistance was rendered by an orchestra composed as follows : Mr. E. H. Clare and Mr. A. Bennett (first violins), Mr. W. Brown and Mr. A. Knowles (second violins), Mr. G. Johnson (viola), Mr. Henry Bond (violoncello), Miss Hackett (piano- forte) and Mr. W. H. The following transfers of licences were sanctioned by the magistrates on Monday :—Cross Keys. from Robert Anderton(deceased) to Ann Anderton; Brewers' Arms, from James Riches to Joseph Helsby; Travellers' Rest, from John Wrench to Thomas Gibbons; Manx Arms, from Thomas Hatton to George Atkinson,—ln regard to the Britannia Inn, the Bench granted an adjournment for a fortnight.—Mr. Browne applied for the licence to be transferred to Frederick Richard Molyneux. He explained that Mrs. Holland, who held the licence for many years, recently died and by her will appointed her daughter, Mrs. Finch, executrix. Mrs. Finch obtained temporary authority, but she had died. Her husband, who had intended to apply for a transfer teat morning, was lying seriously ill. Mr. Steel said he appeared for the executrix under the will of the late Mrs. Finch. The deceased lady be- queathed some furniture to Mr. Finch but the will had not yet been carried out. He therefore felt bound to apply for a transfer to Mr. Finch. When the arrange- ments under the will had been completed, Mr. Molyneux could take charge of the house. Eventually the adjournment as stated above was decided upon.

lIT;TDER the CLOCK for GOOD BOOTS.—Advt. British Women's Temperance Association. A meeting of the above society was held oL Tuesday afternoon in the Church Parlour, Bold-street. Mrs. Norman presided, and Miss Bessie Dutton engaged in prayer. The Secretary read papers, and a memorial form to Lady Henry Somerset was signed, Mrs. Garnett contributing 55., and other members various sums. A deputation was received in the persons of Mr. Chandos Wilson, of Manchester, aud Mr. Pierce Williams on behalf of the Lancashire and Cheshire Band of Hope and Temperance Union to explai.n the effort which is now being put forth by the Union to raise £15,000 to provide headquarters in Manchester and to carry on Temperance teaching in schools. It was decided to hold a rummage sale in June and a- sale of work later, the profits to be shared between the Union and the Association.

Hatton Stack Fire —Alleged Incendiaris m. A forty-ton stack of hay on the farm of Mr. R. L. Warburton, Hatton, was destroyed by fire on Sunday night. Information of the outbreak was received at the Warrington Fire Station at 10.20, and the brigade turned out, under the direction of Deputy-Superinten- dent Turner, with the engine "Major." On arrival two powerful jets were got to work from the engine, there being a good supply of water from in adjoining pit. The fire was subdued after three hours' work. The damage, estimated at £l2O, is covered by insurance.—At the Occasional Court on Monday, Henry Caffrey, of no settled abode, was charged with wilfully setting the stack alight. The police evidence showed that prisoner was seen among the crowd which assembled. He asked an officer " how much he was going to get for discover- ing the fire" and on being questioned, made a rambling statement. Prisoner was remanded to the Daresbury Petty Sessions to be held on Tuesday next. H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC is the KING OR TONICS.-63, SANKEY-STREET, Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: IN AND AROUND WARRINGTON.
div.p: IN AND AROUND WARRINGTON.
The Bridge Question.

[By THE FREE CRITIC.] It was pleasing to notice that the tone of our last Council meeting was a distinct improvement on the previous one. Whether it was owing to the sunny weather we have been experiencing of late or to mine and other people's friendly criticisms in the past I can- not say, but the fact remains that the Aldermen and Councillors were ma more genial and brother-like mood than they have been for the pastsixmonths. The result was that more business was done. In passing I might say that the gift of orchids each Council night by the Mayor to his colleagues and the members of the Fourth Estate is a kindly and graceful act which deserves recording. It also helps to adorn not only the sombre costumes of the wearers, but also brightens up and puts a little colour into the Council Chamber.

The chief matter that came up for discussion was the Bridge. Everybody is agreed that something should be done. This is patent to anyone—but there has been terrible amount of talk and time wasted over how it shall be done. In the meantime minor accidents are continually occurring, and if the bridge is not soon taken in hand there will be a valuable life or two lost— lives that are worth a great deal more than ever a new bridge or what the cost of widening would be. It seems to me that some members of our Town Coun- cil are getting neurotic and unnerved about the spend- ing of money. Their judgment is being warped and too much fear is being shown. They appear not to know when to spend and when to save. I may say at once that if Warrington Bridge can be widened (for anything like a sum of £3,100 to the dimensions as mentioned in Mr. Webster's report, viz.: carriage or roadway from 20 feet to 30 feet 6 inches and its footways from 4 feet to 19 feet, it will be an exceedingly cheap piece of work. I should imagine too,that as it will not cost a farthing in the £ on the rates, that very few, if any ratepayers would object to the scheme. In fact it has been time after time expressed in the town that thes widening of the Bridge would be welcomed. Besides the carrying out of the scheme would after all find some work in the town, as I take it the bulk of the money would be spent in it. The only objections I have heard so far of any moment is to the expence of an entirely new bridge—which would involve a sum of nearly £30,000. The town is not prepared or in the humour to spend any such sum as this and the Council should man- like grasp the facts and face the situation, To leave the Bridge as it is at present, dangerous to everybody, is a Positive scandal and a disgrace to the town. Action in the matter is essential.—On one day alone 7 cyclists came to grief.—Will our Town Council take the warn- ng

div.head: WARRINGTON RUGBY FOOTBALL CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON RUGBY FOOTBALL CLUB.
REVIEW OF SEASON 1903-4.
By " Ovalist."

Some day I shall take up my pen for this annual task with pleasure and alacrity-when Warrington have won the Cup ! On an occasion like the present, however, when all football enthusiasts in the town are smarting under the sting of a second defeat in the final for the Northern Union trophy,one cannot review the doings of the season with anything but chastened feelings. I am not going to admit that Warrington are one of those teams that inspire everyone with con- fidence and then crumple up at the final test with heart-breaking consistency. No! The Warrington men are better than their record would indicate, and it only needs a slight turn of Fortune's wheel for them to obtain the glory they have so narrowly missed on two occasions. Though it has ter- minated with a defeat in the Cup-final this has not been at all a bad season for Warrington. In fact they may reasonably look back upon it with pride, for it is far and away the best they have had under the aegis of the Northern Union. During the eight months just closed, Warrington have won more matches, scored mere points, and played better football than they have done for a good many years. 'Honour too, has not bean denied them, for consistently good play resulted in the acquisition once more of the South West Lancashire Cup. This is certainly, a minor achievement, but it is one full of credit and auguring well for the future. Then the appearance in the final for the blue riband of the Union a second time is no small honour in itself, and furthermore there have been some great performances by the club in individual matches. The League Competition has concluded with Bradford as the winners,and Warring- ton seventh on the list,with 37 points out of 31 games' -two points better than last season's score, itself a record,while the scoring average has improved beyond recognition. Last season Warrington compiled 148 points in the League tourney and their opponents 164. This season the figures are 214, and 153-a vast im- provement. It must not be overlooked, moreover that these figures would have been even better but for the exigencies of the Cup Competition, which caused Warrington to sacrifice points in the matches with Bradford and Salford (home), Huddersfield and Wigan (away). Three of these matches could easily have been won, with possibly a transference of 20 to 30 points from the debit to the credit side. Taking everything into consideration, Warrington have had an excellent League season. At one time they looked like possible champions, but they failed to keep up the high standard of excellence required in order to head the Competition table. An excellent start was made by defeating Leigh (home) and Hull (away), Batley proving the first stumbling block. Thenceforward,for five matches Warrington were undefeated, and then they lost to Hull Kingston Rovers and Oldham in successive matches, the latter club taking the first two points from Wilderspool. Bradford (away) was an unfortunate encounter for Warrington, as in addition to losing by 14-0, they were deprived of the services of Isherwood and Harris. The latter had only just recovered from a broken collar-bone sustained in practice at the commencement of the season, and it was broken again, the two acci- dents keeping him out of the team for half the season. Nevertheless, Warrington frequently scored heavily, victories of 18-5, 11-3, 15-0, 20-0, being recorded in succession against Runcorn (home), Salford (away), Hull and Batley (home). The win at Salford on Boxing Day waione of the finest performances of the season and caused great jubilation. Varying fortune attended Warringtor until the cup-ties commenced, when the team at once jumped into resplendent form. They played Swinton to a draw in the first round at Swinton and defeated them heavily in the re-play. But all this is 'so recent as to need no recapitulation here. I must however, allude specially to Warrington's defeat of Bradford in the re-played semi-final at Huddersfield. This was a feat surpassing anything done during the season, and accomplished by football of the highest class. Warrington won many friends -and it is to be feared backers-by their display at Fartown. A feature of the season's play, which I had i almost overlooked is the ample way n which the Warrington men revenged themselves upon Runcorn for long years of defeat. The two games this season were won by a total of 37 points to 5 points, and the Linnets are no longer feared. Another item worthy of note is that during the whole of the season War- rington have never been fined for a late start, nor had a man suspended for misconduct on the field. I don't suppose another club in the Union can say the same, and it reflects great credit upon the officials of the Warrington Club. With regard to the players who have dorie so well for the Club, there has been no great change. The full-back is still staid, reliable Jack Hallam, and the threequarters the famous quartette, Fish, Isherwood, Dickenson and Harris, who have done the bulk of the scoring for the "Primrose and Blues" during three seasons and they are playing to-day better than ever! Fish and Dickenson have both represented Lancashire during the season, and Boardman also has gained his County Cap. There have been three notable additions to the first team playing strength in Dai Davies, G-. Thomas and Qook, a trio of first-class men who have done much towards cementing the side into a fine combination. The "same old story, nothing new," has to be told once more, however. Warrington have been let down in , the scrummages, though the front rank men are better I than they were a year ago. More bone, brawn, and , muscle are imperative, if the highest honours are to be gained. lam almost tired of r Teating this state- ment year after year, but thq sad recollections of last Saturday may do something towards spurring the executive in the right direction. A good pack of for- wards could never have been beaten as Warrington were by Halifax. While alluding to this topic I should like to quote what the" Yorkshire Post" says of the Warrington team. The comments are instructive and encouraging. Observe! "Warrington have proved themselves to be a clever team, and exponents of the prettier side of the handling game, second probably only to Broughton Rangers and Bradford. They require ano'her half-stone a man in the sc-ummaye, with a greater capacity for wheeling and dribbling to become one of the strongest teams of the day. We trust they will be able to keep their fine set of backs together for the next season, and to infuse a little more weight into the front rank. If that should be so, a third appearance in the final tie, with victory as' the crown- ing point, is not an extravagant forecast." The italics are mine. Perhaps they will impress themselves on the powers that be! Coming to details, Warrington have during the past season played 43 games, of which they have WOD 23, lost 15, and drawn 5. They have scored 40 goals, 69 tries, or 287 points to 33 goals, 36 tries, or 172 points. The teams they have beaten away from Wilderspool have been Hull, Broughton Rangers, Salford, Pontefract, Leigh, Bradford, and Runcorn, while they have been beaten at home by Oldham, Broughton Rangers, Brad- ford and Salford. The otie home draw was with Hunslet and the four draws away were with Widnes, Swinton (twice), and Bradford. To sum up, Warring- ton have beaten Leigh, Hull, Swinton Wigan, and Run- corn twice each, and Batley, Keighley, Broughton Rangers, Widnes, Hull Kingston Rovers, Seaton, Huddersfield, Bradford, Leeds, Salford, Halifax, Ponte- fract, and St. Helens, once each. They have been beaten once each by Batley, Keighley, Broughton Rangers, Hunslet, Mill, Kingston Rovers Huddersfield, Wigan, Leeds and Salford, and twice each by Oldham,Bradford I and Halifax. div.head: DEATH OF MR. E. A. WALLINGTON.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. E. A. WALLINGTON.

The death occurred on Monday morning somewhat suddenly, of Mr. Edmund A. Wallington, of Sutton, near Frodsnam. For 20 years he had been a member of the Runcorn Board of Guardians and had also represented the township on the Rural District Council. He resigned his connection with these authorities a month ago. His geniality and unassuming manner had gained for him many friends. He was a member of the Roman Catholic Church, and regularly journeyed to Warrington on Sun- days in order to attend mass. Latterly he had been a sufferer from heart disease, but it was not anticipated by his friends that the end was so near. REFERENCE AT THE RUNCORN GUARDIANS

div.head: MEETING.
div.p: MEETING.

At the meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians on Tuesday, Mr. Joseph Stokes said that before the commencement of the ordinary business he wished to call attention to the great loss which the community at large had suffered by the death of a very old and res- pected member of the Board—Mr. E. A.Wallington, whom they all knew so well. He had been called away very suddenly, and they deeply,regretted his death. Mr. Wallington was present at the last meeting of the Board, and he (Mr. Stokes) had the pleasure of riding home with him. He also accompanied him from Dutton after the meeting of the Education Committee. Little did he think that that would be the last time he would see Mr. Wallington, for he was then in the best of health and spirits. He had only just ceased to be a member of the Board after many years of public service, and he (Mr. Stokes) thought it would be fitting to pass a vote of condolence with the widow and family. He moved that that be done. Mr. Lewis seconded. .

The Chairman (Mr. A. R. Norman) said one striking feature in Mr. Wallington's character was his kindli- ness and geniality. He always seemed to be in a happy frame of mind, and one of the least likely men to have been called away so suddenly. Mr. Stokes said Mr. Wallington's connection with the Board dated back twenty years. The motion was carried in silence, the members all standing. He was fifty-four yt,ars of age. Mr. Wallington formerly resided at Latchford and carried on business in Warrington. He leaves a widow and eight children. THE FUNERAL.

The funeral took place at Pantasaph on Thursday. Mass for the dead was celebrated at the Francis monastery. In addition to the members of the family there were present :--Mr. and Mrs. Walter Wallington (brother and sister-in-law), M. Thomas Cowdell (Stockton Heath), Messrs. div.head: Interesting Proposals Submitted to the Lords.
div.p: Interesting Proposals Submitted to the Lords.

The Manchester Ship Canal Bill was on Wednesday before a Committee of the House of Lords, presided over by Lord Glanusk, who, as Mr. J. Russell Bailey, was chairman of the Committee on the first Ship Canal Bill of 1883. The other members of the Committee are Lord Hamilton of Dalzell, Lord Yarborough, Lord Romney, and Lord Lytton. The main object of the bill is to authorise the Ship Canal Company to deepen the waterway by two feet, so as to admit of the passage of larger vessels, and to 'carry out certain alterations in the neighbourhood of Warrington. Among the opponents represented by counsel were the Shropshire Union Railways and Canal Company, the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, the Acting Con- servator of the River Mersey (Sir G. Nares), the Liver- pool, Birkenhead, and Warrington Corporations, various traders of Warrington the United Alkali Company, the Salt Union, Limited, Wilson-Patten, and Sir Gilbert Greena.ll.

In opening the case for the promoters, Mr. Balfour Browne, who spoke for the greater part of the sitting, gave a history of the Ship Canal scheme and of the benefits its construction had conferred on the immense district served by it. He believed the railway rates were now about one half what they were when the canal was projected. No damage had been done to the estuary. On the contrary, the estuary was never in a better condition, and what the learned counsel characterised as the silly predictions made, notably by the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, who had always been antag- onistic to the claims of Manchester to become a port, had been signally falsified by the result. Quite recently the London and North Western Railway Company had obtained power to construct a large dock at Garston, which was the best proof the estuary had not been injured by the canal. The depth of the canal as at present authorised was 26ft., the same as the Suez Canal. At the time the Act was passed there were not half a dozen ships afloat that could not have travelled to Manchester. Now there were hundreds, and unless the canal was deepened these ships must go to rival ports, which was, perhaps, one of the reasons the promoters were now being so much opposed. They were only proposing to do what other ports had done, notably Liverpool which had spent five millions to deepen the dock entrances and reconstruct old docks so as to accommodate large vessels It was-proposed by this bill to enable the Company by controlling and regulating sluices and by raising sills of tidal openings, or by other means, to increase the level of the Canal by two feet between the Eastham and Latchford locks, the latter being the end of the tidal portion of the canal, and in this connection to vary the levels of the Weaver and the Mersey—in the case of the Weaver by raising the low-water level as far as Sutton Weir and in the case of the Mersey by raising the level from a dam on the west to Walton lock and to Howley Weir in Warrington 'on the east, including the portion of the old course of the river' between Walton lock and Chester Road. From Latchford to Manchester the canal was an ordinary inland canal fed by the Irwell and other streams, and over this length the Company proposed not to put two feet of water on the top, as in the other length, but to add two feet by dredging. In the latter portion of the work the canal passed undera number of railway bridges and the Company had arranged to do the work in such a way as not to interfere with the stability of the bridges, as a consequence of which undertaking the railway companies had withdrawn their opposition. It was suggested by the Liverpool Corporation that the Company might deepen the tidal portion of the canal by dredging, as was proposed to be done higher up. But there were various objections to this course. One of the objects of the scheme was to improve the naviga- tion of the canal byputting an end to the currants which impeded navigation, and dredging alone would increase rather than diminish these currents. Moreover, the deepening of this portion of the canal by mere dredg- ing would be attended with much delay and expense, as a great quantity of the rock would have to be blasted and dredged. It would take at least six years, whereas the whole of the works proposed could be carried out in about two years. The plan proposed would diminish the velocity of both flood and ebb tide, assist the traffic, and decrease the amount of dredging in the canal. The learned counsel next directed attention to ft clause by which the Company propose that notwith- standing the provisions of the Act of 1885 the tidal and other waters of the Weaver, which shall hereafter flow into the Canal, may beallowed to flow into the estuary of the Mersey at some point above the present outfall of the Weaver and at any time within four hours after any period of high water in the Mersey at Warrington Bridge. In this connection he described a dam, sluices, and other works that are to be created in the neighbour- hood of Warrington. The result of these and other works would be that quantities of water now flowing from the Canal into the estuary over the Eastham sluices and through the Weaver sluices would be dis- charged through nes+ sluices at Lower Walton, and that the water would be really more effective in the estuary for scouring purposes. The present system of inflowand outflcw was a mere oscillation,but by means of the new works a circulation would be established, the water entering at Eastham, swinging round at Walton, and running down the estuary. In order to secure this cir- culation the retardation of the Weaver waters was most important. 'He informed the Cornmittee of the trouble the Ship Canal Company had had with Warrington on the subject of dredging operations, and contended that matters would be much improved by the plan proposed. The Mersey Docks Board objected that the effect of raising the level in the tidal portions of the Canal would be to increas e the reduction of the tidal capacity of the estuary brought about by existing works. It was also objected that by the diversion of the channel and the construction of the new cut and dam at Walton a 'considerable length of the Mersey at the head of the ;estuary would be cut off from the flow and ebb of the tide and that the tidal capacity of the estuary would be diminished at a most important part. Further, that the alteration with respect to the discharge of the waters from the Weaver would seriously diminish the beneficial effect on the estuary the flow from the Weaver sluices was intended to secure. The learned counsel traversed these contentions, and remarked that the interests of the estuary itself might safely be left to the care of the Conservators.

Counsel for the Acting Conservator (Mr. Fitzgerald) stated that he should not take any active part in the discussion of the preamble of the bill, but should the Committee pass the preamble the Acting Conservator would suggest such clauses as miTht appaar necessary for the protection of the great public interests involved in the navigation of the estuary. Mr. Moon (representing the Mersey Docks Board) : That does not soundla very convenient proposal to make Mr. Balfour Browne said that at any rate he protested against the Docks Board assuming the position of the Conservator. The whole object of the dam was to dis- chargathe water at such apoint that the scouring action would be maintained at its maximum, and the plan adopted had been successful both at Richmond on the Thames and at Glasgow. Dealing with the petitions of the Warrington Cor- poration and various Warrington traders, Mr. Balfour Browne said that the opposition of those parties was not really directed against the merits of the bill, but was entirely raised upon extraneous matters. He believed he was right in saying that the Corporation of Warring- ton were thoroughly alive to the Importance to the borough and to the traders of the execution of the pro- posed works, but as regarded the traders he did not think their opposition was bona-fide. They were opposing now because they wanted the Ship Canal Company to give up the benefit they got in the Court, of Appeal and to go back to Mr. Justice Byrne's judg- ment, which was in favour of the traders. What they said in effect was " Let us have the benefit of Mr. Justice Byrne's decision, although it has gone by the board, and then we will support your bill." Some of the petitioners had actually expressed themselves in favour of the Company's proposals, and that being the case their opposition obviously was not on the merits of the scheme. Having briefly referred to other peti- tions against the bill, including those of the Shropshire Union Canal, the Salt Union, and others, Mr. Balfour Browne proceeded to call evidence. The first witness was Mr. W. Hunter, chief engineer of the Ship Canal Company, who gave engineering details of the proposed works. He said that in the last ten years there had been a phenomenal increase in the size of steamers. When the Ship Canal was designed there were comparatively few vessels which could not have navigated a depthof 26ft., but now the limitations imposed by a depth of 26ft. were a serious discount to the value of the canal. There were two or three firms at the present time who were anxious to use the port of Manchester, but many of their steamers- could not come Up the canal on a less depth than 28ft. As regarded the raising of the water level of the canal, he did not think there ever was such an important operation which could be brought about by such simple and inexpensive methods. He had no doubt that the works proposed would be of great benefit to the trade of the Ship Canal,of enormous benefit to the traders in Warrington. and that the effect on the estuary of the Mersey, if anything at all, would be beneficial. The Cimmittee adjourned until Thursday. Mr. T. S. Mr. Steel said the question of there was what appeared to him to be a state of things the wisdom or unwisdom of making application was which was little, if anything, short of a great public a debatable one. The application was granted without ' urther discussion.

- In cross-examination by Mr. on behalf of the Corporation and traders of Widnes, the witness denied that the works proposed in this bill would affect Widnes and contended that it would be unfair to impose on the Canal Company the obligation to maintain the river at Widnes in its present condition. • Sir Benjamin Baker, C.E., gave evidence in favour of the Biil. It was his opinion the raising of the water level of the canal by two feet would not injuriously affect the estuary or any other interest. The proposed works at Warrington simply meant bringing the works up-to-date, and the result would be entirely beneficial. Mr. W. H. Wheeler, engineer to the Boston Docks and Harbour Commissioners, also gave evidence in support of the Bill.

Sir J. Verdi; trustee of the River Weaver, also sup- ported the Bill. He had no objection to the raising of the water level of the Weaver. It would be an advan- tage to the Canal Company to give them a reserve of water for sluicing which would benefit the River Mersey.

div.head: THF WESLEYAN DISTRICT SYNOD.
div.p: THF WESLEYAN DISTRICT SYNOD.
Visit to Warrington.

It is nine years since the Synod of the Liverpool District was last held in this town. Since then the Wesleyans have advanced considerably in number and in influence throughont the country. The increase in membership, judged by the exacting standard of the class meeting, exceeds 6,000 during the last twelve months. There are wellnigh 200 can- didates for the ministry to be examined at these district synods, which are held almost simulta- neously throughout British Methodism. We under- stand that about 120 ministers are expected to attend at Bold-street Wesleyan Church on Tuesday morning next, and they will continue in session on the Wednes- day and Thursday. The Wednesday is known as "layman's day,"and circuit ste wards and other dele- gates will then swell the numbers to almost 300. Members of Parliament, heads of schools, prominent business men drawn from town and city, together with agriculturalists of Lancashire, Cheshire, North and Mid-Wales, will meet together to transact the busi- ness of this great church. Luncheon is to be served in the Bold-street schoolroom at 10 o'clock. The public gatherings at Bold-street and Bewsey-road have been well announced by placard, and large congregations are anticipated to hear the selected' speakers. The official preacher, the Rev. Dr. Burton of Lytham, is the writer of the volume of St. Luke in the Expositor's Bible and has lately written a pleasing hymn for the use of Wesley Guilds. It is to be hoped that the weather may be propitious next week and that the Wesleyan visitors may 'enjoy their stay in the neigh- bourhood of the good old town.

div.head: SHIP CANAL AND THE MERSEY.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL AND THE MERSEY.

With regard to the upper estuary of the Mersey, Mr. Hunter said that the Liverpool people had never done a stroke of work for it. If the Manchester Ship Canal hadnever been made, fourteen million cubic yards of sludge which had been removed from the canal and its approaches would have found a natural resting place in the estuary of the Mersey. With reference to the deepening of the canal between Latchford and Manches- ter, during the two years which would be occupied in the works lower down the dredging operations on the section named could be completed. Those operations would present no difficulties. Dealing with the petitions presented • against the Bill, Mr. Hunter observed that large as were the interests which centred in the port of Liverpool, the interests shich centred in the port of Manchester were much larger. They could, however, both "live." if there was one place more than another which the Ship Canal had saved from extinction that place was Ellesmere Port. The Company were willing to offer any reason- able safeguards to the Warrington Corporation to ease their apprehensions. He believed that the proposed works would be of enormous benefit to the borough of Warrington as a whole. They would give the town a new start. It would be possible to proceed with the other parts of the scheme without the Warrington works, but he was convinced that neither the Warring- ton Corporation nor the traders wished to see the works abandoned. As regarded the traders of Warrington— Messrs. Crosfield and others,—there was nothing what- ever in the bill which would prejudicially affect the interests of the petitioners. The tidal portion of the canal, in your opinion, must be raised if the canal is to continue to prosper ?—lf these works are not carried out the canal must cease to make progress. We cannot stand still, and if we do not go forward we must go back. The scheme can be carried out without injuring a single person on earth, and greatly to the benefit of a big manufacturing district. In cross-examination by Mr. J. D. Fitzgerald, on be- half of the Mersey Docks Board, Mr. Hunter said he agreed that the maintenance of the tidal capacity of the estuary of the Mersey was of great importance. The tidal flow of the canal would be diminished, but he was not touching the tidal area of the estuary. He admitted that the increased depth between Ea,stham and Latch- ford (21 miles) could be got by dredging, and would cost very little more than the proposed work. It would not, however, bring about the improvement to naviga- tion which was so necessary. The witness was also cross-examined by Mr. Hughes, appearing for three traders of Warrington.. The inquiry was adjourned. YESTERDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.
WARRINGTON DEMANDS WITHDRAWAL OF CLAUSES. MR. HUNTER ASTONISHED. WISHES TRADERS WOULD KEEP TO THE RIVER.
The Ship Canal Bill was further: considered yeater, day.

Mr. W. H. Hunter, engineer to the Manchester Ship Canal Company, was recalled and was further cross- examined by Mr. Hughes, K.C., on behalf of the War- rington traders. He admitted that if these works pre- judiced the navigation of the river that would affect the Warrington Traders. He wished the Warrington traders would use the river alto- gether and not the Canal. He would be glad to see the last of them. He contended that these !proposed works would be a great advantage to the traders of Warrington, not only by making it possible for the company to maintain a depth of eight feet of water in the river and reducing the velocity at tidal times, but also by removing the sewage which now seriously affected the quality of the water for the pur- poses of the condensing machinery. Mr. Hughes said the traders whom he represented took a different view of the matter. They thought they would get no advantage, and would run considerable risks. They would be prepared to withdraw their opposition if the promoters would withdraw these clauses. They wished to have these clauses withdrawn. The witness said that having regard .to what had already passed he heard that statement with unbounded astonishment.

In answer to questions by the Chairman, the witness added that these works at Warrington would enable the Canal Company to carry out their obligations and would be more economical than the present dredging opera- tions. He quite admitted that these works had no effect on the main object of the bill, which was the rising of the water in the canal by two feet. The old Walton Lock would hold up the water in the canal as much as was required. Mr. Wedderburn, K.C., representing Sir G. Greenall and Mr. Forbes Lankester representing the Hon, Ellinor and the Hon. Elizabeth Wilson Patten and Mr. J. St. Vigor Fox reserved their cross-examination, stating that an agreement with the promoters was probable. Mr. Balfour Brown, K.C., on behalf of the promoters agreed to submit arbitration clauses for the protection of the Salt Union and the Shropshire Union. Cross-examined by Mr. Hutchinson on behalf of the Warrington Corporation, the! witness said he was willing to give the Corporation all reasonable safeguards. In his opinion there would be no silting in the river above the diversion except at times of flood. If there was he would undertake to dredge the river. He was pre- pared to put in the Bill provisions that the Company should maintain the same facilities for navigation that existed at the present time. In his opinion the raising of the level of the river would not affect the condition of the subsoil water at Warrington. The sewage scheme prrposed in the Bill would maintain the present satura- tion level, and that would be a benefit to Warrington. He did not think that the saturation level would 'be raised if it could be shown it could be raised. He would be prepared to leave it to anarbitrator if they I could not agree to say whether the company should carry out such drainage works as would maintain the present minimum saturating level. As to the construc- tion of the new main to take the sewerage to a point below the dam, no doubt a certain cost would be thrown on the Corporation for 'lumping, but he did not think it would be .£1,600 a year. The Warrington Corporation were under a promise to the Local Government Board to carry out a scheme for treating their sewage and the proposal in the Bill was practically an instalment of that scheme. He did not think it an unfair propor- tion that the Company should be recouped for any expenditure until the scheme as a whole was undertaken. There was no provision in the bill which authorized the discharge of the Warrington Sewage below the dam. He admitted that it would be a serious thing if the Corporation were stopped after these works had been constructed and vested in them.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBALL. By " Ovalist"

Warrington was a sad and chastened town on Sat- urday. There were no brass bands and no conquering heroes—only hundreds of quiet and subdued men , making their way homeward from the various stations They had relied upon the Cup coming home and were prepared to rejoice accordingly. Instead, there was another slip, and the Cup remained in Halifax. I have met local enthusiasts who candidly confess that War- nngton's failure on Saturday was the greatest dis- appointment of their lives, and I can well believe them. Somehow you could not help feeling confi- dent on Saturday, for the sun shone exhilaratingly and everybody seemed to wish Warrington well at Sal- ford. The men themselves were in the pink of conch- tivn and there appeared nothing to stop their triumphant career—except the other team ! And alas! they did. with a vengeance.

Though defeated, Warrington were not disgraced and lam not without hope of seeing them land the Northern Union Cup yet. Oily a little bit of luck was nquired to turn the scale on Saturday, but it was denied. There is no getting away from the fact however, that Halifax were the superior team on the day's play. They had mapped out a plan of campaign which they pursued to the very letter, and by really remarkable forward play the succeeded in bottling up the cleverer men opposed to them most effectively: The Halifax tactics came as no surprise. It was generally expected that they would rely on the old-fashioned cup-tie Methods, but no one in Warrington imagined that they would be so successful in their endeavours. Warrington were so badly beaten forward that the rest of the team was almost wholly on the defensive and never got an opportunity of making class tell. In fact, a stranger witnessing the encounter would, I am sure, think that with a few individual exceptions Halifax were the superior team in all departments. That they are not we all know full well, but Warrington never looked more than a moderate side on Saturday. •

Were Warrington fairly beaten? That is the question in all parts of the town where men do con- gregate, and I think you would get more" Noes" than "Ayes." it ragged the Warrington supporters to see their men treated so unceremoniously, and there is a wide-spread feeling that the methods of the victors were not in accordance with the rules. One of the morning papers on Afonday stated that Halifax won the match by illegal scrummaging, and that is exactly what is said in Warrington. Unquestionably the rapid breaking-up, wheeling, and dribbling of the Halifax forwards had a doubtful look. There was more than a suspicion of wing-forward play, and the dribblers were often off-side. Still they had their, own sweet way. Rugby rules admit various styles of play- ing the game, and Halifax cannot be blamed for not playing the game that suited Warrington.

My own opinion is this. Often the scrummaging was.'" illegal "—or at any rate not as it ought to be. The " blue and white " forwards carefully avoided packing square or parallel with touch, and they ought. to have been compelled to do so. If they broke up more speedily and dribbled better than Warrington after racking fairly I should have had no fault to find. But no ! They laid themselves out to prevent honest scrummaging and succeeded only too well. Naturally amid all this argument and invective the poor referee has not emerged unscathed. I have the greatest res- pect for Mr. Smith and have often- admired his capa- bilities as a referee, but—and it is a.big " but -"—he was not himself on Saturday. He seemed both slow and uncertain—two failings I never knew him guilty of before. Hite was somewhat unstrung I sympathise with him, and I also feel that the " Jack " Smith we are so familiar with would not as a rule permit scrummaging of the kind that he passed unnoticed on Saturday. The Halifax men did as they liked, and. that was all they desired. It is unfortunate for War- rington and for Lancashire that they were not brought to book.

One thing is quite certain. The Northern Union will have to put its foot firmly upon this type of foot- ball if it intends to draw the public to its big games. Rough and tumble tactics may please the advocates of the good old Yorkshire style, but they put skill aid cleverness at a discount entirely. And it is an exposition of the finer points of the game that the crowd nowadays clamours for. If they see Rugby football degenerate into a scramble they will stop at home or go to the " socker " match.

Reverting to the match, Warrington were from first to last bustled out of their usual g,.me, but they stuck to their guns, and aggressive though the Halifax men were they did not look like getting points. Warring- ton, in fact, were the first to become nearly scorers. Ten minutes after the start Dickenson -rushed over near the posts with what appeared a perfectly fair try. It was disallowed, however, and the game proceeded fairly evenly, though the "blue and whites" controlled the scrums and prevented the ,Warrington backs mak- ing any headway. Thirty minutes had elapsed and there was no score, when an unfortunate thing for Warrington happened. Fish was attempting to -field the ball near the Warrington line when it bounced off his knee and over the line. From the subsequent 5 yards' scrummage Joe Riley received and rushed over in irresistible style, Hadwen kicking an easy goal,and giving HaFfax a lucky lead of 5 points. This they maintained until the interval.

On resuming hostilities Warrington infused more dash into their play and appeared stimulated by the cheering of the crowd all round the arena. Halifax tried in vain to drive them back, Fish eventually run- ning down and centreing so cleverly that Little was beaten by Davies who sc3rel near the corner. Fish missed the equalising goal, but his side played up desperately and it was not long before another score seemed certain. Isherwood was seen to break away after the first bout of smart passing seen in the match and run to the line with Harris in attendance. At the right moment he passed, Harris took the ball and the cheering had almost broken out when the wing man stumbled and fell a yard short of the coveted line. It was a cruel misfortune. A try and the lead seemed absolutely certain and so well were Warrington mov- ing at this point that they would probably have won if Harris had scored. Instead, they collapsed like a punctured tyre, and Halifax registered another try close on "time," thus winning by 8 points to 3 points. As I have already admitted they had far the best of the game, but there was just one period after War- rington had scored when it looked as if the tables would be turned. Harris's misfortune was the last straw, however, and WArrington lost a game in which they had been singularly unfortunate from start Us finish.

There were no conspicuous failures on either side. All the men engaged in the struggle did well accord- ing to their opportunities. Morley, the Halifax captain, was about the best man on the field. Be stood any amount of hard work and never made an error in the tactics required to give his side the victory. To crown all he scored the last try by a determined individual effort. Joe Riley at centre was also ill, great form,and Little,the full back,did himself justice both on attack and defence. On the Warrington side Boardman was frequently the most prominent indi- vidual, and it did not appear to be his fault that the forwards were so badly beaten in scrummage work. Davies and Hockenhall stood up to their work man- fully, checking many a rush and dribble by plucky saves. They had practically no opportunity of open- ing out the game, and the three-quarters were gener- ally defending, a sphere of action in which they are as good as the best. Fish was obviously in great form, and it was a source of great regret to the crowd that he got so few opportunities. Hallam was equal to Little, and did more work, one clearance which changed defence into attack earning for him a burst of cheering both spontaneous and enthusiastic.

• Cricket. Warrington continue their victorious career and Bolton had to admit defeat on Saturday. Our local wielders of the willow are to be congratulated upon the success which has attended their efforts so far this season. The, Bolton eleven are accounted a strong combination, and the Warringtonians did exceedingly well in beating them by a margin of 19. The feature of the home clubs' innings was the fine display by P. B. Hawtin. Not a faulty stroke marred his work, and he knocked up the top score of 37. J. Lynes, the professional, was next with 23 compiled in vigorous style. J. Caton placed a useful 17 to his credit.

The mainstay of the visitors was T. A. Howarth who, singular to state, ran up exactly the same total as Hawtin. The bowling analysis does not disclose any remarkable figures. Lynes, as usual, rendered valuable service and seven wickets fell at a cost of 40 runs. B.A. Connor, the captain, was responsible for three wicket for 23 runs.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

GROSS NEGLECT OF CIIILDREN. A case of gross neglect of children was heard by the Warrington magistrates on Monday, the defendant being Charlotte Williams, Clifton-street, Latchford. Mr. Browne prosecuted on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C., and said the case was brought practically for the protection of the woman herself. She had been under the observa- tion of Inspector Hackett since June, 1899, and had been warned from time to time. The children attended St. James's School, and Mr. Stans- field, the head master had, on many occasions been obliged to send them home, owing to their filthy and verminous condition. The othei children could not stand near them on account of the stench. The cause of the neglect was that the defendant was con- tinually drinking. Her husband was a very respectaole man. There were five young children, and one boy was suffering from hip disease through neglect. Defendant pawned the children's clothes in order to obtain drink. He (M-. Browne) asked the magistrates to carry out Sir John Bridge's idea and commit the defendant for the full term—ln the course of his evidence, defendant's husband said that on one occasion he found a pipe and tobacco under his wife's pillow. He himself did not smoke—The other witnesses included Mr. Stansileld, headmaster of St. James's School. The magistrates sentenced defendant to the maximum term of six months imprisonment. A WARRINGTON MAN'S "LARK "—NEWSPAPER SENSATIONALISM AND DRINK.

The Chief Fons Table il-nTolded—a. singular story to the Warrington magistrates on Monday, when Patrick Shaughnessy. of Eldon street, was charged 'with having attempted to commit suicide on Saturday evening.— Mr. Talbot asked for a remand for a week in order that prisoner's state of mind and body might be inquired into and in order to give him time to reflect upon " what an awful ass he had been." It seemed almost ridicu- lous to charge the prisoner with attempting to commit suicide, but he certainly went through the motions of it on Saturday night. He now explained that he did it for a "lark" and for the purpose of frightening hi S wife. He (Mr. Talbot) maintained that that was such a contemptible and mean thing to do that the magistrates would think it was sufficient cause to have his state of mind inquired into At 1.15 on Saturday afternoon prisoner came home from work partly the worse for drink. He went out again at 2.30, returned at 4.30, and commenced to quarrel with his wife about a summons he had received from the County Court. At five o'clock hehad his tea and then sent his step-daughter out for more beer. Ha asked for some writirr, paper and scribbled a few insolent sentences on it, to the effect that he was going to do "this that, and the other "to himself. He (the Chief Constable) did not believe the man had any intention of committing suicide. He was apparently suffering from an]over-dose of newspaper sensationalism and beer. Handing his spectacles to his wife, prisoner told her to take them to a Mr. Quigley adding "I hope he will have luck- with them." Later in the evening he went into an outbuilding fastened some wire rope round his neck and attazhed it to one of the beams. When found by his wife, he was partly black in the face. Producing the wire, the Chief Constable remarked that prisoner patronized local industries as far as possible. He took good care not to put his head far in the noose. He was handed over to the police, after having acted like a "tom-fool or a madman."—Prisoner was remanded to Strangeways for a week.

DISORDERLY BOYS.—Edward Bolton, 45, Haydock- street ; Albert Oakes, 55, Haydock-street ; Alfred Hogan, 16, Ashton-street; and John Litherland, 32, Howard- street; were fined 2s. 6d. each for having been dis- orderly in Legh's-yard on Sunday, April 24th.—P.C. Clough proved the case, and said the defendants and several others were playing football with a bundle of rags and paper and creating a great disturbance. STONE THROWING.—John Houghton, 7,Erwood-street James Quinn. junior, 17, Portland street; John Laff, junior, 16, Erwood street; William Laff, 16, rwood street ; and John Tansey, 11, Ervvood street; all very small boys,were charged with throwing stones in Bewsey street, on April 24th.—Messrs. Greening and Company's watchman stated that he s:.,cv the boys throwing stones. One of the missiles broke a pane of glass in a works window, doing damage to the extent of 15s. Stone- throwing was a daily occurrence in that quarter.—The Chief Constable said the damage done by quite small boys such as these was really remarkable. Works windows, or any other windows behind which there was no one to see the offenders, were considered legitimate prey, and were riddled with stones. He would with- draw the CilS3B against the two smaller boys (Tansey and one of the Laffs) on !Itheir parents promising to punish them.—The magistrates fined the other defend- ants 55., each. MiscELLANEous.—Catherine Doherty, 10, Dial-court, who made her 42nd appearance, was fined 55., for having made use of obscene language on April 24th.—James Quigley, 28, James street, who took part in the savage fight in Arpley fields reported last week, was bound over to keep the peace and ordered to pay costs for having icomrnitted a breach of the peace.--Patrick Richard Moran, of no settled abode, described by the Chief Constable as a loafer, was sent to prison for a month for begging in Bridge street on Saturday night. div.head: LATE ikill. JOHN HARRISON.
div.p: THE LATE ikill. JOHN HARRISON.

The M-.;;RTe-a-d—the following letter:—"l, Egypt- street, Warrington, 14th April, 1904. Dear sir,—l beg to acknowledge the receipt of yours of the 13th inst., with copy of resolution of condolence of your Council. Mr. Harrison was always very proud of his town, and of his long connection with its affairs, and this expression by the Council, coupled with the kind remarks of his Worship the Mayor and Mr. Alderman Bennett, in the Council Chamber, is extremely gratifying to his family. Rlferring to the kindly expression of the feelings of your brother officials and yourself which your letter contains, I should like to assure you that Mr. Harrison had a very deep sense of the many kindnesses he received from you all, during the long period of his official connection with municipal affairs.—Believe me, yours f kithfully, JOSIAH LONGLAND. J. Lyon Whittle, Esq., Town Clerk.

EDUCATIONAL MATTERS.—MORE SCHOOL ACCOMMODATION NEEDED. Alderman BENNETT moved a resolution to the effect that such recommendations of the Education Committee as required the confirmation of the Council be confirmed. He said he did not think it was necessary to say much at that stage of the meeting, at any rate. There were however, one or two matters to which he would briefly refer. One question related to the recommendation of sites, and another to the better accommodation for the training of pupil teachers. It was recommended that an authority should be constituted somewhat resemb- ling the Asylums Board, or the Joint Committee of the two County Councils in regard to the rivers. He hoped the whole question would be considered, and some definite scheme arrived at, by which the whole of the educational re- quirementa of the two counties of Lancashire and Cheshire would be met, utilizing the existing Trai.,ing Colleges as far as possible.On the question of additional school accommodation it was proposed, in order to meet the necessities of the case, that they should erect a temporary iron building, but the committee came to the conclusion that there would be no real economy in that course, and that it would be wise to proceed with the initial stage of the scheme, and that was approved. Within a comparatively short time they :.vould have to erect three new schools. but it did not necessarily mean immediately. They would proceed with the other schools as occasion required. In conclusion, the alder- man said he should like to add his testimony to the valuable services which had been rendered by the late Mr. William Jones, as head official of the School Attend- ance Department. He was for many years in the servica of the Corporation, and he nad been a faithful and zealous servant of the committee. (Hear, hear.)

Councillor ELLISON seconded. Councillor WILKINSON would like to give a word of warning to the Sites and Buildings Committee. Some- how or other he had got it into his mind that they were ratherrushing the matter unduly, and he would like to draw their attention to the report issued by the Direc- tor of Education for their approval. He did not think it would be advisable to read that report before the whole of the Council, because it would be to a certain extent divulging the working of that committee, and he would not agree to such a course. He thought, how- ever, the committee should carefully consider that report and look ahead in Warrington and not build on the spur of the moment or on the peremptory demand of the Board of Education. He hoped the committee would fully assure themselves that these schools they intended to build were really required, and not unduly rush the matter, considering the high rates in Warring- ton. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR said he was chairman of the Sites and Buildings Committee, and during the past twelve months he was sure they had not wasted much of the Corporation money. They were keeping in mind a good deal of what Councillor Wilkinson had said,andhe could assure him the question was in safe hands. Councillor WILKINSON: I ant glad to hear it. Alderman PIERPOINT said after the seriousness of the report. of his Majesty's Inspector of the schools, he thought the committee were quite justified in putting forward the necessity for building new schools. One point mentioned by therlnspector was that the schools were very often too far distant from the homes of the children, whilst a second point was that they must reckon that the overcrowded state of the schools kept a number of children in the streets. In the Inspector's journey around the schools he found two or three cases of this kind,and also the case of a man who was walking from one school to another unable to get admission for his child. That was the state of things in Warrington, and it was at once the duty of the eomraittee to take the matter in hand and the duty of the Council to help the committee in every way possible. Alderman SUTTON said it was quite decided that sooner or later they would have to provide new schools, and he thought it was quite right that the committee should take every opportunity of purchasing really favourable sites whilst they were obtainable, and not sacrifice the ratepayers' money by having to buy at in- creased figures just prior to building. Councillor ARTHUR PEACOCK said there were a lot of children under five years of age who helped to fill the schools, and if these were not there, there would be room. He thought the schools should not be anything like a nursing establishment. Several members pointed out that these scholars had to be accepted. Alderman BENNETT replying, said he could only reiterate the assurance that the committee, so far from rushing the matter, were moving slowly, and if it were at all possible without sacrificing the educational efficiency of the town and endangering the grants—a matter of three-fourths of the whole exnenditure—they would not have undertaken the work. It was, however, absolutely necessary as a point of duty to the rising generation, and in order not to lose this source of income. They had received a number of threats, and quite recently had been within an ace of losing some of their grants. He thought, with other speakers, that true wisdom, was to really look ahead, and secure land at reasonable prices where possible, and not to go blindly on until forced to involve themselves in in- creased expenditure at short notice. The motion was then carried. THE SCALE OE TEACHERS' SALARIES.

Ald-ei:nTan—liE-NTErr— -submitted the following resolu- tion :—" That the recommendations of the Eitication I Committee of the 21st March, 1901, having reference Ito the increases of teachers' salaries be confirmed." I The Alderman, in speaking to the motion. said he did I not think the observations that had been madehad been intentionally unfriendly to the committee, but such a =Me as had been adopted in referring the questions back to the committee placed them in a false position. This he attributed to some misapprehension, and added that the•details of the Education Committee were so multifarious that it ;vas impossible for a busy man to assimilate them. A scale of salaries had to be arranged for the teachers, and in view of the posi- tion in which they were placed pending the adoption of the scale, can3erl them as far back as April 23rd last year to pass a resolution that whatever scale was adopted should be retrospective to the Ist of April 1903. It had at that time become necessary to re-assure the teachers since they were threatened with wholesale resignations. On May 14th a scale for teachers, but not head teachers, was passed,and on February 11th a scale for head teach- ers was passed, and these by the earlier resolution became operative from the Ist of April, 1903. In One : or two cases there were rises which might seem anomalous, but they found some teachers, with all due : respect to those who had employed them, miserably , underpaid, and they could not do otherwise than place them on the same footing as other teachers who were • doing similar work. I In answer to Councillor Tinnion, Alderman BE'sxirrs ; said the scale had not reduced any salaries. ; The MAYOR said it was a misapprehension to think that the members of the Council who were on the I Education Committee were expected to father the mis- takes of that body in the Council. They, as members of I the Council, had to exercise their rights in another ;direction than by pushing the Education Committee's • mistakes through the Council. The estimates of 1993-4 were based upon the salaries paid at that time. The estimates for 1904-5 were on the increased'scale,so that if they paid the increase from 19031 there must be a deficit. The motion was then carried.
