THE STANDARD WAGE QUESTIO.T.
MESSRS. RHODES AND SON AND DIE PAIL CONTRACT. EXPLANATIONS BY COUNCILLORS JOHN EVANS AND STO rr.
INTERFERENCE BETWEEN MASTERS AND MEN. ALDERMAN SUTTON PROTESTS, AND THREATENS TO STOP AT HOME.

At a meeting of the Sanitary Works Committee, on April 13th, the Chairman reported that he had with- drawn from the Council minutes the resolution accept- ing the tender of Messrs. Thomas Rhodes and Son for galvanized pails on account of statements made at the Council meeting to the effect that Messrs. Rhodes did not pay the rate of wages recognised in the district. It was resolved that the Chairman sud Deputy Town Clerk be instructed to visit the works of Messrs. Thomas Rhodes and Son, at Stourbridge, to consider and report upon the whole question.—At a subsequent meeting of the Council, the report of the Chairman, Councillor Stott, and the Deputy Town Clerk on their visit to the works of Messrs. Thomas Rhodes and Son, of Stour- bridge, with reference to the question of the rate of wages paid by that firm to their workpeople was read, and after discussion thereon, it was resolved, that the tender of Messrs. Thomas Rhodes and Son, to supply 500 galvanized steel pails at 9s. 41d. each, and 500 ash- bins at 45. Ild, each, be accepted: Councillor JOHN EVANS, in moving the confirmation' of the minutes, explained that when the tenders for pails had been first gone into, the sub-committee recom- mended the lowest tender, Messrs, Rhodes and Son. Councillor Stott objected on the ground that this firm was not plying the regular wages of the district, and carried an amendment by which the tender of Messrs. Parkinson and Sweeney wae recommended. The Coun- cil referred this recommendstion back,ancl reconsidera- tion by the committee. led to Messrs. Rhodes' tender being again recommended, but it was thought advisable that they should get satisfactory information, and he was appointed to go to Stourbridge and make inquiries. Councillor Tinnion accidentally met Mr. Rhodes in the meantime,and informed him of the contemplated action, and Mr. Rhodes said he would be pleased to see the chairman of the committee, and also Mr. Stott. With Mr. Stott he visited the works, and they were allowed to question any workman they th Right fit, and were in- vited to inspect'the wages book. He could only say that he was perfe3tly satisfied that Messrs. Rhodes were paying the regular wages of the district, and he had pleasure in asking them to confirm the recommendation. He pointed out, however, that in the meantime they had had to purchase 290 pails as a matter of emergency from Messrs. Parkinson and Sweeney.
Councillor rtiOaNT3N : At a htgliar price? Councillor JOHN EvANs: Yes. Alderman SMETHURST formally seconded.

• Councillor PErmt PEACOCK said he understood that the tender had been accepted without the usual fair wages clause. Councillor Jon& Ev.vss &lid the contract6rs had to comply with the Standing Orders, and the contractshad been published in the usual way. The DEPUTY MAYOR said the Finance Committee had had a bill for the expenses of the deputation, and he thought that if they had been misled by wrong information, Councillor Stott should pay theta and not burden the ratepayers with the amount. (" No no.") Councillor STorr said he wished to speak on the matter. He folly agreed with what Councillor John Evans had said, and he was pleased to have had the opportunity of visiting the works. They were received very courteously, and he had also been given an oppor- tunity of going into the shop and conversing with the men. He had made a few notes of the remarks of Mr. Rhodes. _ _ _
Alderman SMETHURST : If you say you are satisfied what do you want to read notes for?

.—Councillor STOTT : If Alderman Smethurst persists, I'll read the whole of them. (Laughter.' Alderman Sm.urturasT : But you say you are satisfied. Councillor STOTT said he was not yet satisfied that Messrs. Rhodes and Sons wore plying the recognized rate of wages. He had seen and questioned several men but could not get a single answer except that they were perfectly satisfied. The men seemed to be afraid to answer any question, and he mentioned that fact to Mr. Rhodos, who selected one man and said "This man will willingly answ4v any question," but he also said that he was prejudiced in his favour. The only other man he was able to get to speak in any way whatever was a man who seemed to have a grievance against the men's union. All he said was that he would be sorry if he could not make more than 30s.a week. With regard to the men baying received notice of dismissal Mr. Rhodes agreed that it was to secure new conditions of labour. He also said there was no such rate as 30s. a week recog- nized in the district. The best wages he paid were from 24.5. to 325. per week. Mr. Rhodes had pointed out that the trade unions were very weak and were not recognized in that district, and had added that he was sorry that they were not strong enough to enforce a standard wage as that would prevent tile "cutting" of prices. Mr. Rhodes said he was p tying as much as other similar firms, but he also admitted that he did not know what other firms in the district were actually paying. Summing up the results, he said the men in thus being questioned had been placed in a very invidi- ous position, and could scarcely give information that would result in loss to their employers. The MAYOR : But we cannot be judges. _ _

C3l.ll2CiliOr ST3TT repeated that 393. was the recog- nized rate of wages in that district for. day av)rk, but 111 r. Rhodes said there was no recognized rate. He (Councillor Stott), however, had a letter from another firm in the district stating that foriron plate work they paid Gd. an hour for 60 hours a weak and he had other correspondarry and a signed statement from 12 work- men in tne district to the eff3ct that 303. was the recog- nized standard for that district. He moved an amend- ment that the recommendation be not confir:ned. Whilst the Mayor was asking for a seconder, Alderman SurroN rose with the remark "Oh, there is no seconder." The MANOR. : Let me conduct the business. The amendment remained without a seconder, sad it was lost.

Alderman SurroN said this was just the result of interference betwesn mister and men, and such a course could not fail to interfere with the success of the work- men. If a workman chose t 3 work for wages that were satisfactory to him why should he not have the right to do so. It was better to htve half a loaf than no bread.
A NIEMBER: That's not the minutes; we are not dis- cussing trades unionism. Alderman SMETHURST: We are discussing it. _ _

Alderman SUTTON said they wore certainly discussing it, and for the last half-hour they had been listening to nothing else. If they were going to have their monthly meetings turned into lecture rooms he should stop from coming to the Council at all. If they were going on in that way over the wages question there would soon be 3 time when there would be no work at all forthe work- men, and foreign competitors would get it. Councillor TINNION: Protection will save us. (Laughter.) Alderman SUTTON: We are not talking about protection. A MEMBER: Well, you are very near it. (Laughter.) Alderman SMETFIURST : Well protection will do it. The MAYOR: That is politics. Councillor Dons said he sympathized with Coun- cillor Stott, but was not sufficiently satisfied with whet he had said to second the amendment, but he felt that they ought to listen to what was said on such matters. Councillor Stott was the Trades Union representative and was entitled to speak on their behalf. Alderman SUTTON: But not to listen to lectures.

_ Councillor DODDS: Not altogether, but perhaps the "good old father" himself got a little wrong too. (Laughter.) Councillor A. Pr.A.cocK said the deputation should have got the information they were sent to get and have been thoroughly convinced. Councillor MAOINN said he objected to the principle, which he urged was opposed to the interests of the rate- payers. Their first duty was to consider the money of the ratepayers. Conneillor PENTHICRTON said he did not agree with Councillor Maginn's remarks. (Laughter.) He also contended that the fair wage clause materially helped employers of labour, since otherwise those paying good rates would find themselves thrown out of the market by nrices being cut. The MAYOR pointed out that the Standing Orders did not say who was to judge in these matters. The master accepted the contract, he signed the agreement, and with that they carried out all the formulm they had. On the evidence before them a judge would say that the case must fall to the ground. Councillor STorr : If it was brought before a judge I should have witnesses. I cannot bring witnesses here.

Al erman Surrox: Surely not over a matter like this. Councillor TINNION suggested that it would have been a fairer statement if Councillor Stott had said there was no trade union in the Stourbridge district for these men. _

Councillor STOTT : But there is. Councillor TINNION said it was probably something like the union of the printing trade in Warrington. There were two firms who paid union rates, but they did not employ anything like the bulk of the printers of the town. Councillor STOTT: There's no comparison at all. Councillor TINNION : Perhaps not, because the other case is worse. Councillor JOHN EVANS, in his reply, pointed out that in the Stourbridge district thore were no appren- tices employed in the trade. He was, however, con- fident that the firm was paying the standard rate. The trade union, he pointed out, had a very small member- ship. The minutes were then adopted. "A GROSS BLUNDER." COUNCILLOR TINNION AND CONCESSIONS TO PROPERTY OWNERS.

The Paving and Sewerage Committee submitted a resolution to the effect that the Town Clerk apply to the Local Government Board for sanction to borrow £6.000 for private street works. Councillor TINNION proposed the confirmation of the committee's minutes and remarked that the Borougk Surveyor had submitted plans, specifications, &c., for he forming and paving of several streets, and that was what part of the £G,OOO was required for. Other streets

were to be made ready and would take no the remainder of the money. They could not go any further with the streets until the Government la3pec.tor had been down, but as soon as things were in order the work would be carried out. Councillor ROBERTS seconded.

Councillor STOTT hoped-aie-Carrying out of the pav- ing of the streets would not be the same as in the case of Elaine-street which had been exoavated and then left for nearly twelve months before the paving was done. Councillor TINNION sad that was not altogether the committee's fault, but was partly because of the diffi- culty in getting sAtts, &c., at reisonahle prices. The Committee seemed to stand between the ratepayer or householder on one side and the property owner ol the other and they tried to do their best for both. (Hear, hear.) Personally he had never agreed with the resolu- tion which gave seven years to the property owners to pay the bills for street making,and he thought it was one of the grossest blunders the Girporation ever made. It had done in.)re, in his opinion,to hamper the Committee in their work than anything else. At a meeting of the Electricity and Tramways Committee the members considered the Electrical Engineer's report on the "one man" cars,which was not favourable to the introduction of such cars ,when it was resolved thtt the matter be left -in the hands of the Engineer for farther iniairy; anl also that a charge of not less than El 103. per weak be made for the use of advertisements in the cars not exceeding two innumber and not exceeding 18in. by 221 n. in size.—The Tram- ways Manager reported that he had given 16 men a week's notice to terminate their services, and it was decided that each man should be given an extra week's pay. The report of the Mana,gar as to the running of the cars on the Llngford rout 3 ws approved.—ft wis resolved that the Nlayor and the Cb.airman beappninted to attend a Conference to be held at the Westminster Pal :V.30 Hotel on Tuesday;the 19th inst.. to consider the decision ofia committee of the House'of Lords in giving a private Tra.rnw.ty-Company running powers over a Corporation's lines.

- The Chairman, Deputy Oh-Lim-yin, and Councillors Evans, Tinnion and Pemberton were appointed a com- mittee to consider and report on the utility and cost of the working of the destructors at Howley. At a meeting on April 23, the report of the Engineer giving the result of the tests made by him of the four samples of coal selected by thA Committee was read ; and instructions givcn that if the Engineer finds it necessary to purchase any coal ho be authorised to obtain his requirements from Messrs. Fletcher, Burrows and Co. at the prices quoted by them.—The Engineer presented a report showing that economy could be effected by the use of mechanical stokers and it was resolved that tenders should be obtained for the supply of mechanical stokers to boilers Nos, 1. 3,4, and 6. It was also resolved that the Engineer be authorized to lay a main for the purpose of supplying current to a 30 horse power motor belonging to the Whitecross Co. Limited, at Quay Fold Pumping Station. Alderman SMETHURST' proposed the adoption of the minutes. He was pleased to say that of the men who had been discharged nine of them had been found situa- tions in various places, and they expected that in a very short time they would have found places for the rest. (Hear, hear.) With reference to the 30 high pressure motor—(latighter) Councillor TIN. NION : Horse power, you mean. (Laughter.) Alderman SmETHuRsT : Yes, high pressure horse power. (Renewed laughter.) Continuing, the ALDERMAN, referring to the laughter at the slip of the tongue, said it was all very well for the Council to laugh, but they had not the difficulty of managing such an important committee as he had to look after. The MAYOR interposed with a remark that Alderman Smethurst should keep to the minutes. Alderman SMETHURST : I am not going to al w you, even if you are the Mayor of Warrington, to p ut me down. Continuing, he said it was not fair for he

me:ubers ta keep making jarring r3rnarks. The com- mittee instead of playing arid" larking," were working hard and trying to make some profit. (Hear, hear.) In would cost about £l5 to lay the cable to the motor he had referred to, but they would gat a good return f) r their money. They were not going to spend the rate- payers' money for the purpose of satisfying a few people, and AO far as their committee was concerned if they spent any money they must see a profit for it. The "one main" motor would mean a saving of £5 a week at least on etch car. They had ordared two of these motors at Halifax-

Councillor STOTT : They won the cup. (Laughter.) Councillor TINNION : They can afford it. Alderman SAE NIURST said he thought that if they had one of the motors they could just about clear the expenses of the Longford route. With reference to the mechanical stokers, they not only reduced the con- sumption of coal, but caused much less smoke. The committee were going to try and show the people of Warrington that they could work live or six boilers without turning out a very large volume of smoke. The saving already affected by the use of the na.chanical stoker for one boiler was about £3 a day. They could therefore SO9 what a large amount would be saved by the use of the stokers on all the boilers. Coun3illor WILICINSON secon•led the adoption of the minutes, and pointed out that the mechanical stokers were not an experiment. They had one of them work- ing, and it was using slack at Gs.2d, per ton and keeping up the same pressure as was obtained from the other boilers which required coal at 12s. 101 a ton. Their coal bill was £2,030 last year, so that they would effect a saving of about .£1,20J by having these mechanical stokers, which would cost £930. C)uncillor PE NIBEIZTJN said it was not often that he s§oke in praise of an olficial, but he thought a great deal of the credit for the change in the consumption of coal was due to the engineer. H.e(Councillor Pemberton) had kicked against the enormous coal expenditure several times, and urged that slack could be used. Mechanical stokers hart been usel in this district for five years, and ncr.v this change on the part of one or two with reference t coal was rather surprising him. They had been buying coal in the department for tic) years without a contract at a cost of 12s. a ton. Councillor WthluAoN: What has that to do with the question at issue.

Coiacillor PEMBEEtr%)N: Socno people wanted to cry me down a few weeks ago wh3n I brought it before the Council. Nov they have come round to my way of thinking. Continuiug he expressed pleasure that the cotnmittee were puting their shoulders to the wheel and trying to make things pay. The engineer had effected many savinss and he (Councillor Pemberton) was pleaselto give honour where honour was due. Councillor Wirarssos explained that they could not obtain the sameamount of pressure fro:u slack unless they used the mechanical stokers.

Alderman BENNETT did not think the Ceuncil gave Ald3rman Smethurst quite fair trettmeat, and he was afraid they were apt to treat him with a jocularity which was as unbecoming to the dignity of the Council as it was unfair. He thought great credit was due to Alderman Smethurst and the vice-chairman and mem- bers of the Electricity Committee for th 3 improvements they had made, and he was pleased to see they had taken up things which he (Alderman Bennett) had often advocated amidst the same rude interruptions which greeted his friend Alderman Smethurst. (Laughter.) fie had always maintained that by the use of proper appliances th?re might be an enerraTas economy in the consumption of coal and a dimunttion in the dense black smoke which was such a source of trouble and inconvenience. His view had now been confirmed by a stern practical basin4ss man (Alderman Smethurst) and a practical business committee.lt seemed like a fairy tale that the mechanical stokers would save 23 a day,but even if they did not save% penny the improvement/ would be worth while if it diminished the smoke nuisance. It would also be an encouragez-neat to manufacturers to adopt the same methods. He thought the Council might be told what approximately was the result of the working of the Electricity and Tramways Department for the year just ended.

Councillor BurtioN suggested that, as the Council now had a public analyst, it would be more satisfactory for him to test the coal samples. He would rather rely on his decision than on that ()fettle engineer testing from the boilers. With reference to the mechanical stokers the saving they were said to effect.was a revelation to him. It seemed to point out that the'Y had been radically wrong before in not availing themselves of that economical method. He bad, however, heard of private firms who had these stokers, and they had come to the conclusion that they could raise more steam by hand firing. He was not at all satisfied with the information which had been given. He would like more proof ,before they spent that £9OO. Councillor PETER PE A.COCK said that with reference to the tram service on the Longford route, he thought they ought to consider the r itepayers there. Their ser- vice of cars had been curtailed 50 per cent., and they had no workmen's cars. The public were complaining strongly that they were not receiving preper attention. He had w. itten to the committee but had received no reply. Tin NlA.Yoasi,id that mater would receive the atten- tion of the committee at the next meeting. Councillor STOTT referred to the appointment of the gayor and Chairmin to attend the conference at West- cainsi,er Palace Hotel, and said he thought they, as a , Council, ought to take every means of resisting private companies being allowed to take advantage of munici- pal undertakings. (Hear, hear.) Councillor JAMES EVA.NS inquired how long the mechanical stoker had been in use.

The NIA-Yoa pointed out that if the Council objected to the stokers being obtained they could take action when the tenders came up for consideration. Councillor MINION said he was afraid Councillor Wilkinson looked at things from a too rosy point of view. He (Councillor Tinnion) had no 'hesitation in saying that the use of the stokers would reduce the coal bill, but whether it would reduce it £9OO or £1,200 as Councillor Wilkinson said-he very much doubted. They would certainly decrease the smoke nuisance, but Alderman Bennett must remember, in his desire to get rid of the smoke, that there were some processes and trades in which it was almost impossible to prevent smoke and the law recognized that it was impossible. It should be borne in mind ,that the firms which made the most smoke generally paid the most wares. Councillor LORD pointed out with referen-ce to Long- ford trams that two cars (ten minutes service) took £22 a week. One car (fifteen minutes service) took £l7 15s so that there was a loss on the receipts of £4 ss. There was a saving on wages and running of £9 10s. and that' left a net gain of £sss. per week, on the fifteen minutes service. Councillor DODDS Said the hilarity which had been exhibited that evening was not because they had any fault to find with Alderman Smethurst, or wished to laugh at him. He was the chairman of an important committee, and he realized that fact. He came to the meetings of the Council prepared to anticipate any possible objection; they admired his almost juvenile in- terest in the questions coming before the committee ; they enjoyed his enjoyment, and that was why they laughed. He (Councillor Dodds) suggested, in order to save ;time in future,that the alderman should not antici- pate the objections that were likely to be made, but, like the other chairmen of committees,state his case as briefly as possible and then reply to the criticisms of the members atthe close of the discussion. If that were done it would save the time of the Connell, and there would be less hilarity. (Hear, hear.)

Alderman SMETHURST said he was much obliged to those who assisted him in carrying out the work of the committee. Really so much time was wasted talking about a few refuse buckets that when it came to the minutes of an important committee they could not listen while he referred to them properly. He had intended merely proposing the minutes and sitting down. but he had to refer to the extra matters he had mentioned. He would have got through what he had to say in half the time if he had not been interrupted. He would sooner go two or three miles in the other direc- tion than come to the Town Council. In reply to Alderman Bennett he was sorry to say that for the year ended March 31st the tramways showed a balance on the wrong side of £640, that including sinking fund and interest and all expenses. The Electric Works had made a profit of about £l5O, but there was a debit balance from the previous year of about £5OO, so that they now hada debit balance of £340 13s. He hoped next year it would be the other way. (Hear, hear). The minutes were approved. GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of this committee a re;Oin-ti-eii, passed at a public meeting, was submitted requesting the Council to petition Parliament against any interference with the discretion of licensing justices, when it was resolved that no action be taken in the matter; also that the bylaws under the Employment of Children Act, 1903, as allowed by the Secretary of State, be now formally confirmed and adopted.—A letter was read from Mr. r. T. Williams, district goods manager of the London and North-Western Railway Company, inform- ing the Council of the improved service of trains to and from Warrington. It was agreed that the thanks of this meeting be tendered to Mr. Williams for his continued efforts to improve the train service.—The Town Clerk reported that the Cheshire Electricity and Power Gas Bill had been rejected by a committee of the House of Commons. The minutes were confirmed. A discussion on the proposed widening of Warrington Bridge is reported elsewhere. COUNCILLOR MAGINN AND THE ACCEPTANCE OF TENDERS. Councillor 11,1AGI:s1N had given notice of his intention to move: "That it be an instruction to each committee of the Corporation when they have obtained tenders for goods, or for labour required, or both, to accept the lowest tender except only in cases where any person tendering carries on business within the borough and in which the committee for special reasons may con- sider it advisable not to accept the lowest tender, and that in accepting any tender each committee shall require the person tendering to give the names of two responsible sureties who shall guarantee the due execu- tion of the contract. That the standing orders be amended so as to give effect to the above resolution." Councillor MAGI said he would prefer to adjourn his motion till the next meeting. Listening to that Council for two hours drove away the little bit of wit that he had. (Laughter). It was too heavy a job to speak tg that motion at that hour. He had seen one councillor there asleep for the last fifteen minutes (laughter), and he might snore if he took that oppor-

div.p: MRS. RILEY TESTIFIES.
Mrs. Riley, of Clashmore, Dornoch, Scotland, is a strong witness for Dodd's Kidney Pills, the remedy that has caused so much talk recently by its wonderful Cures. - _

Mrs. Riley says:—" I have great faith in Dodd's Kidney Pills and would advise anyone suffering from rheumatism to try them. I am sure they would be grate- ful for the result. When a child I fell on the ice and hurt my spine, and I have been weak in my back ever since. I am now over fifty years of age and I have suffered a great deal of pain. Sometimes I have been able to work, and at other times my strength would all leave me the moment I tried to do any of my ordinary household work. The rheumatism came in my arms and caused me great suffering. "I began to use Dodd's Kidney Pills and in a short time my arms Were quite free from rheumatism and I felt my strength increasing, so that I kept on using the pills. lam feeling much stronger now, and I know that besides curing my rheumatism, Dodd's Kidney Pills have greatly improved my general health. They are splen- did."

to mention. It xv,-)uld be within the recollection of some of the members that the Clerk and himself were appointed as the committee's representatives at the conference of Lancashire Assessment Committeesjin re- spect to the proposed Government legislation in the direction of altering the law of valuation. They would probably know:that the Government Bill was read a first time and put down for second reading last ruesday.So far as he could (-rather from the Press, the Bill had not been read a second time. Hastily, in view of the first reading having taken place unexpctedly, the conference wag convened on Monday last. The Clerk and himself atten- ded, and it was on that he wanted to say a word. The avowed nun of the Bill was the promotion of uniformity of valuation, but it was open to doubt whether the Bill would secure that end. The recommenda- tions of the Royal Commission on local taxation which sat for several years had not been accepted nor had their suggestion that the geographical County of Lancashire should form a special area on the lines Of the Metropolitan area. At present there were 30 Union Assessment Committees in the geographical County of Lancashire and if the administrative county were divided into committee districts, as the Bill suggested might be done, the number of assessment committees in the area of Lancashire would be actually increased. That, obviously would go against rather than in favour or securing uniformity of valuation. At the conferencq,differences of opinion emerged but ultimately it was unanimously agreed that strong representations be made to the Prime Minister, the President of the Local Government Board and a copy of the representa- tion sent to every Lancashire member, deprecating hasty action on such an important subject and asking that the second readinr, might be deferred until time had been given for the full consideration by the authorities which would be affected of the provisions of the Bill. The reason he (the Chairman) mentioned the matter was in order to ask the committee to approve of the action of the clork•and himself in atteßding on their behalf and to empower them to attend an/ adjourned meeting. The nhole thing had been done"' rather a hurried way and as prompt action might be desirable, he thought the committee would empower them to join with other Lancashire Assessment Cour mittees in pressing upon the Government and their Lancashire members such amendments and modifications as would be likely to secure greater efficiency of administration and to secure that any legislative changes should be beneficial. It might be necessary to take joint action by Lancashire unions before the nest meeting.

Mr. kATHER proposed that the Chairman and Clerk be empowered to attend the conference. He welcomed the Bill because there was such a great difference in the rating in different townships and a great difference between the county basis and the local basis. Mr. DAVIES seconded. Mr. FORSHAw supported and said it was rarely thel got reports from deputathns. The resolution was passed.

A meeting of this committee was held vesterda—y• Mr. A. J. Jolley presided. There were also Present : Messrs. S. Davies, T. H. Ashcroft, R. Forshaw, Houghton, G. 11/father, J. Billings, and .T. C. Sutton (clerk), Wm. H.! Woodcock (assistant overseer), and W Owen (valuer). THE GENERAL WOLFE.

Councillor ROGEES appealed against the assessment of the General Wolfe, Church-street, which stood at £165 gross Ind £l4O rateable. He stated that the pre- vious owner, Mrs. Brundrett, was rated at £76, and he would remind the committee that Mrs. Brundrett was a brewer, and had wholesale and retail profit. Mrs. Brundrea did not care twopence for her retail profit. She got the wholesale profit and could afford to give what would ruin him. He could not afford to pay the present assessment. After his last appeal he went to the brewery And told them that the house would not stand the expenses, and he could never pay it. Mr. Down thereupon reduced the rent by £3O. He would also remind the committee that customers who used to call at the house, now went past on the tramcars, and he could not expect them to get off to oblige him. His rent was now £lOO.He had stabling for eleven horses,but he had never had eleven horses in the stables since he had been there. His trade had gone down independent of bad trade.
Councillor DAVIES moved, and Councillor Ashcroft seconded that a reduction be made from £165 gross to £l5O but the proposition was lost. _ _

Councillor itoaEns was called into the room and the chairman informed him that the committee could not see their way to reduce the assessment. The committee were tagreed that if Mr. Rogers saw his landlord and the rent was reduced the committee would consider that as satisfactory evidence to justify them in reconsidering the case. Until Mr. Rogers did that the committee could not interfere.

Councillor ROGERS said he would go to the brewery and endeavour to get a further reduction. If he could not, the only course open to him would be to appeal to Quarter Sessions. He believed his case would be con- sidered there.

The CHAIRMAN: It has been considered here. Councillor ROGERS: I mean no disrespect to this committee, but I believe it will be gone into fairly at the Quarter Sessions. I shall be well represented and I belilve they will form the same opinion that I have formed, that I am over-assessed. The CHAIRMAN: You see the brewery people first to get a reduction of rent. Failing that, you must give due notice.
THE KINGS ARMS. THE EFFECT OF A MUSIC LICENCE.

Mr. J. W. PLINSTON made an appeal on behalf of Mrs. Elizabeth Plinston of the Kings Arms, Buttermarket- street, the assessment of which stands at £9O gross £76 10s. rateable. He pointed out that since the music licence had been taken away the takings had been about half what they were formerly. The trade was now only about twelve barrels a month. The rent was £4O and Mrs. Plinston had been promised a reduction—Mr. Billinge : This reduced trade owing to the withdrawal of a music licence must prove that the people are musically inclined in that district. (Laughter.) It was decided to postpone any alteration of the assessment until the brewers had reduced the rent. THE BAY HORSE.

Mr. J. WI. PLIssToN then appealed --against the assess- ment of the Bay Horse Inn, Winwick-street, of which he is tenant. The assessment is £9O gross and £76 10s. rateable. During the last twelve months, he said, his takings had been from £lO to £l2 a week less. He now sold 7 barrels a week and about 5 gallons of spirits. His rent was £7O a year. The CHAIRMAN: What you have been telling us rather tends to show that your assessment has been too low. If your assessment were £95 net it would be more in harmony with others. If the committee altered it at all, they would raise it. The CLERK: You had better withdraw your appeal. The appeal was withdrawn. THE VALUATION BILL. STATEMENT BY THE CHAIRMAN.

div.head: "I REALLY MUST USE VI-COCOA."
div.p: "I REALLY MUST USE VI-COCOA."

Thousands of men and women, after reading the particulars published respecting the merits of Dr- Tibbles' Vi-Coooa, have been induced to become regular drinkers of this popular food beverage. But many have said to themselves," I really must use Vi-Cocoa," and have failed to do so. Why? There is no more agree- able and inexpensive cocoa on the market. A 9d. packet or a 9d. or Is. 6d. tin is value indeed, for Vi-Cocoa does all that it is claimed to do, and there is no so-ealled concentrated or foreign cocoa in the world to equal it. It is highly nutritious, imparts stamina to the systems is refreshing to the weary brain-worker, and recuper- ates the body after physical fatigue.
Girls' Club Silver Street.

This club, which has been doing a good work during the winter months, was the scene of a happy gather- ing on Monday evening. A .successful season was brought to a close with a tea and concert to winch seventy girls, who have made the best attendances, were invited. After a substantial meal had been served, a capital programme of vocal and instrumental music was submitted. Item; were contributed by Mrs. Griffiths, the Misses Fairclough, Miss G. Sloane, the Misses Hampson, and the Misses Bishop and Moore. Afterwards the stockings knitted and the garments made during the winter, were distribUted by Miss B. Dutton, who spoke highly of the long-continued and acceptable services of the matron, Mrs. Davies- A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to all who had supported the entertainment, and specially to Miss Ashdown, the hon secretary, who had arranged the tea,while kind friends wit') had c-mtributed articles for the use of the club were gratefully mentioned, notably Mr. Z. Armitage and Mrs. Gough. Thanks were accorded to a generous unknown friend who each season sends a handsorne gift of oranges.

Advice not Appreciated. At the County Petty Sessions on Wednesday, Danie Cooper, pf Woolston, was charged with having assaulted William Gatley at Woolston.—Complainant said he was standing outside the gate of the defend- ant's brick yard. The engine had broken down and he offered some information as to how it should be mended. Defendant thereupon struck him a blow o the jaw and knocked him down.—Defendant alleged that complainant was standing where he had no right to be. He admitted pushing Gatley, but denied striking him on the jaw.—Defendant was ordered ta pay the cost of the summons.

div.head: ALTERATION IN THE TIME OF MEETING
div.p: ALTERATION IN THE TIME OF MEETING

Mr. Spruce moved that the meetings of the District Council be held on alternate Tuesdays in the summer 'months at 3 p.m. and during the winter at 2 p.m. If the proposal were adopted hewould also move that the Board of Guardians meet on the same dates in the summer months at 1.45 and during the winter at 12.45 ; the House Committee during the summer at 12.45 and the Relief Supervision Committee monthly at 1.15 (meetings to be held on days when there is no house in- spectien.) The present arrangement was very incon- venient especially for members who had other business to attend to. Under the existing system the Highways Committee and House Committee'met at the same hour and it was impossible to give the necessary attention to both. Mr. Collier seconded. _

Mr. Linaker said he would agree to the proposition on the understanding that every other meeting of the Council should be purely for highways and public health business. The estimates for the ensuing year provided for hn expenditure of 26,000 on the highways, and it was incumbent upon them to devote at much time as possible to the spending department. The Clerk pointed out that hitherto the Council had met once a month as a Highways Committee, and the consequence was that decisions ,on some highway matters had to be recorded in both the Highways Com- mittee and Council minute books. It -would facilitate the keeping of the minutes if the Council met one Tuesday for highways and public heath business, instead of as the Highways Committee.
• The resolution was carried unanimously, the clerk's suggestion being embodied. The arrangements for the summer months will be in operationfrom April to the end of,.September.

div.head: DUTTON WATER SUPPLY
div.p: DUTTON WATER SUPPLY
The Clerk informed the Council that the Water supply had now been extended to Dutton .and small portion of Aston.

The Council fixed the charge for the water at 3d. per week for cottages under £l.O per annum in rateable value, and at 124 per cent. on the rateable , value for occupiers of other property. Air. Roylance asked If the pipes had been laid to the .satisfaction of the Council, and if the roads were in a good state of repair. The Clerk said the pipes had been laid to the satis- faction of the engineer of the scheme, and the roads were under maintenance at the present time.
PRECrPTS FOR CONTRIBUTIONS. The precepts for contributions by the overseers were zigned.
COUNCIL AND CONTRACTORS.

The Clerk said that at the last meeting, the Council passed a resolution that he should take proceedings agaiast Messrs. Jowett Bros. for the recovery of the amount of the certificate of the surveyor for the repair of Kingsley and Norley roads after extraordinary traffic by the firm. He wrote to Messrs. Jowett Bros. stating that he should commence proceedings on a certain date. Before that date he received a letter from the firm who, after withdrawing any previous letters on the sub- ject, statdd that they would be plr.ased if he could arrange a meeting between the Council and the firm to discuss the matter without prejudice. The Chairman said Mr. Edgar Jowett interviewed him on receiving the Clerk's letter, and he advised him to withdraw the other letters and the offer made to the Council. The best course for the Council to take would be to appoint a strong, small committee to meet Messrs. Jowett Bros. He thought that Mr. Jowett was now at least capable of looking at the matter from another standpoint, and he anticipated that probably they would be able to secure a satisfactory settlement of the case. It was decided ta appoint the following committee to meet the firm :—Messrs. Woodward, Pilling, Baxter, Linaker, Mounfield, Guest, Stokes, and Chrimes.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
The Making of Beef Tea.

A meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was hel.l on Wednesday morning. Mr. A. Brooks presided and there were also present: Mrs. Clay, Mrs. Wilkinson Miss Broadbent,Dr.Murray.Rev. Dr. Mereer,MessrsAsh- croft, Bminge, Bent, Bolton, Davies, Flanagan, Forshaw, Houghton, Jolley, Mather, Tutor:, Thompson, and S. Sutton (assistant clerk), F. Awhery (master), and A. Wright (master.) DEATH oFAN ASsISTANT OVERSEER.

Mr. BILLINGE referred to the death of Mr. Edwin Jackson for over a quarter of a century the assistant overseer and collector of rates for the township of Havdock. He proposed a vote of condolence with the widow and family. Mr. WILLIAM HOUGHTON seconded.
The ASSISTANT CLERK remarked that the late Mr. Jackson Imd been an excellent officer. The proposition was carried. •
. GRATVITIES TO MR. AND MRS. WRIGHT.

it was resolved to grant gratuities of £5 ss. each to Mr. and Mrs. Wright, the superintendent and matron of Padgate Schools, in recognition of extra work per- formed by them during the last half-year, in the laundry, consequent upon the washing of the Work- house clothing at Padgate during the alterations at the. Workhouse. A DEPUTATION TO SEE HOW BEEF TEA. IS MXDE
Mr. and Mrs. AWBERV, master and matron, were instructed to visit one or two neighbouring Workhouses to asceitain the best method of the preparation of beef tea.
THE TEA CONTRAC"r.

A letter was read from Messrs. Henry Milling and Co., Ltd.. stating that in consequence • of the Budget they would find it necessary to increase their quotations for tea by the amount of the additional tax.
It was agreed to allow Messrs. Milling and Company to increase the price accordingly.
THE POOR LW CONFERENCE
The Chairman and Clerk were.appointed to attend the meeting of the North Western Poor Law Conference to be held in Manchester.
VACCINATION

A printed circular, conveying cony of a petition to Parliament from the Reading Union, was submitted, The petition was against the provisions of the Vaccina- tions Acts and against vaccination generally. • It was ordered to lie on the table. .

.An eleven-year-old boy who was before the Scar- borough Bench on Wednesday on the charge of theft had an unpleasant experience. Found behind the counter of a shop by a lady assistant, he was locked up by her in a cupboard until the arrival of the police.

div.head: GREAT SANKEY PARISH COUNCIL.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY PARISH COUNCIL.
This Council met on Monday evening under the presidency of Mr. George Thompson. There were also present Messrs. H. Fairclough, F. T. Jefferson, and J. Smith (clerk.)

div.head: BUTTERMILK BRIDGE.
div.p: BUTTERMILK BRIDGE.

Mr. Thompson said that at the last meeting of the Rural District Council he called attention to the con- dition of Buttermilk Bridge, and the matter was then referred to the Surveyor, who had taken prompt action, and had had the bridge repaired temporarily. He had been down to the bridge and found that some portion of the timber was decayed, and would have to be renewed. The whole of the repairs would be carried out as promptly as possible. With regard to the foot- path leading over the bridge, that portion on the War- rington Corporation's side was not fit for use. He did not notice much wrong with the footpath on ..heir side of the bridge. The Clerk said that in reply to his letter with regard to the footpath, he had received a letter from the Rural District Council informing him that the Surveyor would give the matter his attention.

div.head: EDUCATIONAL APPOINTMENTS.
div.p: EDUCATIONAL APPOINTMENTS.

Thb Clerk stated that he had written to the Clerk of the District Education Sub-committee at Earlestown informing him that Mr. J. Fulton Smith had been ap- pointed representative of the Great Sankey Parish Council on the Education Sub-committee, and that Messrs. George Thompson and Arthur Birch had been appointed the two representative managers of the Sankey school. He had also submitted the names ofthe following gentlemen as recommendation for appointment by the sub-committee as managers of the school.—Rev. J. R. Jones, Messrs. William Furness, F. T. Jefferson, and H. Fairclough.—ln reply to a letter written by the Clerk informing him of his appointment, Mr. J. Fulton Smith wrote thanking the Council for their kind ex- pression of confidence, and said he would continue to give his best consideration to all matters affecting the interests of the parish. (Hear, hear).
THE WATER SU PPL Y.

A letter was iead by the Clerk which had been re- ceived by the Rural District Council's Sanitary Inspec- tor, Mr. F. Kerfoot, from the Water Engineer of the Warrington Corporation, Mr. James Deas, with refer- ence to the supply of water for Brow Farm, occupied by Mr. William Taylor,and stating that the Corporation would run a main to a point opposite Brow Farm if the Council would guarantee eight per cent. on the cost of the main for a term of ten years. The cost was estimated at £75.
Mr. Thompson said the letter was read at the District Council, and it was thought advisable that the Parish Council should take up the matter, because it affected them more thananyone else.
After discussion-it was decided to appoint a commit- tee consisting of the Chairman and Messrs. Jefferson and Fairclough to go into the matter.
THE USE OF THE WARRINGTON FIRE ENGINE.

The Clerk drew attention to the resolution passed by the Warrington Town Council relative to the use of the fire engine by parishes outside the borough. Mr. Thompson reported that the Clerk of the Rural District Council was instructed at their last meeting to write to the 'Warrington Corporation asking what sub- scriptions would be required for the use of the brigade.

div.head: DELAYED LETTERS.
div.p: DELAYED LETTERS.

Mr. Thompson proposed that the Clerk write to the Warrington Postmaster, calling attention to the great inconvenience caused by letters for Great Sankey being forwarded to Penketh, thereby being considerably de- layed.
*Mr. Fairciongh seoonded, and the motion was agreed to..

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
The Piano Fund.

This Board met at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday under the presidency of M. A. R. Norman. There were also present :—Messrs. S. Taylor, T. Lea, J. W. Timperley, S. Woodward, G. Pilling, T. Wright, J. Stokes, J. Moun- field, C. Roylance, J. Bolsha.w,. H. Eyes, J. Whitlow, A. Broome, H. M. Davies, T. Lewis, J.Smith, H.lVlavvdesley, J. T. Collier, W. Harrison, J. L. Jones, C. Horton, R. A. Chrimes, G. Fryer, W. M. Morris W. Turner, A. G. Guest,.J. Whitley, J. Spruce, W. Fletcher, R. Billington, P. Mounfield, with Messrs. aF. Ashton (clerk), W. E. Hough (deputy clerk), T. Cooke, J. Riley and W. dePrez (relieving ,officeis.) THE MAINTENANCE OF P./AMER LUNA.TICS, It was reported that nt a meeting of the Committee of Visitors of the County Asylum, the rate of mainten- ance of pauper lunatics for the quarter ending June next was fixed at Bs.sid. per week.

AN ANTI-VA:CCINA.TIONIST PROTEST. The Guardians of the Readiag Union wrote asking the Board to support a petition to Parliament stating the following views on the vaccination ques- tion :—(1) That your petitioners believe that vaccination is dangerous to life and limb and useless to prevent the infection of smallpox; (2) that the enforcement of vaccination as a condition of ser- vice in the public departments, civil., naval, and military, is a grievous obstacle to those who believe it to be dangerous and useless; (3) that smallpox as well as fever and zymotic diseages have been greatly diminished by the improvements of the Public Heath Acts in the 19th century which affords hope that small- pox may be by such means further,diminished until it is extinguished ; (4) that your petitioners view with unqualified disapproval the proposal to enforce re-vaccination, asa useless expedient to pre- vent the spread of smallpox, as dangerous to public health, as means of spreading disease, and a further breach of parental and individual liberty. Your peti- tioners pray that your honourable house will repeal the Vaccination Acts, 1867 to 1898, and reject the Re- vaccination Bill of 1904. Without discussion, it was decided that the letter should lie on the table.

COMBINATION AND CLASSIFICATION OF WORKHOUSES. A letter was read from the North-Western Poor Law Conference District (Lancashire and Cheshire) inviting the Board to send representatives to a meeting to be held in Manchester to consider the report of a sub- committee on, the combination and classification of workhouses. file formation of the committee was the outcome of a paper read by Mr. Cleaver at the Black- poolConfe.renco of 1903. The Chaarman and the Clerk were appointed to attend the meeting on behalf of the Board.
THE TIME OF MEETING. The Board approved Mr. Spruce's motion that from April to the end of September the Board should meet fortnightly" at 1.45 and during the Lwinter months at 12.45.

• THE LADIES' VNITING COMMITTEE. GIFT OF A PIANO IN PROSPECT. At a meeting of the Ladies' Visiting Committee the resignations of Mrs. Baxter, Mrs. Linaker, and Mrs. Milner were received. A vote of thanks was accorded these ladies for their past services. Miss Dutton reported that the. piano fund had reached about £B. The committee hoped the Guardians would subscribe to the fund. Miss Dutton was re-appointed president and Fletcher and Mrs. Whitley were elected hon. secretaries. Mr. Woodward moved the appointment to the com- mittee, in place of one of the ladies who bad resigned, of Mrs. Arthur Edelsten of Norton, and also that Mrs. Milner be requested to reconsider her resignation. With reference to the third vacancy, he hoped to be prepared to nominate a lady-at the next meeting. Mr. Fletcher seconded,and the proposition was agreed

to. t The Clerk said he was instructed to write to the mem- bers and retiring members asking if they were willing tosubscribe to the Workhouse piano fund. The Chairman said he did not know the Clerk was going to mention the subject. Before it went any further, he ought to say that he had had information that led him to believe that before very long a piano 'would be generously presented to the committee for use in the-house. In that case there would be no necessity for subscriptions. Mr. Piling: I beg to withdraw my subscription. (Laughter.) The Chairman: The thing cannot be decided for a few weeks at any rate. I propose in the meantime that the whole matter be deferred till we see the develop- ment of the offer. Mr. Collier: I On a subscriber std. I have great .pleasure in seconding. This course was agreed to. FINANCIAL. .

Mr. Woodward presented ill; ial statement,show- ing a balance in hand of .£873 Os. 2d. The balance actually appearing in the treasurer's book was £62195. 3d. more than that, being accounted for by cheques not presented. THE SALARY OF THE INDUSTRIAL TRAINER. The House Committee considered the application of Miss Hayes, the industrial trainer, for an increase of salary. The committee did not see its way to recommend an increase, as it was the opinion that the salary com- pared favourably with the amounts paid in other unions. The minutes were approved. At a meeting of the House Committee it was reported that the water supply had now been extended to the workhouse gates. The committee recommended that Messrs. Timmins, of Runcorn, be asked to prepare an estimate of the cost of hydrants andappliances necessary in order that the supply would be available at the house in case of tire and also for domestic purposes. This course was agreed to.

ALLEGED HOUSEBREAKING AT ST. HELENS. At St. Helens on Tuesday, Peter White, a labourer, of 72.Fenton-street, was charged with burglariously enter- ing the dwelling-house, 3, Wilson-street, and stealing wearing apparel, SCc.. value ..-‘24 45., the property of Enoch Lawrenson. Chief Constable Wood said that on Sunday night Mr. Lawrenson and his family v‘ ere absent from home from half-past six to half-past nine and on their return they found that a hole large enough to admit a man had been broken' into the kitchen win- dow. Detective Hall said he arrested the prisoner and found some of the stolen property concealed under the staircase. He asked for the case to be remanded until Friday. White asked to be tried at once, but was ordered back to the cells.

div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
NOTICE TO CO RRESPONDENTS.

Authors of letters intended for publication must mall cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith. Matter intended for publication must be written Imo ride only of the paper and seat in, if possible,not than Thursday.

div.head: Mr. Monks and the "Long Pull,"
div.p: Mr. Monks and the "Long Pull,"

Sir,—l think it is a great pity that Mr. Monks cannot leave the poor publican alone. The latter's difficulties are great enough to contend with in trying to carry on his business in a respectable manner with those wham he ha 4 to serve both inside and outside his house withont being constantly harrassed and threatened by mernbers of the Bench. There are many in the licensing trade like myself who are strictly carrying oat the agreement come to some time ago to give what is termed the froth measure' over, which is only fair to the public; And if this is not being carried out by some, then it is unfair to those who are. No one except tied houses oan atter& to give more than this. If they do,aienthe business is not worth having, for there would be so little margin left. If the brewers 'interested would only see that their managers were exact in the over-measure agreement, there would be no cause for cormilaint. With regard-to the public, they only want educating up to this agreement, and the publican being firm, matte,?rs would go on smoothly. Mr. Monks.and the Licenaing Bench surely would not object to this agreement. If they do, then I hope they will state distinctly what they de want, an enforce it. I would saggest a conference between the Bench and the trade. It is very annoying and distressing to the latter to keep having these complaints, Mr. Monks has not been an enemy to the licensing trade hitherto, and I am sure both he and his 'colleagues on the Bench woald listen te reasoz.—Yours Scc., 'ONE IN ME TRADE..

div.head: Warringtoli Bridge.
div.p: Warringtoli Bridge.

Sir,—lngsupportine• the above scheme, Mr. Editor, uthouldlikeito bring before the notice of ratepayers ele necessity of all classes uniting together to bring about one ofthe most•important amprovemfnt for safety to be lives of those people who may use the Warrington 13ridgeas root passengers. It is a well-known factotbat we are not in a position at the present time to build a 'few bridge which may cost any wherelrom £20,660 to £30,000, but the defrand for the safety to life compels those who have .the bestinterest, and the interest of thenown only, at heart to act at once. If it had been decided to build a new bridge'this wolfs.- would not have been carried out for at least the next 15 to 20,years. Thus we are compolled to widen the bridge by cantilevers as being the most favourable scheme at the present time to suit the rate- payeri''pockets. Accidents are continually happening • on or near the approach to the bridge of which I append a few. First, a-youth coming rout of Mersey-street collided with a cart, his bicycle .was destroyed. but he escaped with a shaking. Second, cyclist eollided with a cab, be *as badly 'bruised abc,ut the feet, and for sometime he was unable to more. Third, b..youth slipped off the footpath, the path being so narrow, and fell up against the side of an electric car, which-threw him on to the footpath again. These -tare some reasons why this work should be proceeded with and carried out at once. More- over I um quite confident that I could procure 700 or 800 signaturesiin favour of this scheme from Let:llford alone. Thanking you in anticipation, I remain yours faithfully,
NV. J. WILSGN. 6, Lyon-etreet, Warrington, 6th teay, 1904.

div.head: Cobden Centenary.
div.p: The Cobden Centenary.

Sir —Armonth henceithe Centenaty of the birth. o Richltrd.Gebden will afford a happy occasion not only for honouring the memory of the statesman to whom the country owes so much of its well-being, but also for a national rally of progreseive forces:in favour of Peace. Retrenchment, and Reform. The past yearhas seen the beginning, .end apparentiy the end, of the "raging, tearing propaganda"; and although we do not for ft moment snppose that this means the end of the Protec- tionistatitation—evidencelis not wanting of its con- tinuance in dovieus and secret ways—there is yet goad reason to rejoice that another open assault upon oar freedom of tcreig,n trade has been repulsed. But this is not enough. A policy of ales and privileges at home and aggression and adventure abroad requires a prodigal expenditure; and prodigal expenditure has always been the main cause of protective •tariffs. Not only have certain leaders to be checked, therefore, but a whole policy has to be reversed. We have then, a triple aim in celebrating the Cobden Centenary—to honour Cobden's memory; to mark the failure of Mr. Chambe- rlain's agitation:; and to demand a Government pledged to resolute reform, to Imperial and internationalpeace, andto a large reduction of the wasteful expenditnre on armaments. If we condemn the present Government in other respects we shall at leest be able to give them credit in regard to the conclusion of Arbitration Treaties with France, Italy and Holland, and the epoch- making agreement with France. The Cobden Club Is actively engaged, in concert with many sympathetic bodies, industrial, political and religssus, in organising suitable gatherings throughout the country on Friday, June 3rd, and Saturday, June 4th, and there will also be many pulpit references to the ethical aspects of Cobden's work on the preceding and following Sundays. In London our chief meeting will be held in the Alexandra Palace, on the Saturday evening, when Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman will be supported by Mr. Lloyd George, Mr. Winston Churchill, Dr. Clifford- .and other well-known public men. In some cases several towns or districts are combining to snake a greet county detnonstration, for instance, at Midhurst, where free traders from Brighton, Horsham, and other Sussex centres will gather to hear Lord Davey and Mr. Bryce. Every town in the country owes something to Richard. Cobden, and in every town a meeting of some sort how- ever humble, ought to be held on the Centenary of his birthday. Warrington ought not to be behind-hand in this matter, but if anything is to be done there is no time to lose. I shall be glad to supply further inform- ation, and to give any possible assistance in finding influential speakers and in providing suitable literature. Faithfully yours,
G. H._PERRIS, Secretary.

div.head: Cobden Club, London, May sth. he Royal Commission on Disorders
div.p: Cobden Club, London, May sth. he Royal Commission on Disorders
in the Church.

Sir,—lt cannot be denied that it is humiliating to a religious community to have its affairs overhauled by the secular power for the suppression of disorders alleged against it. And were the Anglican Establish- ment what it claims to be—a continuation of the Church and ministry founded by the Lord—l would be amongst the first to oppose any such interference by a hybrid Parliament. But it would be too wide a stretch of imagination to endorse the claim. I have some know- ledge of the New Testament scriptures, but I cannot find anything there to countenance a mortal headship of Christ's Church, with Right Reverend and , Most Reverend Fathers in God sitting on thrones as his sub- ordinates! Whatever professions the Church-may make offher Apostolic origin the fact is that to-day, as we see her, she is as much a creature of the State as the army, and equally under the control of Parliament. Even in the matter of history her record is comparatively short. Instead of going back to the time of Christ she appears to have come into existence only in the Reign of Henry VIII., 370 years ago. Prior to that date the dominant religion of this country was the Roman Catholic, over which the Bishop of Rome was the supreme head and ruler. But as that prelate refused, and rightly refused, to sanction the divorce of one of Henry's wives (queen Catherine) that self-willed and arbitrary monarch at once set about to overthrow his power and jurisdiction in this realm. And so success- ful were his efforts that in 1534 his obedient class- parliament invested him with supreme authority in all matters ecclesiasticat as well as civil. Thus was the Roman faith disestablished in this country, and the pre- sent State Church set up upon its ruins by a process of injustice and spoliation perhaps unparalleled in modern history. And from the days of Henry until now, the sovereigns of England, male and female, irrespective of character, have presumed to lord it over God's heritage as if they had a divine right to do so, not even allowing the Church to elect her own chief pastors:as all inust have the Royal stamp. The ecclesiastical change introduced by Henry is called par excellence the Reformation. The methods of reform adopted, whether riddling or winnowing. do not appear to have proved quite effectual. At any rate, consider- ably less than four centuries have sufficed to develop the tares that were either left or sown in the vineyard by the overhasty. husbandmen. Indeed, judging from the Reports of Convocations and other ecclesiastical gatherings, and also from the Royal Commission itself, the Church seems to be in a bad state in our days, and calling loudly for reform. Then why not try another drastic Reformation! Thel successors of the good king and parliament who set up the Church in the sixteenth century would have no difficulty in breaking down their image in the twentieth. And what a change for the better would result from their handiwork! One of the first results of disestab- lishment and disendowment would be to promote a better spirit among Christian men, and more co-opera- tion in Christian work. Then when State patronage and State pay had disappeared the church would begin to understand the glorious liberty of the gospel and corrupting hirelings would disappear. And then think of the enormous amount of money that would be set at lib6rty, and could be applied to a sound secular educa- tion, properly based on the divine principle of love to God and man, which is the very essence of the Christian religion.—Yours truly, May, 1904.

div.head: MESSRS. GROSFIELD'S EMPLOYEES.
div.p: MESSRS. GROSFIELD'S EMPLOYEES.
RECOGNITION OF LONG SERVICE.

There was a unique gathering in the Parr Hall on. Monday evening, when the firm of Messrs. Joseph Cros- field and Sons, Limited, recognised the long and unbroken service of some of their 'oldest employees. Three veterans with over 50 years' service behind them were each the recipients of a money gift of £25, and 21 employees whose length of service ranged from 25 years to 44 years received" £5 note each. The hall was filled with employees and their friends. Members of the,Board of Directors and the heads of departments were also present. The proceedings were of an interesting and entertaining ,character. A musical programme was provided by the employees themselves and they acquitted themselves admirably. A mixed choir under the conductorship of Mr. E. B. Ogden sang several part songs ina manner which reflected credit on all concerned, and the firm's prize band, conducted by Mr. W. Halliwell, played up to their reputation in several selections. Solos were efficiently sung by Miss C. Hastings, Miss Marsh, Mr. E. Pownall, Mr. J. Allan and Mr. A. V. Baxter. The humour of the evening was supplied by Mr. J. P. Hignett, whose songs" caught on" with the- audience. The accompanists were Mr. J. Carter and Mr. G. F. Chapman. The presentations for long service were made by Dr. Markel (managing director), and as the recipients stepped on to the platform to receive the firm's hand- some recognition of their services, they were loudly cheered. The proceedings were presided over by Mr. A. H. Crosfield (chairman of the Board of directors)and 'he deliveredan interesting speech, prior to the presenta- tion.

Mr. Arthur Crosfield, who had every heartyreception •said:—" I have first of all to thank the Works Councils and through them yorrselves, for your kindness in ask, ing me to preside-this evening over a meeting which 1- very eventful, and which would be eventful and inter- esting if oaly because of the presentation which is about to be made .by Dr. Markel. (Cheers.) I think that this great gathering has a farther significance beyond that cererneny,intereating as it will be in itself, because I think it marks the extraordinary progress which ow: firm has made of recent years. (Cheers.) The very numbers in which we are assembled to- night bear testimony to the material progress that has been made, butt do not refer only to that, I am speaking more particularly of the remarkable pro- gress which the last few yearn have witnessed, (if I may say so without seeming to blow our own trumpet), in the firm's capacity as employers of labour. (Cheers.) A few years sines I was reading a summary of what has been done by some of the most enlightened employers of labour in America and lam bound to say that what I read there caused me to rub my eyes. But I will say this, that if you look through this interesting little ,1 pamphlet on our works which has been compiled, I think you will honestly agree with me that we are not far if at all behind some of the most eilightened empleyers of labour in the States. (Hear,' hear.) The ether iday .we were compering notes with Sir John Brunner upon what had been done at Bank Quay and Winnington. And although to some extent we are handicapped, when pitted against ,these whose works are in the country, still lam happy to tell you that while in some important respects Brunner Mond's are ahead of us, in other respects we are ahead of them. (Chews.) The first time I ever had the honour of speak- ing to a representative gathering of employees at Bank Quay was in 1E92, and I 'remember on that occasion expressing the hope, that as time went on our employs would cultivate a taste for music and drink deeper from that fountain which Professor Huxley has called,the most enduring of all the refined pleasures of life—literature. (Hear, hear.) At that time I little thought of what twelve years would bring forth, and what splendid progress would be made in the develop- ment of thetalent of our employds,asahstrated by the beautiful music we have just listened to with such joy and suck pleasure. (Hew, hear.) Literature, no doubt, will follow in its turn for I do not doubt that the stimulus which educationlas already given will tend in this direction. May I just say that by 'literature lam not referring to that scrappy sort of reading that you get in the halfpenny evening press. which if useful in its way, le, lam afraid, very often apt to lead to an occupation which is very .unsatisfactory and; I aim sure very unprofitable, and which is known as " spotting" winners and backing losers. (Loud !laughter). The pamphlet I have referred to is so suggestive, that if I had not had a warning word from my friend Mr.Rigby,l might have been tempted to detain you a good deal longer than I intend to de. There are many topics one could deal with. There is the fine work done not only for the benefit of our own place, but for the benefit of Warrington by our Fire Brigade. (Hear, hear.) Then I think the work that has been undertaken by our Ambu- lance Corps is beyond all praise. (Hear, hear.) It is a very unselfish and admirable work. A great deal is be- irig done besides this,which I must not touch upon, but it is most satisfactory to seethe public spirit which has been shown by the employs at Bank Quay in support- ing the auxiliary forces of the country—(hear, hear)— even though my brother George may have wished to see them do a bit more. I have only time to say a passing ward on this matter, but I believe everyone of us will realise that it has become a ‘uestion of vital import- ance to us that our auxiliary forces should be strong in numbers, thoroughly well equipped and thoroughly efficient. I do not know whither every one realises that the total expenditure upon the defences of this country and our Empire has now reached the enormous total of £90,000,00Q,a year. ("010") That is jest double the entire expenditure of Germany, and far beyond what other rival nations spend. The time has come when we must,if possible,check this expenditure on the army, and certainly check Mhg. alarmingly increased ex- penditure on the navy. Fvfm an economic point of view therefore, as well as from other points of view, it is absolutely necessary to strengthen our auxiliary forces so that we may depend mainly upon them and somewhat less upon our costly army and navy for home defence. (Hear, hear.) And so let us be glad that our firm has played its part in this patriotic work. (Cheers.) There has been a lighter side to all this. We have our sports and athletics which have done so much for the character of Englishmen, and which, I venture to say, do teach the average Englishman to play the great game of life fairly and squarely. (Hear, hear.) Further- more in the winter months, we have pretty frequently these charming dances, two of which I had the pleasure of attending this season. lam told that an unlooked for aonsequence of these social pleasures has happened. There is now, I understand, an enterprise shown at Bank Quay, not amongst those who are too young—we don't want that—but still a remarkable amount of matrimonial enterprise amongst the manhood and womanhood of our works. (Laughter.) lam informed that this has had a very appreciable effect upon the matrimonial average in this town. (Laughter.) I must confess r was very glad to hear it. (Loud laughter.) Now I have a ward of warning to give you on the matter. (Renewed laughter.) There had recently been published a book upon the subject of matrimony, which I trust everybody here will avoid, because if you read it I am not sure that this spirit of daring will survive. (Laughter.) I got hold of this book the other day, and as "to be fore- warned is to be forearmed"—(laughter)—l arulgoing to give you a bit of warning in advance. This is what an American writer has to say upon the subject of matrimony. He heads it with the line,—" Balm of Gilead," and it reads as follows : "A radiant smile appeared upon the face of the dying Mormon as the Elder read to him words of hope and promise from the Bible. There 'shall be no marriages in Heaven, re-read the Elder. Again the radiant look suffused the visage of the much married sufferer. Oh ! Death, where is thy sting',

he gasped, and fell back lifeleSs." (Loud laughter): I wish to observe that none of my colleagues on our ' Board of Directors so far as Tam aware have anything whatever to do with Mormonism. (Laughter). But they are all married men except myself, and yet I be- lieve they entirely and heartily repudiate any sentiment of that kind. (Laughter). Here is one other quotation: "The fact that there is no marrying in heaven goes still further to prove, perhaps, that" Fools rush in where Angels fear to tread." (Loud laughter). Now suppose that some young, fellow who has won his spurs feels a stirring of matrimonial ardour and ambition within his breast. (Laughter). He comes across this wretched book and learns that " Matrimony is a game in which one side cheats from the beginning," or he hears of " Single blessedness and married cussed- ness !"—(laughter)—who, I ask ybu in the face of such discouragement is going to take this great leap in the dark? (Laughter.) So I beseech all our girl friends and men friends here to shun this book of "Bachelor Bigotries," and rather to follow President Roosevelt's excellent advice in the matter, so that in matrimony as in other things we may take the lead. (Laughter.) I have referred to some of the work that has been done. May I say that our Board who are res- ponsible for the conduct of affairs are very gratified at the hearty way in which the Wotks Council have thrown themselves into what is described in our works book. For tike creation of this Works Council ; for bringing the conditions of employment well up-to-date, and into line with the most advanced and enlightened employ- ment elsewhere—as we intend to do, and I hope to a large extent have done—(cheers)—for this, as well as for the scientific development inside our treat works I am sure it is quite unnecessary for me to tell anyone in this hall how largely we are indebted to the energy and initiative of Dr. Markel. (Loud cheers.) Dr. Markel has far too big a mind to care for flattery, nor is there any need for it because I am very certain that every thinking man and woman in this hall who reflects upon the progress of the last few years must feel that at any rate an honest attempt has been made at our factory to civilise the conditions of industry. (Hear, hear.) Ladies and gentlemen, it is often said that a company has no conscience. (Laughter.) I should just like therefore to take the opportunity which this evening affords to tell you that all this progressive work has had the unanimous and hearty approval and sanction of our Board. (Cheers.) As for the great commercial progress that has been made by our firm, I am sure that not only our Board but everyone of us at this great gathering is proud of it, and confident of yet greater progress in the future. (Loud cheers.) I do not think this evening we shouldaltogether forget
