battle of life would be easier for our children in year to come. (Applause). The CHAIRMAN said Warrington could be won for Liberalism if they had the earnest, intelligent and ener- getic support of the whole of the Liberals in the town. He would like all present to associate themselves with the Liberal organization, so that when the time came they would be able to act as one solid body. He would now call upon Mr. Crostield, whom he hoped would be the great standard bearer of the cause at the next elec- tion. (Applause.) Mr. CROSFIELD said he had proposed votes of thanks a good many times in his humble efforts at platform work, but he never proposed a vote of thanks with more heartfelt sincerity than the vote which he moved not only for himself, but on their behalf, to Mr. Howes for the address he had given them. The Chairman had called it inspiring and eloquent, and it certainly had been a most eloquent address, relieved by those delight- ful touches of humour for which Mr. Howes surely had a special gift, and full also of the most instructive matter which must afford food for reflection to every- one in that room. For himself, although Mr. Howes touched upon so much, he would specially like to thank Mr. Howes for the long address he gave them on that very. important question—the pernicious attempt to introduce what was closely allied to slavery into the British empire again—(applause)--a pro- position which was so absolutely reactionary from the paint of view of every workingman, be he skilled artisan or labourer,who had at hisheart the good of all the workers of the world. (Hear, hear). He thanked Mr. Howes for the incisive and exhaustive way in which he handled the question, because be (Mr. Crosfield) had had the good fortune to post himself up to some extent, not only from the Press and from whet was published, but from men who had been eye wit- nesses upon the spot, and men of influence amongst the traders in South Africa, who had lived there all their lives,land with whom he had been associated in com- merce for the last fifteen or twenty years. He had an account from two of them—one a very able commercial traveller who had been all through the Transvaal and the Orange Free State, the other a merchant with a very large stake indeed in the country—and he must say, without detaining the meeting at that late hour with any particulars, that the sum total of the account they had given him of those broken hearted people, of the desolate country that that hideous war ha? left behind it, was truly heart-rending. (Hear, hear.) They as Liberals were not arming at a Utopia but, after all, one of the root principles of Liberalism, one of the planks in their platform which was the very foundation of their Liberalism, was a determination to try and reduce the sum total of undeserved misery and destitu- tion in the wqrld. (Hear, hear.) He could admit they all knew there were wars which were what were called just and necessary, but they were few and far between. As a rule, wars were not just and necessary, and the more they looked into the way in which those utterly unscrupulous men upon the rand—whose intrigues Mr. Howes had exposed point by point in his splendid speech— the more they lookedinto the way those men pulled the strings from 1895 onwards, from the date when they organized the raid, up to the date when they organized the war—because they were equally responsibly for the one as for the other—the more they felt how terrible Ii was that they should have sacrificed 20,000 fine British lives and squandered the savings of British statesman- ship for the last thirty or forty years, and, he would add, caused the unspeakable suffering and the ,terrible agony which those innocent 20,000 helpless women and children went threugh during the timewhen that nation was being slowly done to death. (Hear, hear.) As re- garded our soldiers, they did their duty, and he had always said,and he would repeat it, the tighter the place we got into through that bluster- ing, hectoring sort of diplomacy that had been the order of the day, the greater the honour to those soldiers who got us out of that tight place. He hadalways felt, however, that one could not but regret that terrible waste of lit., and that frightful'expendi- ture of treasure for purposes which had been so splendidly exposed by Mr. Howes. In his address Mr. Howes had touched upon other questions that were be- fore them. He (Mr. Crostield) had heard workingmen friends of his in years gone by complain, and justly corn- Dlain,that there was not in Warrington that opportunity for education on political matters which ought to be afforded by those who were responsible for the conduct of the Liberal party in the town. He was sorry to say he did think there were considerable grounds for that complaint made a few years ago, and on the other hand, he must honestly say that during the last twelve months, at any rate, and particularly since a. gentleman whom they all deeply respected and whose ea-nest Liberalism was doing a great deal to bring about the victory which they intended to achieve, since their friend the President of the Association—(applause)—threw his energies into the work of the Liberal party,and week after week had given them in the Press admirable letters sifting and examining every important topic as it came up, he (Mr. Crosfield) had felt the time had gone by when working- men friends of theirs could come to them and say "You are not doing your duty in the educational line." Besides the work that had been done in the Press, they had had the most splendid support,—for which he felt personally deeply grateful, and he thought they all felt deeply grateful—from their friend Mr. Howes—(applause)—who had given them not once, but many times this winter, those wonderful addresses that Nw.re amongst the most eloquent, stirring, and impoVant that had ever been delivered in the town by any politician. (Apola.use.) Other men taking a leading part in the politics of England had also come down and assisted them with true statesmanlike and instructive speeches—in fact, he did not mind telling them that he did not give them very much peace at Liberal headquarters unless they gave the workers in Warrington a good backing. (Hear, hear.)Ele very nearly sat on their doorstep—(laughter)— and he inten led to continue doing so. (Applause.) He did not want to have the slightest responsibility upon his shoulders when the critical moment came; he did not want• anybody to be able to say "You have not done your share in getting us down political streakers to instruct and to inspire us in the work before us." During the last few months a great change had come over the state of affairs in Warrington. They were not lacking now either in instruction or in inspiring speeches. The organization was better than it was. (Hear, hear.) They had against them as their chief obstacle the dead weight of apathy and ignorance and political inertia upon which Toryism had been founded in this town, They had as against that, sub- jects that must appeal now to those who perhaps were inclined to shelve politics in years gone by and say that they would not bother with them. When they got the question of education, when • they knew how it ,came home to every e family and how it gave every man's child a good chance or a bad chance of earning a good position for himself; when they knew how this question of Free Trade meant fair supplies of cheap food in the households, then they were coming down to the questions that must stir men, if any questions would stir them. (Hear, hear) In addition, at previous meetings, they had touched upon those other questions, each one of whieh would he a sufficient rallying cry for the whole of their party. It would, he respectfully submitted, be grate sucficiont for the trade unionists of Warrington, and for all men who had at heart the interests of labour, if they had as a rallying cry that simple little Bill which Mr. Shackle- ton had introduced. (Hear, hear.) Chinese slavery itsel' would be a sufficienerally cryingets would Free Trade and Education. When they had those questions in a total- ity, their programme and what they had to fight for was as he had said at two or three meetings lately, not only affording them as fine a cause and as great a cause to induce them to put their backs into the work as they had in 'the elections of 1880 and 1818, but they actually had a greater and a more far-reaching cause to fight than even their predecessors had at the elections he had named. "So the long and short of it is " continued Mr. Crosfield "that it mainly depends now upon how far the captains in our party will realize the importance of the work that devolves upon each one of them, how far they will throw themselves into the work, and realize that in politics, as in. business, if youlare going to succeed you must remem- ber it is necessary to grasp veer opportunities. (Hear, hear.) The opportunity which is given to us is the opportunity of a lifetime. I do hope every one of us will feel that though mistakes have been made in the past in the Liberal party, though people have sometimes trotted out their hobby horses at inconvenient moments there is now a greater unity in the party all through the country as in London, and people are content to sink their own particular fads and work for the general good of the party. So all we have got to do in Warrington is to fall into line with the progressive tendencies of the rest of the country and determine that this time, at any rate, we will be wise before and notafter the event. (Applause.) You know, gentlemen, we have no candidate at present, and we think it is much wiser to defer the formal selec- tion of any candidate for the present. I wish to say without any affectation that my position is simply this —that while we are leaving the question an open one for the time being, if it should be thought that with my great political deficiencies, of which I am well aware, if it should be thought by you and our friends who have the control of the party work on the executive that I can give any real assistance by fighting again the Liberal battle for this constituency, I shall most cer- tainly be there when the bell rings. (Cheers.) In 1900 it vas hopeless, and I did not fail to realize that from A the first moment. I thought the result was only amazingly good under such ten ibly difficult circum- stances. (Hear,hear.) To me, I can assure you, as long as I live it will be, I think I can say without any ex- aggeration, the greatest honour of my life to have alear,hear.) I did not funk was proud to fight the battle, tfhoeugdhetfetahtat one losaintogm b.ltatntale i though I lost h. But if it should fall to me to fight again, I would be a jolly sight prouder to fight and win." (Loud cheers). Mr. W. CLEGG seconded the motion which was carried with enthusiasm. The CHAIRMAN:having been thanked for presiding,the meeting concluded.

Li- the members of the Liberal party for some time Darwin, Ka., of West Didsbury, Manchester. had felt, that it would be a great thing to win Warrington. Mr. Howes proceeded to allude to the growth of enthusiasm in the Liberal cause, and said there was no doubt in his mind that this town was very much like all other towns in which they had a mass of working people. Only two things were necessary to ensure victory. The first was that the working people should have placed before them the facts of the case, and the second that the oreaniza- tion should be made as perfect as possible in order that those who were willine to work might be shown how they could work, and in order that the work they did might bring about the greatest results. He frequently said that the only cause for the existence of Tory Governments was the short political memories of the people. Working people who had to struggle for their existence, would never dare to vote for Tory. candidates if they thoroughly understood what Toryism meant. and if they could carry in their recollections the develop- ment of Tory work from administration to administra- tion. All the horrors of the present Government were 'merely a repetition of what previous Tory Governments had done. Toryism was the same yesterday, to-day and for ever. (Laughter.) Mr. Howes proceeded to urge the importance of efficient registration work, and gave elaborate details of how districts should be survey d and canvassed. In conclusion he dealt briefly with current politics. Alluding to the Chinese labour ques- tion, he said that if they once admitted the principle of allowing the Government to provide cheap labour for employers, everyemployer woald have an equal right to demand it. After criticising the Licensing Bill and the Budget, Mr. Howes said they in Warrington would be gloriously happy when the votes were counted, if they saw the name of Crosfield at the head of the poll— (applause)—and knew they had rescued this important borough from the thraldom of Toryism. The Liberal leaders in London would rejoice with exceeding great joy when they in Warrington could flash over the wires the knowledge" Warrington is Liberal." (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN hoped they would not forget the good counsel Mr.flowes had given them in regard to organisa- tion. Whether the name of Crosfield would be at the head of the poll at the next election really depended upon all the Liberals individually. It was for each one to take his part and not depend upon the officers of the Association. For the good cause that was before them and for the great issues that were involved, he trusted there would be a determination on the part of every Liberal to do what he' could in the important spade work that was before them. (Hear, hear.. l Mr. ARTHUR H. CROSFIELD proposed a vote Of thanks to Mr. Howes, who he said, had paid several visits to Warrington, andeach visit had had great effect. He thought the effort that Mr. Howes had made ought to help them to be wise before the event. One thing that he (Mr. Crosfield) had learnt in his commercial experi- ence was this, that if you were going to succeed in this life you had got to know how to grasp your opportuni- ties and you must be wise before and not after the event. Referring to the remarks of the Chairman and Mr. Howes with reference to himself, Mr. Crosfield said the Liberal party had not chosen a candidate yet, but he was aware that his name had been brought forward perhaps because he had the great honour—the greatest honour of his life—in being allowed to fight the battle last tieie on behalf of the Liberal party. On that occasion he supposed the Liberal party had the most terrible ordeal to face that even MrHowes with his wide politicalirecollection could recall,and as Councillor Evans put it the other night at Thewlis-street, it was fought through the mists of Jingoism. There could beno doubt that the working c:asses of this country were largely blinded by the smoke of that Jingoism and by the sub- tlety of the mostastuteelectioneerer,—Joseph Chamber- lain—one of the most dangerous men who ever had con- trol of the fortunes of this country. (Hear' hear.) At the time he was speaking of. Mr. Chamberlain certainly was swaying the destinies of Englandand breaking down the level and the whole tone of our politics, as he (Mr. I Crosfleld) had heard not only Liberals say, but Conser- vatives also. One Coneervative said that Mr. Chamber- laid had vulgarised English politics more than any other powerful statesman had done for a century. He (Mr. Crosfield) was talking to "Yin John Morley about the events of the war and took occasion to tell him of the capital that was made against them at the last election by the deliberate attempt to persuade the people that because Liberals condemned the policy that steadily led up to the war, therefore they were condemning the men, who by their bravery and persistency during that terrible warfare were endeavouring to pull us out of the tight place in which Great Britain had been put. The more he read about the events that led up to the War, the more he was convinced that the position he took up at the time was the correct one. Fresh issues were now coming up, but it was better to considerthese ' events in our own day and not to wait, as we did over the Crimean war, fifty years to discover that "we had put our money on the wrong horse." Mr. Crosfield reviewed some of the chief events in the South African imbroglio, and in referring to the rand magnates, said a set of men less praiseworthy could not be found to deal with the question of Chinese slavery there. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion, he appealed for cohesion amongst the progressive forces in Warrington in order to put a stop to the retrogressive policy which now predominated. (Applause.) Councillor EVANS seconded the vote of thanks which was carried unanimously.

Appropriately enough, the \Farrington Band of Hope' has welcomed the " merrie month "by holding a festi- val reflecting something of the spirit of the old time- revels which Warrington, in common with other industrial centres, never sees. Bright and picturesque' was the scene at the Parr Hill oi Thursday evening when youthful members of the tem- perance ranks made merry at the Court of: the Band of Hope Queen. The coronation was in-- vested with a quaint ceremonial and stateliness, and it was evident that the spectacle gave pleasure to the' large audience. The platform was gaily decked with.— streamers, and the dresses of the DO chit-ken seated • on the gallery m ide quite a wealth of nolonr. A fitting Opening hymn' was "Soldiers of 9'emperance " (composed by Mr. F. Podmore.) The sprightly • ' chorus " Come lassies and lads" preceded the evening'& ceremonies, and a group of boys and girls danced to the familiar air. After a flourish of trumpets the retir- ing queen and the queen elect entered, attended by the Chancellor and other dignitaries, and maids of honour. Tile retiring queen was escorted to the throne, and the- beautiful floral crown which sparkled with electric lights, was placed on her head. Having spoken words of fare- well to her subjects,"l-ler Majesty" vacated her exalted position, and the queen elect was conducted to the throne and crowned by the Chancellor. The stirring chorus " Hail to our queen" was given with a fine swing, and then homage was paid to the queen by the court, and representatives of the B.W. Temperance- Association and the Order of Rechabites. There was- also a pretty procession of characters familiar in nursery rhyme and children in a variety of costumes. A speech by the newly-crowned queen was followed by a series of interesting musical items. A company of diminutive soldiers sang and drilled under the direction' of ex-private D. Smith and came in for a round of applause. The navy did not go unrepresented and one of the hits of the evening wis the hornpipe by little sailor boys. Their leider (T.Richmond) acquitted him- self with special credit. A group of sturdy railway men told of their calling in a well-rendered song. Then a number of tiny tots tripped round to the strains- of "Here we go round in a merry rush," and soon found favour with the audience. For the second part of the programme some enjoy- able miscellaneous items had been arranged. Master Tom Barton, Cert. R.A.M., displayed consider- able ability as a violinist and his solo Romance et Bolero "called forth an encore. Lavinia Hewitt feel- ingly sang "Daddy" and Flarry Colley gave a creditable interpretation of "Angels ever bright and fair." • A duet The night bells" by Elsie Spruce and L. Hewitt was appreciated and Harry Griffiths gave Jack's the" boy for work" in good style. A popular humorous item was Reggie McCollam's song "The horse that Misses' dries the clothes on." A novel and enjoyable feature was a selection by Master Toni Barton's boys'orchestra, the youthful performers being recalled. lathe conclud- b inr, song and chorus' " Gad bless our band of hope," the leading narts were well taken by Harry* Griffiths and May Isherwood. The royal procession having been reformed and left the platform the National Anthem concluded a successful entertainment. - The cantata reflected great credit upon the children and their instructors. The queens (Elsie Wright and Ethel Cooper) took their parts with dignity, and recited well- Great praise is due to the conductor (Mr. A. Spruce) and the organist (Mr. F. Podmore, M.1.U.M.). A prtomising pupil of Mr. Podipore (Master Clativorthy) assisted at the organ duping the evening, and also accompanied several items on the..piano. During an interval an address was delivered by the President of the Union(Mr. R. A. Naylor) who presided,. and was accompanied by Miss Naylor. He thanked the audience for their warm reception which, he said, was certainly (-railed if not excelled by the great pleasure which it afforded him to come from London to stand on the platform as president of that Union. (Applause.) He con,gratulated everyone connected with the diltnon- stration upon the success which had attended their en- deavours. He expressed the hope that the children would grow up to be good men and women and always keep the pledge of total abstinence. (Applause.) The Band of Hope movement was a very important work, and he only wished they could throw a little more life and activity into the main, sustaining endeavour of the great term:mance effort for the promotion of national sobriety. If they could only get the childr en to le irn the ways of temperance and encourage them to stick to those habits they would soon have a sober com- munity. That seemed to him to be the best way of accomplishing the great object they had in view, and would urge noon the band of hope workers not to allow anyone to influence them to forsake the substance for a shadow. They had a grand opportunity of doing some- thing for the benefit of the great nation of which they were a part, for nothing could elevate a nation- more than real temperance. (Applause). When they looked at the causes of the failure of so many lives and viewed the horrible scenes that Christian workers were brought face to face" with, and asked themselves the question "What bag brought these poor peeple so low down IT they would find in the majority of cases that it was because they had S'pent their money" for that which is not bread,- and their labour for that which satisfleth not." In con- elusion be urged all connected with the Union to 0- forward in the great work they had undertaken. He hoped and trusted they would do their part to save the children, and that their noble endeavours would have - the blessing of heaven to accompany them. (Applause). The arraingements were admirably carried out by the' following committee)—Messrs. T. Dale, G. Whitfield,

R. P. Williams, Mesdames Davenport and Whitmorer and Misses Wood and Ward, Mr. F. Gandy was an energetic hon. sec., and he had able assistants in Messrs H. Woolley and R. E. Jones. The work of training the children devolved upon Mesdames Davenport and Whit- more, Misses Wood and Ward. Mr. E. Whitfield and Ex-private D. Smith. The cantata was repeated last evening when lqrs- Simpson presided. In the course of her address, Mrs. Simpson said gatherings like that augured well for the temperance cause. She made an appeal for support of the effort which is being put forth by the Lancashire and Cheshire Union to raise £15,000 for the purpose of providing scientific teaching in the schools and erecting headquarters in Manchester-. Parents and guardians might materially help the temperance movemement by never offering intoxicants to children. If they did not put that tempation in the way of the young people there would be no •!more sad scenes of child drunkenness in their midst. In addition to the children already mentioned, the miscellaneous programme was contributed to by 3. Whitmore.

div.head: INTER-RAILWAY AMI)ULANCE COMPETITION,
div.p: INTER-RAILWAY AMI)ULANCE COMPETITION,
Warrington Win the Third Prize for the Cheshire Lines Railway.

The final competition for the inter-railwa.y ambu- lance shield took place yesterday at the Portman Rooms, Baker-street, London, and Warringtonians will be glad to hear that the Cheshire Lines team from the Warrington Central Station carried off the third prize. It would, of course, have been much more satisfactory if they had won the shield, but nevertheless they are to be congratulated upon attaining such a high position—the highest yet attained by the Cheshire Lines Railway in these com- petitions. The competitions are open to all railway companies in the United Kingdom, and there is keen rivalry for the coveted honour. The "Warrington teatn was selected by the Chesh:re Lines Com- mittee to again represent them in the contest. They did remarkably well in the preliminary contests, which were recently held. There was a record entry, 23 railway teams competing in three groups on three •suocossive days. One group com- peted at Chester and the other two at St. John's Gate, London. The Warrington team representing the Cheshire Lines Railway, competed at London, and was composed as follows : --FL T. Williams, ticket collec- torH. Holloway, clerk ; J. ; J. Fogg, signalman ; Robertson, parcel porter,and J. Nutter, clerk. At the close of the preliminary comp?tition which had been held in private, the following rastilt waq announced : Cheshire, Lines 251, Lancashire and Yorkshire 247, Great Western 210, Mersey 215, Great Eastern (holders) 241. On Wednesday the Warrington men had the honour !of being introduced to Mr. James Pinion, the new ; manager of the Cheshire Lines Committee. He expressed a desire to see the team that was going to I represent the Cheshire Lines Railway in the final com- petition for the handsome shield given by the St. John I Ambulance Association. Accordingly the five members of the team journeyed to Liverpool on Wednesday after- noon and were introduced to the new manager by Mr. E. 0. Lloyd. Mr. Pinion expressed his pleasure at I meeting the team, and addressed to them a few words of encouragement. He expressed sympathy with the aims and objects of the Ambulance Association, and , hoped the Warrington team would bring credit upon ! the Cheshire Lines Committee in the impending contest. It may be stated that the inter-railway shield com- petition was inaugurated in 1899. The Cheshire Linea Railway has competed each year. Owing to the great counter att‘action in the shape of the Cup Final at Weaste, there were no matches in connection with the Works Bowling Competition on Saturday, and the committee of the association decided to hold a friendly gathering themselves. A main was arranged, and this took place on the green at the Stocks Inn, Padgate, the games proving highly enjoyable. Tea was provided by Mrs. Fryar, the hostess, after which there was a little speech-making. Mr. Samuel Taylor, a vice-president, occupied the chair, and Mr. Joseph Foster the vice-chair. Tne Chairman spoke of the enthusiastic way in a hich the working men of the town took up bowling, and said he considered it one of the finest outdoor pastimes there was. Speaking of the president (Mr. G. Crosfield) and Mr. A. H. Crosfield (one of the vice-presidents), he could not help saying how much they were indebted to the Crosfield family for the encouragement they gave to sport generally. If other gentlemen gave their patronage to out- door snort so largely he believed the community would greatly benefit. Mr. Willett, chairman of the Icommittee, then presented the prizes won in the main, which were as follows :-1, Herman Williams; 2, Tom Bridge; 3, John Monks; 4, F. W. Scarisbrick : 5, W. H. Smalley; and 6, George Holbrook. Mr. F. W. Scans. brick. hon. secretary, in proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. Willett, spoke in the highest terms of the way in which he (Mr. Willett)didhis work,and said the associa- tion ought to be proud to have such a man as the head. Mr. Rigby supported the proposition,and endorsed what the Secretary had said. He had known Mr. Willett a long time, and he thought they had got the right man in the right place. The rest of the evening was enjoyably spent, the following contributing to the programme : Messrs. George Ball, John Monks, A. Peters, W. H. Smalleyand Oakes, the latter causing much amusement with his comic songs. A vote of thanks was accorded the chairman and vice-chairman and host and hostess. The first prize was given by Mr. Fred Clare, the .econd and third by Mr. George Crosfield, and the fourth by Mr. John Willett. WORKS COMPETITTON. NEXT SATURDAY'S MATCHES. Tho following matches will be played on Saturday afternoon, on the green at the King and Queen,Padgate- lane : Houghton's Wire Works v. Pearson and Knowles No. 3. Referee, Mr. George Holbrook. Thewlis's File Works v. Whitecross Netting Depart- ment. Referee, Mr. I. Makin. Cockheclge Factory v. Richmond's. Referee, Mr. John Monks. After six o'clock on Friday evening the green will be reserved for the players in the above matches.
